div.head: MoDOUCALUS PATENT SELF RAISING FLOUR FOR DELICIOUS The Examiner, Saturday, June 7, 1913. IN THE COURTS
div.p: MoDOUCALUS PATENT SELF RAISING FLOUR FOR DELICIOUS The Examiner, Saturday, June 7, 1913. IN THE COURTS
The longer Kidney Trouble is neglected,
the more deeply rooted it becomes.
AN EXPERIENCE WITH

station prisoner seized him by the neck and tried to trip him up several times.—Prisoner: How could you tell it was me when there were 300 or 400 people behind you shouting " shame " ?—P.C. Flaherty also gave corroborative evidence.—Prisoner said it was "nothing but a lot of his." —The Chief Constable said that he had investigated the case himself. The prisoner had admitted that she had obstructed the police and alleged tbat the officer had struck her with his staff. She could not show any marks of a blow. She also admitted that she had attempted to release Sutcliffe. Prisoner and her husband were the cause of all the scenes of disorder in Winwick-road on Saturday night. Her husband was arrested the same night on a charge of stealing a cash boa r.t Rochdale. They had been in Warrington spending the money.—A fine of ss. and casts was imposed. FURNITURE SMASHER. James Mitchell, SO, Winwick-street, was charged with having been drunk and also with doing wilful damage to his wife's furni- ture on Saturday.—P.C. Sankey proved the charge of drunkeeness.—John Ditchfield, yard foreman, employed , by Mr. E. Isherwood, said Mrs. Mitchell complained to I him about 5 o'clock on Saturday that her husband was I doing damage. On going to the house he found the I stairs blocked with broken furniture. He saw the prisoner standing in the bedroom, and eventually he removed the furniture. Prisoner was then taken into custody by P.C. Sankey.—Elizabeth Mitchell, the wife, said her husband came borne drunk at 2.15 on Saturday afternoon. After sleeping until 5 o'clock he caste downstairs and threatened her, saying he would " make ber head as big as two," if he could get hold of her again that night. She was afraid of him and went for the last witness. She valued the sideboard which prisoner broke and which was a present from him, at £5. He had been very much addicted to drink of late. Three months ago she arranged to take all the furniture and she paid him £2O (signed agreement produced).— Prisoner: What about that £2O I lent you to start business filth ?—Mrs. Mitchell : I did not have it.— Prisoner: She gave me the money because she thought I was going to Australia. She is always ill-tempered and I cannot do any good with her.—The Chief Constable: The damage was really disgraceful, very much over £5. His wife was hoping he would emigrate.—Prisoner was ordered to pay £5 damage and the costs of the case, or in default to go to prison for one month.—Prisoner: I will go down.

div.head: DOWN THE CHIMNEY.
div.p: DOWN THE CHIMNEY.
End of a Novel Case After Long Adjournment.

At the Borough Court on Saturday, before Messrs. A J. Jolley (in the chair), T. Pemberton and J. Upson, an echo of the remarkable case in which a man entered a house by getting down the chimney was heard when James Bate, 23, Lord Nelson-street, appeared after his case had been adjourned for three months.—The Chief Constable said the charge was one of being found on the enclosed premises, 11, Norman-street, on Saturday, March Ist. Prisoner got down the chimney, and when found by the occupier of the house said he was looking for non-union inert. He was under the influence of drink at the time. There was a second charge of having done wilful damage to the extent of £lO to the roof of the property, and the case had been adjourned in order to give the man a chance to pay the money. The damage had been repair( i, and prisoner had paid £4 17s. at the rate of 3s. or 4s. per week. He (the Chief) suggested that justice would be met if prisoner paid another 3s. It was questionable whether it was wilful damage, seeing that Bate was in drink. It had been hard for him to pay the money.—Mr. Cowdell, the agent for the house, expressed agreement with the suggestion.—Bate was ordered to pay a further 35., and wps dismissed.— The charge of being found on enclosed premises waa then withdrawn.

div.head: STREET BETTING.
div.p: STREET BETTING.
Smart Penalties at Warrington.

Fines amounting to £B4 4s. Gd. were imposed on three defendants, for street betting, at the Borough Police Court on Thursday, before Mr. W. Roberts (in the chair) and other magistrates. John Hill, labourer, 36, Aiken-street, answered three charges of loitering in Priestley-street or. the 7th, Sth, 9th, 10th, 13th, 15th, 16th, 18th, 21st and 28th May, for the purpose of betting. The Chief Constable said that on the dates named P.C.'s Anderson and Moody kept observation, with the result that on almost all the dates they made bets with the prisoner. He was carrying on the business the previous day and was arrested. Prisoner had nothing to say. The Chief Constable said prisoner was a most impudent customer with regard to street betting. He had previonsly been fined £lO for a similar offence. Hill was fined £lO and costs in each case—a total fine of over £3O. Joseph Appleton, 7, Baxter-street, answered two charges of loitering in Baxter-street, on the 21st, 22nd, 23rd,27th, and 28th May, for the purpose of taking bets. The Chief Constable withdrew a further charge of using the yard of his house for betting purposes Prisoner had " worked " in the vicinity of the Rail- way Inn and had conducted the business with great impunity. Officers had also given him betting slips. Prisoner : I never go near the Railway Inn. The Chief Constable: You were in the vicinity of the Inn. Prisoner was fined £4O and costs in 1912 for keeping a betting house and had also been fined 50s. and costs in two cases of street betting. The Chairman: We are going to do our duty and do all we can to stop these offences. You will be fined £4O and costs or in default four months' imprisonment. Thomas Robert Belshaw, 28, Po wys-street,was charge d with a similar offence in a street off Atherton-street on the 19th and 20th May. The Chief Constable said the police were not very anxious to press the matter as they understood the prisoner couid not follow his ordinary employment. A fine of £lO and costs was imposed, with an alterna- tive of a month's imprisonment.

div.head: Borough Police Court.
div.p: Borough Police Court.
MONDAY.
Before the Mayor (in t-b-e- chair), Aide!man Smethurst, Bolton, and James Evans, Councillor Wilkinson, Messrs. S. Wright, W. Roberts, G. Pilling and W.

Farness. MAINTENANCE CASE.—Ia the case of Thomas Phillips, late of Middlesbrough, who was charged with being in arrears of maintenance to his wife the Chief Con- stable said the prisoner was before the Court on Mon- day last and the case had been adjourned to enable him to undergo an operation at Darlington. The Darling- ton police estimated that he had had to go in the Infirmary where he was daily inspected.—The case was adjourned for a further four weeks. STREET ROWDYISII.—SamueI Sutcliffe, 21, Bowes- street, was charged with having been drunk and dis- orderly in VVinwick-street and further with assaulting P.C. Harrison on Saturday.—Harrison stated that at 11-15 p.m. he was called to the shop of Mr. Russell, butcher, Silver-street. The prisoner was drpnk and shouting, and refused to go home. He was very rough and kicked witness several times about the lower part of the body. It was only with the assistance of several officers that he got prisoner to the Police Station.—Prisoner : You got hold of me and &shed me to the floor. I never said anything to you.—P.C. Flaherty corroborated the first witness's statement.—The Chief Constable said that after 12 o'clock on Saturday night he heard a tremendous row and on going into Museum-street saw a crowd of 150 to 200 people creating a lot of disorder. They were following the prisoner down to the Police Station. There were several people who alleged that the police bad handled the prisoner roughly, but when he interviewed some of them in separate rooms their statements proved to be false. Certainly prisoner's wrists bore marks where the handcuffs bad rubbed against them whilst he was struggling. It was the dis- gusting and disgraceful behaviour of the crowd that excited the prisoner and made him worse. The bother began through another man, who was with prisoner, stealing a piece of meat, which prisoner had to pay for. They tried to steal meat from Mr. Russell's shop but were given into custody. Two of the ringleaders in the hostile crowd were in custody for serious offences at Rochdale.—The Mayor, in fining prisoner 10s and costs with an alternative of 14 days' imprisonment, 'aid that no doubt the crowd excited prisoner and made him worse. PRISONER'S CURIOUS DELUSION.—Martha Sutcliffe, wife of the last prisoner' was sent to prison for 14 days for assaulting William Warren, 9, Fortland-street.— Warren stated that when Sutcliffe, his wife, and a com- panion went into a butcher's shop, witness warned the shopkeeper that t'ley had attempted to steal meat else- where. Prisoner scratched his face, saying that he had no right to say what he bad. She also assaulted him in the charge office, giving him two violent blows in the mouth.—Prisoner : I have not touched him. He ill- used me scandalously. I have not been well since.— After Acting-Sergeant Woollacott had given evidence, prisoner said : It's all lies they are telling. I have bad three electric batteries on me since 11 o'clock last night.—Tho Chief : That would be the after effects of the beer. She has been evidently drinking very heavily of late.—Prisoner : There have been three or four of them going past the cell, never mind drinking. They have been doing something to me and my husband was as bad as them.—The Chief : There was a gallon of beer in the house when Sergeant Woollacott went for this woman. She was having it all for her own use after the others were locked up. It was evidently the last lap. ALLEGED WoUNDING.—Henry Edelston, 32, Lord- Nelson-street, was charged with unlawfully wounding his wife Amelia.—The Chief Consteble said that about 2-5 the previous day there was some disagreement between the parties. Prisoner picked up a knife and slashed his wife's arm. She had been taken to the Infirmary where it was reported that. she was progress- ing favourably. It was essential that the case should be adjourned.—Adjourned for seven days.

div.head: TUESDAY.
div.p: TUESDAY.

Before Councillor H.Fir;be-r-t-a-(in the chair), Mr. C. Jackson Holmes and Colonel Edelsten. FOOTBALLER'S DOMESTIC TROUBLES.—The adjourned case in which Thomas Knox Gibbs, Hume-street, was summoned at the instance of the N.S.P.C.C. came up for hearing.—Mr. Browne, who appeared for the society, said the case bad been adjourned for a week on the application of Mr. Steel for the defendant, and Gibbs' father bad now intervened. If Gibbs carried out the pr amises he had made, they v ere quite content to have the case adjourned. The 'j cts f the society were preventative and they desir- d • gye him a chance of sticking to his work and keeping straight, giving up his" pals, "and making every eft la to do as a father should towards his wile and children.—The case was adjourned for eight weeks. CA USE OF WINWICK-ROAD BRAWL.—Margaret Taylor, stranger, was charged with stealing a piece of beef value 45., from the shop of Mr. Russell, 45, Winwick- road, on Saturday, and also with obstructing P.C. Harrison.—The Chief Constable said he desired to offer no evidence in regard to the larneny.—The Clerk (to priscner) : Do you plead guilty or not guilty to obstructing the police.—Prisoner : I was only just behind him when he tried to bit me with a truncheon.— P.C. Harrison said he was taking a man named Sutcliffe into custody and on the way to the police

div.head: WEDNESDAY.
div.p: WEDNESDAY.
Before Mr. J. W. Hayward (in the chair), Alderman
Smethurst and Mr. W. T. Williams.

HUNGER AND DESPERATION.—Edward Gill, no fixed address, was charged with being a suspected person and with loitering in a passage at the rear of Pickmere- street, for an unlawful purpose.—The Chief Constable said prisoner was seen coming out of a dust store. He said he was on his way to Liverpool and that he was only resting tbe night. On the way to the Police Station he admitted that he had been there for an unlawful purpose and said that if he had had the oppor- tunity he would have got into the house. He added, " If a man is hungry he is bound to do something." The case was adjourned for seven days in order that prisoner's antecedents might be inquired into.

div.head: THURSDAY.
div.p: THURSDAY.
Before Mr. W. Roberts (in the chair), Messrs. J. Upson,

A. J. Jolley and Dr. Naden. TEMPTED AND FELL.—Cbarles Henry Foster, 8, Ellen-street, was charged with being on the enclosed premises 38, Green-street, for an unlawful purpose on June 4th.—The Chief Constable said that about 11.15 ,the previous morning, Polly Gearing, who was in charge of the shop, went out. On her return she saw the prisoner round the counter with a cigarette box containing money in his hand. He said he had come for some cigarettes. In a few minutes he ran away, but was eventually caught by Samuel Balmer, labourer, 18, Milner-street, who seized him by the legs and threw him to the ground near the Post Office in Springfield- street. He sustained injuries to his hand in doing so.— Sergeant Holland said that in reply to the charge prisoner said: " I am very sorry. I went for some cigarettes and finding no one there I was tempted and tried to take the box."—The Chief Constable said the prosecutors had from time to time lost money from the box and prisoner had been caught in the act of stealing a packet of baking powder from one of the shops.—He was sent to prison for one month. The magistrates commended Balmer for his brave action, and it was left with the Chief Constable as to what reward he should receive from the Poor Box. "ALWAYS DRUNK."—Joseph Ford, 2, Oakland-street, was charged with having been drunk and disorderly the previous night.—P.C. Gibbs said prisoner stood in the middle of the tram track in Buttermarket-street and would not move when the driser sounded the gong.— Prisoner said he had stopped to light his pipe. He was not drunk.—The Chief Constable: As a matter of fact he is always drunk. For a man to stand a yard in front of one of the tramcars is sufficient corroboration of the officer's statement that he was drunk.—A fine of ss. was imposed. ALLEGED SUSPICIOUS CONDUCT.—John Quinn, 22, Old-road, and William Carey, 22, Back Crossley-street, were charged with being found on the enclosed premises, 41, Bridge-street, for an unlawful purpose.—The Chief Constable said that at 12.40 that morning P.C. Dixon was in Bridge-street and saw the prisoners acting in a suspicious manner in Dolman's-lane. They climbed over a hoarding into the yard of Mr. E. Richardson, grocer. Quinn was caught in the yard, but the other man was successful in evading the police for a time, but was subsequently arrested by another officer. it was neces- sary that prisoners be remanded as the police had received information of a bacon store being broken into.—Prisoners were remanded for a week. DID NOT KNOW WHAT INSURANCE CARDS WERE.— John Taylor, no fixed address, was charged with having been found wandering in Mersey-street.--The case aving been proved, the Chief Constable said the prisoner spent his time in prison and in workhouse all over the country. He did not know whet Insurance cards were and openly admitted that he did not work. He did not want to work and he, the Chief, suggested that the magistrates should give him time to think over it.—Prisoner: I do more than you.—The Chief Constable: That is not much. It is no compliment to you. (Laughter.) The Chairman said they thought prisoner ought to do some work, and sent him to prison for three months. GIRL ATTEMPTS SUICIDE.—Annie Cartwright (15), daughter of George Cartwright, 25, Pier- point-street, was charged with attempting to commit suicide the previous day.—She was employed at the Imperial Hotel, and the ptevious afternoon she complained to a fellow-servant that she had a severe headache. She suddenly put a bottle to her mouth and drank a quantity of camphorated oil. The other girl gave her salt and water acd prisoner was removed to the Infirmary.—The girl's excuse was that the other servant scolded her.—This statement was denied, and the Chairman (41r. J. Upson)—only he and Naden now adjudicating) said that if the other girl had charge of the kitchen, it was her duty to see that the work was done properly. The prisoner should not do anything so stupid, because she was reprimanded, reproved or instructed, as to go and take poison.—The girl, who appeared sorry for her action, was dismissed on her parents promising to look after her. STRUCK WITHOUT PROVOCATION.—Ferdenand o Dement°, Dial-street, was charged, on warrant, with assaulting William Vernon. The evidence for the com- plainant was that he was coming out of the Raven Hotel' when the defendant struck him a violent blow without any provocation. He was knocked to the ground and his arm was broken in two places.—Mr. Steel, who appeared for defendant, admitted the technical assault, but stated that all the defendant did was to push the complainant, who was wearing clogs at the time and fell.—A fine of 10s. and costs was imposed. ORGAN GRINDER'S PLEASANTRIES.—Rose Dement°, summoned Mrs. Joseph Chriscoli, for using obscene language on Sunday evening last and Joseph Chriscoli for wilfully breaking windows.—Mr. Steel appeared for Mrs. Demento.—Evidence was called on both eider, and in the case of the female defendant, the magistrates said that evidently some very bad language had been used but they were not in a position to say whether the defendant toed it. She was dismissed. The husband was fined 2,1 and ordered to pay 103. damage.—The parties were all organ grinders, and the Chairman said that if patrons of street organ grinders could have heard the evidence that had been tendered in those cases be felt sure that they would not give them the support they usually did.—The Chief Constable said that for the past fortnight there had been continual bother between the Italians and if they had had to pay for the extra police duty that had been required in that neighbourhood it would cost them a considerable sum

div.head: LITERATURE AND POLITICS.
div.p: LITERATURE AND POLITICS.
Gifts that were Neglected to Become a

div.head: Mere Prime Minister.
div.p: Mere Prime Minister.

Whenever Lord Morley speaks upon literature his words make very good reading. At the annual dinner of the Royal Literary Fund he talked in a most enter- taining way to the learned ones who were assembled. A reference to literature and politics brought forth the following : In England there had been one man who combined signal brilliance of airy imagination, of social savoir of mockery of the follies and prejudices of man, with the achievement of the position of being the decisive and supreme master of the policy of this realm—he meant Mr. Disraeli. A great friend of his, the most competent of critics, said: "Mockery. insight, spirit of humour. and so forth—is it not deplorable to think that the man who could write books of that kind should have flung them all overboard in order to become a mere Prime Minister ?" (Laughter.) Whether that was a right judgment he did not know, but there was something in it. France did more honour in many ways to literature than was common in this country. The other day, turning over a list of the European battleships he found that France had three battleships called by the names of three old friends of his with whom he had more than a bowing literary acquaint- ance—Voltaire, Condoreet, and Diderot while Victor Hugo and Michelet gave their names to armed cruisers. Eager as he was for the glorification of men of letters, who were also capable of being men of affairs, he rather trembled to think of approaching his adventur- ous and open-minded friend the First Lord of the Admiralty with such a list. The selection would be most invidious. The only name he could really think of was Carlyle. It would be a splendid name for a Dreadnought. By a great and extraordinary piece of magnanimity the Prime Minister of the day offered to make Carlyle a Grand Cross of the Bath in a very admirable and interezting letter, to which Carlyle replied in a perfectly worthy way. But Carlyle in private said—he was then very old —" What should I do with G.C.B. ? They would say Grand Cap and Bells." (Laughter.) So he was afraid Carlyle would not have appreciated the honour that he would give him.

div.head: SMOKE NUISANCE.
div.p: THE SMOKE NUISANCE.

Sir,—Compared with the typical South Lancashire town, Warrington is favourably circumstanced with respect to the smoke evil. Our town is surrounded, not by dispersed pit-heads and power-houses, such as commonly obtain in the vicinity of the coal centres of Lancash4e, but by a wide belt of unbroken country. Hence, there is no augmentation, from extramural sources, of the smoke locally evolved. This circumstance of remoteness from the ultra-industrial areas should secure for Warrington every advantage in anti-smoke crusade. J.C.

div.head: MARRIED WOMEN IN WORKS.
div.p: MARRIED WOMEN IN WORKS.

Sir.—l think if Parliament would pass a law prohibiting young married women from working in factories and workshops away from home there would be a decrease in infant mortality, thate, curse of Lancashire. Men should be paid better wages so that their wives could stay at home to look after their infants. Besides being better for the infants this would give work to single women. Manufacturers employing young mothers rob the country of its useful citizens. If they have consciences let them prevent young mothers working away from home. Let laws be made for the mother as well as the father and give single women a chance to earn a
WOMAN WORKER.

div.head: EXPENSES OF HEALTH WEEK.
div.p: THE EXPENSES OF HEALTH WEEK.

Sir,—The accounts for the Warrington celebration of Health Week have now been audited by Mr. J. A. Ransome, and Task for the hospitality of your columns in order to inform those who have so kindly subscribed to this municipal enterprise how their money has been expended. The expenditure wag. very small, consider- ing the widespread influence of Health Week, and only totals £5 14s. This was covered by donations from the following :—Mrs. Vere Davies, 10s. 6d.; Mr. C. E. Parker, 10s. ; Academy Lynchers, Se.; Captain Crosfield, Sc.; Mr. F. W. Monks, 55.; Mr. Gordon Roberts, Se.; Mr. John Taylor, 55.; Miss Broadbent, 2s. 6d.: Mr. J. Hesketh, 2s. 6d.; Dr. Joseph, 2s. 6d.; Mrs. Rylands, 2s. 6d.; Canon Willis, 2s. 6d.; Mr. and Mrs. Kingdon, 10s. ; Mr. W. N. Hutchings, Bs.; Alderman Bennett, Sc.; Mrs. Eddowes. 55.; Mr. J. A. Ransome, Sc.; Mr. J. W. Slack, Sc.; Mr. B. S. Townroe, Se.; Mr. W. E. Brown, 2s. 6d. ; Mr. J. S Hill, 2s. 6d.; Mr. R. H. Meldrum, 2s. 6d.; Mr. F Smith, 2s. 6d.; Mr. H. Gray, is. To all these ladies and gentlemen, may I, as Hon Treasurer, express my thanks. Warrington, June 4th, 1913.
B. S. TOVi'NROE.

div.head: DOMESTIC SERVANTS AND THEIR GRIEVANCES.
div.p: DOMESTIC SERVANTS AND THEIR GRIEVANCES.

Sir,—l saw an article in your paper a few months ago on the Domestic Servant Problem. I will give my views to try and solve that question. First, I think a servant ought to have a nine-hour day like the mill girl. . Second, I think domestic servants ought to bi+ respected more and not looked down upon with con- tempt as a good many of them are at the present day. I also think they need a day of rest like other working girls. Another thing, the cap ought to be done away with, and references ought to be exchanged. Girls ought to came home evenings or else get a room away from the place where they work. It is no wonder there is a scarcity of domestic servants. A few more of them ought to emigrate until mistresses know how to treat them better in this Christian land of ours. Let all the servants work for a nine-hour day and they will get it. There is dignity in all honest laboar even in domestic work. Girls now-a-days would rather work in a noisy, stuffy mill or workshop; so would I rather than go to service until service is made more attrac- tive. MAGNA EST VERITAS ET PREVALEBIT.

div.head: "Privilege and its Responsibilities."
div.p: "Privilege and its Responsibilities."

There was a good attendance at the meeting of Wycliffe P.S.A. Society on Sunday, when Mr. B. Farrar presided and spoke on "Time an.: its good uses." The Rev. T. T. James took for his subject "Privilege and its responsibilities," pointing out that the two words should be indissolubly linked together. We have privileges in our day of which our forefathers knew nothing. Our own land was once governed by an absolute monarch. Sometimes when men seriously differed from the King they paid the penalty by decapitation. We have had government by rulers for the people, but now we had governments ruled by the people's will. This went to prove how great was the responsibility resting upon the people; we individu- ally have great privileges, won and purchased for us by our forefathers, but which now added greatly to our personal responsibility. He had heard men sing at meetings most enthusiastically "When the roll is called up yonder." He had not a word to say against that immortal truth, but what about the roll call here and now ? As soldiers did we hear the call to fight for tie right, to combat error and sin in our own lives and in the lives of others ? _ _
The Secretary proposed a Tote of condolence with Mr. and Mrs. Starkey on the death of their child. Mr. H. Osborne read the lesson and Mr. Beswick led the prayer.

div.head: Indispensability of Righteousn ass.
div.p: Indispensability of Righteousn ass.

The Rev. W. Reid from time to time presents short series in the pulpit in which a sequence of thought or succession of historical fact is followed. On Sunday week the morning congregation at St. John's Presby- terian Church was asked to consider the relation of Christ with God as the "Image of the Invisible," while on Sunday morning last the relation of Christ with the universe was presented under the appellative of "The Firstborn of Creation." Mr. Reid promises to bring the series to a close on Sunday week when the relation of Christ with the" new creation "will be considered. On Sunday evening in considering the search through the streets of Jerusalem for a righteous man as described by Jeremiah, the preacher made reference to Isaiah's ideal and actual Jerusalem a century previous, and to the Jerusalem of Jeremiah 's day, as illustrative of the possible extent of human corruption. The anxiety of God to pardon was emphasised, but so also was the indispensability of righteous- ness. The seeking of truth and executing judgment were the prophet's own definition of the righteous man, which was at once complete and catholic, and if to be found was at once ths assurance of the pardon of Jerusalem, even as the imperfectly righteous Lot became Zoar's temporary Saviour. Such a one, however, was only found in the Lord Jesus who at once vindicates the prophet's search and teaching of the doctrine of mediation, being Himself "Mediator, Model, and Power to realise." In Him. His people preach not from pulpit only, but in actual expresiion of life, that, not the presence of evil, but the absence of good is that which proclaims doom. - -

div.head: Bold-street Wesleyan Church. Sunday School Anniversary.
div.p: Bold-street Wesleyan Church. Sunday School Anniversary.

The anniversary services, in connection with the Sunday echo orattached to the Bold-street Church,were held on Sunday last, when the Rev. Henry Haigh, D.D., an ex-president of the Wesleyan Conference, and one of the foremost men in Methodism, occupied the pulpit, morning and evening. The event is one to which the children of the Sunday school look forward with eager anticipation, and the scholars presented a very attractive appearance, as they sang the special hymns for the day. The singing throughout was quite equal to the standard set in past years, and the large choir refideied valuable assistance in making the musical portion of the service a success. Especially interesting were the two hymns sung by the tiny tots of the primary department, and, considering their very tender years, they acquitted themselves even better than their seniors. The anthems rendered by the choir were good, the evening selection being very creditably sung. Speaking at the morning service, Dr. Haigh said the lessons to be derived from the study of the child were wonder, receptiveness and trust. The true child is filled with the spirit of true science in that it possesses the nnbiased desire to know. Christ teaches us that the charge of a child is a religious vocation—not" another mouth to feed," but another soul to mould. Parentage is the most solemn responsibility of life, and a good influence is better obtained by example than by precept. In the evening the reverend gentleman based his remarhs upon the story of Es.au's lost birthright. It was pointed out that in many ways Esau was a splendid personality; stalwart, athletic, of striking presence, with an eagerness for adventure and a fearlessness, that all combined to make a sticcessful sportsman. But Paul described him as a "profane person,' because there was nothing sacred in his life, either in aims, in

child. Defendant had lost several situations through his own neglect. Eighteen months ago he was employed as a stud groom at Hull, where his wife lived with him. He was discharged from that position, without any explanation. For the last twelve months be had been working at a Sheffield lauadry as a vanman and had sent his wife only two half-crowns. He had practically ignored his wife, who had had to rely on her mother and friends for assistance.—Defendant said he was quite prepared to make a home for his wife if she would go back to high.—The case was adjourned for four weeks. THEFT Or BxEß.—Richard Meyers (19), Collins Green, pleaded guilty to stealing, at Burtonwoorl, on May 28th, two bottles of beer, the property of B. Cunningham, brewer, Warrinston.—Edward Thomas Maley (20), Collins Green, pleaded guilty to receiving them. Meyers took the bottles out of a box on a cart belonging to the firm and made off with them. Astley followed and afterwards took the bottles home.—Both men were bound over for 12 months and ordered to pay the costs of the case.

div.head: GOVERNMENT AND THE FAIR WAGE CLAUSE IN CONTRACTS.
div.p: THE GOVERNMENT AND THE FAIR WAGE CLAUSE IN CONTRACTS.
INSURANCE COMMISSION ACTION.

A fair wage and a living wage are not necessarily the same thing, but we think the recent action of the National Health Insur- ance Commission has a direct bearing upon the demand to which we recently drew pointed attention, the demand that is being made by labour for an adequate recognition of the services it renders to the community. The Clerks to the Insurance Committees in England have just received from the Com- mission, a circular drawing the attention of all committees to a memorandum embodying the resolution passed by the House of Commons, March 10, 1909, on the subject of fair wage clauses in Government contracts, and the recommendations made by the Advisory Committee of representatives of Government departments, which was estab- lished in accordance with a suggestion in a paragraph of the Report of the Fair Wages Committee of 1908. The Advisory Committee, it is specially pointed out, recommend that clauses such as those inserted in Government contracts should also be introduced into contracts which are not entered into by Government departments, but involve the expenditure of public money or other considerations granted by a Government department. div.head: LLOYD GEORGE AND JOHN BRIGHT.
div.p: LLOYD GEORGE AND JOHN BRIGHT.
Sympathy the Cause of the Chancellor's
Popularity.

One passage in Mr. Lloyd George's speech at Criccieth deserves to be quoted for the singular beauty of its language and feeling When he came from London the other day he visited, as he always did, the neighbourhood of his old village ; and the valley, adorned in the new clothes given it by Spring, was intoxicating in its beauty. He felt that nothing but health and delight could po'sibly dwell amidst such surroundings, but he was appalled to recollect how many of those who were contemporaries of his at school had been stricken down in the hopeful days of youth by the white plague. From the cottage amidst the trees consumption had dragged a promising boy to a cruel doom; and again, further en, more ruthless than an Egyptian plague, it had not been satisfied with stealing the firstborn, but had left the inhabitants childless. He remembered what had happened in his own home, and looking to the east, west, north, and south, he ' saw everywhere dwellings—some humble, some ample —where this disease had found a tranquil home and had left it desAated. As he thought of these village tragedies the beauty of the landscape faded, the verdure withered, and he could see the grim monster still stalking defiantly through the glen challenging any power to save from his poisonous fangs the victims he had marked for destruction. _

The " Westminster Gazette " justly remarks that the rassage explains the appeal which Mr. Lloyd George makes to his fellow citizens. " For the eloquence—reminiscent of John Bright—is clearly the product of an intense sympathy, the sincerity of which writ large in every \Toed of it."

div.head: LABOUR INVOLVED IN BUILDING A BATTLESHIP.
div.p: THE LABOUR INVOLVED IN BUILDING A BATTLESHIP.

Sonic interesting figures are given by Mr. Alex. Richardson, of" Engineering," in the first chapter of the "Naval Annual," edited by Viscount Hythe, regard- ing the number of mau-hours required to build battle- ships in order to support the contention that two years is too short a period for the completion of the larger and more powerful ships of the present day. The battleship of fifteen years ago, having a length of 390 ft. and a displacement tonnage of 12,950 tons, involved in the construction of the ship 5,273,368 man-hours; at 52 hours per week and 50 weeks per annum this required, for the hull alone, the etnpl ,y- -ment for two years of over 2,000 workmen. The first Dreadnoughts required 5,489,863 man-hours, and the Iron Duke class, of 5801 t. in length and 25,000 tons displacement, involved 7,200,000 man-hours, or about 2,800 men for two years. Only about 2,000 men can be engaged on a ship without getting in each other's way. The corresponding fitzures for the construction of propelling machinery are equally interesting. The reciprocating engines of the battleship of fifteen years ago, of 13,500 horse-power, required 1,789,000 man- hours, while the turbine machinery of to-thy, of more than double the power, requires 1,850,000 man-hours. The small increase is explained by the fact that whereas in the case of reciprocating engines only some 55 per cent. of the cost was for material, the remaining 45 per cent, being ft ,r labour, the material fur turbines, much of it machined ready to hand, notably the blading, absorbs 72 per cent. of the total cost, leaving only 28 per cent. for labour. In the case of the hull there has not been the same advance in the cost for matelial, the propor- tion thus absorbed having increased from 46i per cent. to 54 per cent., leaving for labour 53 per cent. and 46 percent. of the total cost of the hull respectively of fifteen years ago and now. The twin gun-mountinga for five barbettes in each ship require 21 to 24 months to complete, and in connection with armour-plate it is pointed out that from the casting of the ingot to the completion of each plate ready for the ship three mouths are required. These figures seem to establish the view that two years is too short a period to allow for the completion of a ship of the line; although this is the contract date, it is in near:y all cases exceeded.

div.head: KING'S BIRTHDAY HONOURS
div.p: KING'S BIRTHDAY HONOURS

The list of birthday honours issued on Monday evening comptises three new Privy Councillors—Lord Welby, Mr. J. Herbert Lewis, and Sir Alfred Mond— seven baronets, and twenty-six knights. Mr. J. M. Barrie, the famous novelist, becomes a baronet, and a knighthood is conferred upon Mr. Forbes-Robertson, the actor. Mr. William Vestey, one of the new baronets, is honoured in recognition of his efforts to organise relief for the poor of London and Liverpool.

The Examiner, Saturday, June 7, 1913.
FARM AND GARDEN.
LANCASHIRE FARMERS' ASSOCIATION.

According to the yearly report of the Lancashire Farmers' AssociatiQn, recently published, the total membership now Lumbers over 2,900, the number of branches being thirty-nine. The net result of the year's working was an excess of receipts over pay ments of ;£135 12s. 11d. There was a total of £1,141 to the credit of the association on January 1 last' During the year a large number of members had made use of he privilege of making inquiries regarding the financial position of persons with whom they intended to transact business, and few bad debts would be made if greater use were made of this benefit. Members had been urged to demand higher prices for milk owing to the increased cost of production.
INFECTIOUS UDDER TROUBLES OF COWS.

"Dairymen would save themselves an immense amount of worry, work, and loss if they instantly isolated a cow when anything is seen to be wrong with her udder," says Dr. A. S. Alexander, of the College of Agriculture of the University of Wisconsin. "Infection from germs is present in nearly all cases of mamtnitis (garget) of the udder. The infection is often carried from the diseased cow to other cows by the milker's hands ; or the infection spreads from stall floors and gutters contaminated by milk, or pus from a caked udder. The contents of a diseased udder should never be milked on to the stall floor. The ofTected cow should be milked last, or by someone who does not milk the other cows. All milkers should be careful to wash their hands frequently, and to keep their finger-nails short and clean. Shit floors should be kept clean, disinfected and adequately covered with fresh, clean bedding material. If cement stall floors are used, the rear third of each should be boarded over, else chronic con- gestion and gsrget may result from chilling or bruising of the udder. Beware of the non-sterilised milking tube. It carries infective matter, and leads to loss of the quarter or udder. The milking tube is a mcst dangerous instrument unless cleansed by boiling for twenty minutes bef,re use. Lastly, remember that immediate, intelligent, persistent treatment must i.e given to the diseased udder; that the m at good is accomplished in the first twenty-four hours of treat- ment; that delayed treatment usually I roves futile, and that the cow should not be stabled or pastured with other cows before her udder has become perfectly sound."

div.head: FOOT-AND-MOUTH DISEASE RU MOURS.
div.p: FOOT-AND-MOUTH DISEASE RU MOURS.

Breeders of pedigree stock have been considerably perturbed by the rumoured outbreaks of foot-and- mouth disease. Momentary auxiety says the "Times ' was followed by resentment that the dissemination f such reports should be p0551b13, for it is feared that the official contradiction may not overtake the reports or entirely remove the suspicion created abroad. In the view of these breeders it would be time enough to give currency to reports of outbreaks when they are confirmed by the veterinary insrctors of the Board of Agriculture. They do not hold the Board responsible for the dissemination of these local suspicions—on the contrary, they recogni-e the difficulty that confronts the authorities in. NN, bite- hall-place in suppressing premature public notification —but they feel aggrieved that publicity should be given to occurrences harmless in themselves, but which, magnified as some of them have been, may mean serious injury to a great industry. It is to the credit of all concerned that alarming incidents of the kind are so few in proportion to the number of cases in which local uncertainty as to diagnosis arises, and this fact suggests that it should be posaible to prevent any premature report from gaining publicity. No good, but a great deal of harm, may result from the spresa of unconfirmed suspicions, and stockow nen, as well as the Board of Agriculture, have every reason for feel- ing that secrecy should be observed until an (facial pronouncement can be made.
SOOT, SALT, AND LIME. Much has been written and said as to the benefits

likely to accrue from the application of agents such 8 lime, salt, soot, etc., to contaminated gt ass lands .with the object of purifying it from disease, while it is claimed by some commercially interested in artificial manures that some of these are effective. Laboratory experiences, writes a correspondent in "Farm and Home," do not indicate that lime, salt, or soot applied in such amounts as are comparable with the life and well-doing f herbage and live stcck are likely to destroy all the disease-ptoducing agents polluting grass land, but, as instanced in case of the effect of salt on the fresh-water snail, which entertains the immature fluke, it is, perhaps, possible that either or all of the materials named may provide circumstances unfavourable to parasites in some phase of their development. The effect of lime on soil, we know, is sometimes remarkable. Our knowledge of its deleteri- ous effect on soil bacteria is far from complete, but it has been seriously suggested very recently that it is capable of effecting some measure of soil sterilisa- tion. While the addition of lime to many soils is often followed by growth of superior herbage, its applica- tion to "tainted " pasture may be advisable, though in our present state of knowledge we cannot suggest that-it should take the place of other manures named, but used in conjunction with them at the rate of two or three tons of slaked lime to the acre. We have no know- ledge of the special effect of any chemical manure on the organisms which pollute pastures, but when it is realised that grass land may be contaminated by organisms discharged in the excreta of infested animals, it will be evident that most of the chemically prepared manures are far less likely to convey the seeds of disease than animal manure. It will be realised that top dressing of grass land with farmyard manure made by animals discharging disease germs may prove a. facile means of ret.dering it dangerous to grazing animals.

div.head: IN THE GARDEN.
div.p: IN THE GARDEN.

CoLorns IN FLOWERS—The effect on the colour of flowers of certain mineral matters is a subject of some interest. Iron is perhaps the most potent of these, and affects, as we know, the colour of apples and the chlorophyll of the leaf. Carbonate of soda reddens hyacinths, and superphosphate of lime is said to alter the hue or bloom of other plants. Charcoal is remark- able in this way; it is said to darken dahlias, roses, petunias, and some other plants when applied to the soil and to-enrich the bloom. Similarly peat is said to change red Hydrangeas to blue, and probably many chemicals used in small quantities can be used to modify the colours of flowers.—" Agricultural Economist and Horticultural Review."

PLANTS IN ROOMS.—These should now be growing away freely, and in order to maintain the plants in health well-rooted specimens should be fed with liquid manure. Soot water is an excellent and cimple fertiliser to apply at this period, and it is also perfectly safe to use. Soot water may be made by placing half a gallon of soot in a bag in six gallons of water, and after Finking for three to four days the liquor may used quite sifely. On very hot days it is well to shade window pants in sunny windows. Fuchsias that are well rooted will be considerably benefited by an application of soot water, especially is this the case when they are coming into bloom.—" Agricultural Economist and Horticultural Review." THE BARDFIELD ONLIP.--This is the most beautiful of our native primulas, and one that is by no means widely distributed. In common with the cowslip, it has been flowering very freely this year, and recently, when in the Bardfield district, we noticed a very beautiful colony in a rather thickly-wooded plantation. Curiously enough, the natives of Essex call the cow- slip Pegglo or Paigle, and the Oxlip is known to them as the cowslip. The true Bardfield Oxlip is a plant well worth a place in the best gardens, and will thrive well in moist, loamy soil. It is generally regarded as a natural cross between the pimrose and 'cowslip, but of this there is some doubt.—" The Garden."

div.head: REVOLT OF THE FARMERS.
div.p: REVOLT OF THE FARMERS.
Hostile to tariff" Reform" that Excludes Agriculture from its "Benefits."

The revolt of the farmers from the "New Procedure" grows apace. Stimulated by the sympathy and advice of the fervid " whole hoggers " in Parliament, such as Mr. George Wyndham, Mr. Charles Bathurst, Lord Willoughby de Broke, the Right Hon. Henry Chaplin, and Prof. Ilewins, and led by Lincolnshire (the first to break away), Worcester, Sussex, Kent., Stafford shire, Hanapshira and Shripshire have all declared their determination to eschew " any scheme of Tariff Reform which excludes agri- culture from its benefil s." This sentiment was endorsed by the National Union of Farrn-Ts,representing 20,000 farmers of England and Wales, at their meeting on Februaly 26th. The Essex farmers have ben the most recent to range themselves beneath the revolters' standard. At the meeting of the Braintree Branch of the Farmers' Union, held on May 21st, it was unani- mously resolved : "That, in the opinion of this meeting Tariff Reform, to be just and acceptable to the agricul- tural interest should 113 on the lines of Mr. Joseph Chamberlain's fiscal policy." The Chairman, Mr. C. W. Gray, J.P., introducing the resolution, said the new departure from the policy of

Mr. J. Chamberlain came as a great surprise. It was not to be supposed, however, that the new policy arose with Mr. &Aar Law; he was squeezed into it, and only adopted it with great reluctance, while the Right Honourable Henry Chaplin had dissociated himself entirely from it.

div.head: RUNCORN BOARD OF GUARDIANS.
div.p: RUNCORN BOARD OF GUARDIANS.
HOSPITAL IMPROVEMENTS.
The fortnigl.tly meeting of the Runcorn Board of Guardians was held at Dutton or, Tuesday, Mr. Linaker, jun., presidinr. THE TREATMENT OF IMBECILES.

The Clerk submitted a report of the visit of Ne. 13. T. llodgson, one of the Lunacy Commissioners with respect to a vinij paid to the workhouse on the 24th just. Ho said that he found one man and five women detained on permanent orders under section 21 of the Lunacy Act, 1890, three of the women being fresh cases since the visit of his colleagues in 1908. Two of the women slept in the body of the house the other three and the man ii the horpital. Their beds and bedding were clean and generally in good order, but the pillowcase and sheets of one of the beds in the dormitory in the house were much worn. The dayrooms in the hospital were comfortable and tidy, but the one used by the tvio women in the body of the house were very bare and cheerlcsq, with no books or papers. The health ef the imbeciles was good, only the man being confined to bed, and he on eccount of some restless excitement whim, he bed developed recently. He regretted to learn that the imbeciles were very seldom taken beyond the worlhonse premiser. The bathing amengements were satisfactory. There bad been no employment of mechanical restrain. The C'erk said that the Visiting Committee bad gone into the points raised by the Commissioner and they recommended that his suggestions should be carried out Mr. W. M. Morris said that the whole of the matters raised in the report had bcen very carefully gone into. Phere vas nothing very contentious aeout them and practically the whole thing had been left in the hands of the Nlit,st3r and the doctor to be duly carried out. He nmered the resolu• ion of the committee. The Chairmen said that the Master had given them son e information about the cheerless rooms cud the ques;ion of bo. ks and that p jut in the report was rather misrepresented. Illuatrated periodic tls were taken there regularly, but o i the particular d.y that, the Commissioner came there was none. The day pre- viously books had been taken in and they were torn up. Notwithstanding this he continued to take in the bcoks as usual. The reulution was confirmed. THE HOSPITAL STAFF.

The Master presented a report concerning the staff- ing of the House. The hospital staff consisted of a saperintendcnt nurse and two assistants. The average number of patients was fifty, including a number who required feeding, w ushing and frequent changing, and some children. In the opinion of the Medical Officer the staff was insufficient. It was suggested that a matren be appointed. nig wculd give an average cf one nurse to twelve patients, not including the matron. It was reported that the nails of the male and female wards and the kitchen on the male side were in a very bad conditkn and needed urgent attention. The Medical Officer considered it desirable that a glass- () everad verandah should be erected on the south side of the female day ward, so that the children might get out in the fresh air more frequently. Suggestions for lavatory improvements were included. The Visiting Committee recommended that the suggestions he carried our. air. Morris raid it generally fell to his lot to move some expenditure. The committee had met and gone very fully into the recommendations and there was no doubt that the resolutions arrived at had been very necessary for some time past. They wanted to have a controlling hand over the hospital, and for that reason they recommended the appointment of Mrs. Parsons, the matron, es superintendent nurse at an increased salary of £lO. She was a fully, certificated nurse and thoroughly understood the work. With regard to the male and female wards they were in very good order and they recommended that they be plastered and the outside painted. With regard to the quest ion of the glass veranda!), they were often a lot of children in the hospital ward and they had not been able to take them out under cover. This was strongly recommended by the Medical Officer. If they had a glass verandah erected they would he able to enjoy the sunshine and _ _ .
fresh air with tatety. _ Thu Chairman ascured the Board that there Wag nothing extravagant about the recommendations end nothing was Leing done that did not require to be done. _ _
lhe report and recommendation were adopted. Mr Morris gave notice that at the next 'netting he would move that the salary of the matron be increased from £4O to £5O. FEWER VAGRANTS IN THE HOUSE.
The House committee reported that there were st present 122 inmates in the house compared with 127 last year; there were 76 vagrants compered with 128 lest year.

div.head: WATER FOR PIGS.
div.p: WATER FOR PIGS.

It is absolutely essential that all pigs under every condition should get what drink they care for. If sloppy food be served no other liquid will be asked for, but with any other articles of diet there may be desire for extra fluid. If the pig is ill it is all the more necessary than any craving for think should be gratified, although, of course, the right kind must be given. Cold spring water is rarely good for swine or for any other animal, therefore such as is pumped from the deep well or is taken from the cold spring should be in some way tempered a bit before put in the trough. When pigs are being made up for bacon on meal stifled so thickly that the contents of the bucket have to be shaken out, pure water should always be served once a day, say at mid-day, and the animal will be Lund to drink heartily and fatten all the faster for it. Suckling sows, too, need a lot of fluid, but it is dean supplied in the shape of wash, which answers well enough if of decent quality.—Warwiek- shire in" Farm and Home."

div.head: LETTERS AND LITERATURE
div.p: LETTERS AND LITERATURE
I-I

During my many years at sea I was continually exelcising the calling of a letter writer. I had no one to write to myself, but I wrote much for others. In this connection I may say that when I did get a chance to correspond to my own account I did not neglect it, for my first letter to my wife, from Calcutta, numbered fifty-two closely-written pages. But though letter writing is usually literature, it is in a class by itself, which, though a high class, is quite distinct from literature generally. The first attempt I ever made at the latter class of writing (unconsci, usly, cf course) was in St. John, New Brunswick. I was mate of an English brig, which, during a black stormy night, dragged her anchor, fouled a Calais (Maine) schooner, and eventually the whole brutal tangle took the ground opposite the ferry slip, where it stopped all the ferry traffic. I was oidered by the harbour authorities to send in a report, which I did, writing wilh a running pen. Afterwards, I was amazed to be told by some potentate whom I did not know that the story of the happenings of that night had afforded the Harbour Board much pleasure, but they did not believe it because it read so well !—Frank T. Bullen in "Howl Began," in " T.P.'s Weekly."

div.head: MiliiLmL
div.p: MiliiLmL
FROM SCHOOL TO WORK.
Town Council Sanctions Juvenile Employment Bureau. TO GIVE ALL CHILDREN A CHALICE.

The Warrington Town Council on Tuesday evening gave its approval to the establishment of a Juvenile Employment Bureau under the Education (Choice of Employment) Act, 1910. The scheme is an elf art to place children, on leaving school, in the situations for which their capabilities best fit them, and thus to pre- vent them drifting into blincl alley occupations. There was some opposition to the proposal on two different grounds—one that the expenditure, which is estimated at from £7O to £BO a year, ought not to be borne by the municipality, and the other that the establishment of a bureau would ILA do all that was chimed for it. However, the great m ljotity of members were con- inced of the util.ty of the scheme, which 1,1,13 accord- ingly approved.

div.head: SCHEME EXPLAINED.
div.p: THE SCHEME EXPLAINED.

Councillor H. ROBERTS (chairman of the Education Committee) in commending the scheme to the accept- ance of the Council, briefly outlined the reasons which had actuated the members of the Education Committee in introducing it. Ile was sure that all the members of the Corporatton would desire to fncilitate as far as they could the provision of proper and suitable employment for the boys and girls of the town, and the only differ- ence of opinion that could arise was as to the methods to be employed with that end in view. He ventured to suggest that as the Council speCalised Es work, through the medium of committees, it was only doing bare justice to those who gave special attention to the particu!ar subject entrusted to them that their views should rcc?ive favourable con- sideration, if not active support. The so eme sought to promote two or three objects. 'I he serious difficulty with which a very preponderating number of parents in Warrington found themselves faced, with regard to the provision of suitable employment for their children, proved the necessity for some assistance in that direc- tion. The scheme not only suggested the careful filing of particulars of all the children who left school at the usual :age, but the Education Authority was also furnished with a large amount of information, throu, h the system of medical inspection, as to the physique and characteristics of the children. Such information might be utilized, under proper conditions, in the selection of suitable occupations. If the scheme were adopted, anl the control left in the hands of the Education Committee, there would be unrivalled oppor- tunities for urging upon the parents of the children the desirability of the education of the latter being continuei in the continuation schools for a year or two after they had left tbe elementary schools. POPULARISING EVENING SCHOOLS.

A most marked result had arisen from the carrying out of a similar scheme in Glasgow. Prior to the establishment of a juvenile employment bureau in that city there were only 3,500 scholars in attendance at the continuation schools—and that number had been practically the average SULItla I number for the preced- ing ten ytars.. With n a very short time of the estab• listirnent of the bureau the attendances had increased to 10,555—an advance of 300 per cent. It was impossible to estimate the enormous advantage to citizenship of that increased period of education, and he had no hesitation in saying that they expected to obtain similar results in their ovrn town. NO INTERFERENCE WE EI PARENTAL CONTROL.

The chief objection which bad been urged against the scheme was that it would interfere with parental control. That was, he submitted, an entire misunder- standing, and he was certain that the members of the Council, on carefully reading the proposals, would see that such a suspicion had no foundation in fact. The Education Authority had no locus stand/ in the matter until the parent came to them and asked for their assistance. It would be an impertinence and foreign to the characteristics of English life if any authority were set up and arrogated to itself the rights which fairly and preperly beleneed to the rarent. Tbe Educa- tion Committee asked for the support of the Council in enabling them to codify tho information now in their possession, and to organise a system by which they might bring together the employer and the child, find suitable employment for the latter, and thus give nsaistance to a large number of parents who were not able to do this kind of work. Ihe ordinary working man was engaged from 6 a.m. to 5 30 p.m. each day, and until neon on Saturday, therefore what chance had he of seeking employment for his child in a proper channel ? In a large number of cases the duty was relegated to the mother, and frequently to the child, who did tot ard could net look to the future. Of cours-, the bureau could not mike a job whno one did not exist, but these who worked it would be in sympathy with the children, and the bureau would also enjoy the confidence of the vast majority, if not the whole of the employers. The alternative to the scheme now proposed was the setting up of a similar autho.ity by the Board of Trade. lie submitted, however, that the Education Authority's methods, position and influence, all being home made, were influitely preferable to any assistance which might be given by en aliea authority which did not know the requirements and the special facilities obtaining in the town.

div.head: COST.
div.p: THE COST.

The expense could not be large, as he Lad no doubt that the information as to children leaving school would be cheerfully supplied by the head teachers, without involving any additional cost. At the ouLkide limit, the initiation of the same could not involve an expenditure of more than .£7O or LSO a year. He asked the Council to give the committee authority to go on with that beneficent work, which was, if possible, even more important than elementary education in its effect on the lives of future citizens. Alderman BENNETT seconded the motior. COUNCIL SHOULD "PUT ITS FOOT DOWN." Alderman JAMES EvANS moved an amendment that the scheme be not approved. He said he agreed with a great deal that Councilor Roberts had said in regard to the cheerful work that would be done by the teachers, but, nevertheless, it should be rememboted from time to time propositions and suggestions were received from veriour offices of the Uovernment. They were sometimes readily accvted by the Council, but in the majority of the cases the Corporation had to pay part of the bill. lie thought the time had nos arrived when an authority like the Warrington Corporation should put its foot down—(" hear, hear," from Councillor Pemberton)—and s "We cAnnot allow suggestions and Acts to become eperative unless we have a voice of our own as to the payment of part of the bill 'l' He did not quite see the necessity for the proposition that bad been made by Councillor Roberts. Under the Children's Act they could have aer advisory committee which he believed was capable of doing much useful work. Already they could enlist the cube. ion and co-operation of the Labour Bureau, which bad now a juvenile department. For the time being such work as an advisory committee could do would meet all the needs of tne case in Warring on. THE RIGHT OF THE PARENT.

Councillor Roberts had rather over-stat_d the possibilities of a wise tolection cf employment by the committee or the head teacher. If a father did not know the natural bent and cliabi!ities of his child there was not much hope of tl.e le 'char knowing tem. Those who had only a caFull knowledge of the boy might more rtailily make mistakes than the p trent in selecting a suit tble calling. The p treats chAce bhould come first. Councillor ROBERTS: It deer. Alderman EVANS said that had not ben his experi- ence of the working of each dipaitments. He was inclined to think that the bureau would mystify and hamper the parents when they Lad to fi,ce the question of thi-ir children leaving school. How many of the very poor contemplated taking their children from school at a specified date? His experience was that they let their children remain at school until they could make a successful appt al to the School Attendance Committee for exemption and then looked out for situations for them. If any committee could devise means, in voluntary lines, to keep boys and girls at school until they were seventeen he wished them well in their purpose, but he was afraid there were considerable difficulties in the way. Councillor GOUGH seconded the amendment that the scheme be referred back. lie contended that the Council had not been given sufficient time to consider the question in all its bearings. He regarded the scheme as a great interference with parental control ; it was taking out of the hands of the parents their right of choice and giving it to a committee.

div.head: GIVE THE CHILD A CHANCE.
div.p: GIVE THE CHILD A CHANCE.

Alder Min BENNETT,in supporting the scherne,ad in itted the necessity for a readjustment of taxation so as to relieve the local ratepayers of some of the burdens imposed by national schemes. At the same time it would he absurd to cut off their noses to spite their faces, and decline to do a good thing because it might cost, as in this instance, a small Burn. Tnere were great possibilities for good in the proposal. If they accepted the doctrine that, on no account must parental con- trol be interfered with, they would cease to educate children or to look after their health and would allow them to grow up like savages. The one dominant policy of all intelligent people to-day was to give the child a chance. There would he nothing approaching equality of opportunity in this country until every child—rich or poor—had an equal chance of rec?iving a good educa- tion. Learning the three R's and mere school know- ledge was only the beginning of education, nud be sighed regretfully for the time when the old ssstein of apprenticeship was olserved. lie believed that gradually we would get back to that, but in the mean- time we wanted to escape from the chaos in which we were at present involved, Thousands of children were,

by the more necessitit s of the situation; doomed to lives for which they were utterly unfitted and would perpetuate a population which was not making the best of itself, either from a purely selfish point ot view or from the standpoint of the good of the community. If they c -uld, by friendly advice and assistance, help a few of the children to realise their life, to lice it in ft fuller degree—in a hqppier, healthier and more intelligent manner—they would, he contended, be doing a good work. (floor, hear.) COUNCILLOR PEACOCK GIVES A LOCAL INSTANCE.

Councillor PE.toocK was grieved to find Alderman James Evans moving an amendment to the scheme, as he Fad always found him kindly disposed towards poor children. If ever a scheme had been proposed to do good to the poor children of Warrington it was the present one. (Hear, hear.) It was a great trial to many parents to know what work to put the children to after they had left school. lie contended that the teachers know more than the parents about the capabilities of tho children and the callings at wLich they were likely to sucm.ed. Only that afternoon he received a letter from an educated young man who was engaged in an ironworks in the town—he would not say which. Ile was 19 years of age, sod be pointed out that he could not make any more progress or make nay more money, Could lar (Councillor Peaccck) do something to enable him to get a situation in which he could get on ? In the case of the children of the poor they bad no influence to enable them to appronth suitable employers and the) drifted flit) blin 1 alley eccupatiorr. Vl hat was more difficult to a boy of 14 year 3 of age than to go into e Labour Bureau ? It was like going into a rolice curt; it terrorized him and very often he would not go. Consequently, he took the first errand boy's place that presented itse'f and so eventually went to swell the ranks of the unemployed or the casual workers. Councillor HAWTHORN said it was not intended to take from the parents any control which they now possessed. The o-trnmittee would be one to which they could appeal for advice, and for what higher purpose could they appeal than the finding of employment for their childr, n ? The bureau would do a grett service not only to the parents but to the generations that were yet to come. The teacher knew a great deal of the aptitude end capabilities of the young, as they bad developed in his hands. They could best gauge whether a boy was fitted for manual or mental employment. The scheme had proved of value in Glasgow, Liverpool and other great centres, and Fad prevented, to a great extent, the follow log cf Hind alley occupations. Under present conditions many youths were forced to begin their working career over again at the age of twenty, as they bad reached the end of their tether in the occupations in which they had originally been placed.

div.head: MOTHER'S SACRIFICE.
div.p: A MOTHER'S SACRIFICE.

Councillor PEMBERTON, in supporting the amendment, said the speeches which had been made sounded nice and beautiful, but the practical side of life muet be looked at. Someone would have to do the labouring seri the blind alley work, ualess some clover engineer invented a mechanical boy to suit the purpose. (Laughter.) Appeals were made to give boys a higher education, when it must be known that there was no occupation for them. There was a deplorable amount of unemploy- ment among the educated classee. If there were only a thousand jobs, what was the use of educating B,COO for them, and leaving 7,000 disappointed? It was a scandal, and made his blood boil when he thought how people were being misled. lie knew of one widow who stfieted herself of food to give her son what was called a superior education. Councillor ROBERTS : All the more credit to her (Hear, hear.) Councillor PEMBERToN : Certainly, if there is the promised reward at the end of it. lint is there ? C n- tinuing, he said that boys who received the superior education were not fit for other woe,. The new bureau would not be able to find opening, even as hricli :yers, plumbers and other skilled artisate, because the trade unions regulated the number of apprentices and would not allow work te be created in that way. le re were clerks who had all the qoalifl3ations referred to who were working at a pittance—for less money than he paid a bricklayer's 1 .bourer. They could get lawyero, doctors and accountants at £2 a week, and— The MAYOR : Better not touch upon contentious subjects. Councillor WILKINSON: They should join a trade union. (Laughter.) Council or PEMBERTON added that the whole subject was contentione. lie protested against the insiduous way in which fresh burclene were constantly being imposed upon the ratepayers, and he asked the members es business n,ers not to have dust thrown into their eyes, but think for themselves and put their own every-day experience to work. The ()est was said to be £7O or £BO a year, but the Council knew what it would be in a few years. The rates of the borough were Bs. in the 2. and it was only by a squeeze this time that they got through with that sum. Councillor WILKINSON : You know nothing about it. (Laughter.) Councillor Pemtertnitoef said he had no objection to the Board of Trade taking the scheme in hand, provided the Government would pay for it. After all the expenditure on education he questioned whether the yoang men of to-day were of more value for practical business pet poses than their pr«lecessors. The municipalities were being drbgged at the tail of educational facilities and it was time they called a halt. Councillor BROADHURST, in opposing the amendment, said it was not claimed that the bureau would do away with bl:nd alley job.. They would always exist. As a strong supporter of Labour Exchanges, he admitted that they c mid not give that sympathy whieh they as the workingclase of the town desired. The committee could extend sympathy to the poo. children, who in the past, had not had equal oppertunities. Every hasl oug ht to have a fair chauce. Ha had seen youths drae'.;ing 30 tone of iron per dal when their talents might have been directed into much better channels. Ile appesled to the members of the Council to banish all political feeling and do their best for the children of the working-classes. .

Al lertuan BURTON contended' that thm-e would be a possibility of the committee m 'king favourites among the boys and recommending them for good positions, to the distdvantage of other. Ile did not object to the expenditure on education, if a benefit was derived from it, but he questioned whether it, would be possible for a committee to sty avLether a certain boy would make a good eneineer or mechanic. £l,OOO A WEEK ON EDUCATION. Councillor lIENSHALL thought it would be agreed by all of them that there was to be no interference with parental authority, and there was not a shadow of the shade of a suggestion that parents should be dictated to or even advised unless they asked for it. They were spending roughly £l,OOO a week on education, and yet lads who had reached the seventh standard were being allowed to take up work in which their training would be lost. lb e did not, of coursej wish to deprecate the errand boy. "I began as an errand boy myself and look where I am," added the councillor amid great merriment. If the new bureau were an attempt to make doctors, lawyers and pro- fcs3ioaal men, there would be a great deal of relevance in what Councillor Pemberton had said. hut it was not. It was not even an attempt to make butchers, bakers, and candle-stick makers. (Laugher.) It was, however, an attempt to find—probably the corn- mittee would often fail—what a boy or girl had an aptitude for. Not only would they seek to find them the right class of work, lytt to keep in touch with them during those formative years between the ages of thirtcen and seventeen. Rigid economist on education as he was, he was prepared to risk £75 a year on the scheme. TO MITIGATE UNENIPLOYMENT.

The MAYOR explained why, although he was origin- ally unfavourable to the scheme, he had been led to support it. No one felt more strongly than be against the interference with parental control or the placing of additional expenses on the heal rates by Imperial legislation, but no one raho realised the personnel and functions of the proposed committee could have a shadow of a doubt that it • as admirably ad losed for the purpose set forth by Couecillor Roberts. The teachers, who were acting in loco parcntis, a large proportion of the Education Committee and every possible source of assistance and sympathy would be brought to bear in this difficult matter. The expendi- ture wonli he small—although, of course, that should not affect their judgment on the question of principle— and inasmuch us the benefit to be derived was purely local,they ought not to begrudge. The question of unemployment was a vexed and difficult one to deal with, and it was in a great measure duo to the evils which the scheme was intended to mitigate. (Hear, bear) The proclivities of boys and girls in this and in other towns were not considered and led into the proper channels, rind on these grounds he must vote for the minutes of the committee. DANGER OF AN UNEDUCATED DEMOCRACY. Councillor Rolizras, after expressing satisfaction with the tone of the discussion, expressed surprise that Councillor Pemberton should have advanced such arguments. his speech largely amounted to this: That because there would always have to be "hewers of wood and drawers of water" somebody with the gifts of Providence should discriminate as to those who were not to be allowed to rise above that position and say to them "Education is no use to you." flow anybody could justify such an argument at the age when the child's faculties were undeveloped and the future an unknown period to him, he could not undentand. Even if there ware any justification for the assumption that there must always be men of low grade capacity, he was a believer in evolution, and he hoped thrt some day the standard of general ability and capacity would be greater than it was now. Whether that were so or not, it was no reason why they should not educate the people. We were 'getting rapidly an educated democr•tcy. An uneducated democracy was a danger to the State and to the world. It was far better th it the people, from top to bottom, should at least have a fair modicum of education. Education was not to he solely applied for the purecrae of earning a living. It brought with It a broader view of life, a greater perception of the beautiful things of life, arid au appetite for better things that deft:m.l4°d recognition in a material way, at the hands of the State. He was glad a reference had been made to the widow who was denying herself to educate her son. They wanted to help these widows and others. What had (Continued in next column )

It forms an essential constituent of most vegetable and animal organisms, and ranks next to air in ministering to life, for it forms the chief ingredient in all living tissues and animal juices. Children require more proportionately than adults, and the keen demand for it, among local juveniles, is vividly depicted above by our photographer.

div.head: HOT AFTERNCO
div.p: A HOT AFTERNCO

Since we drew attention t) the manner in which the drinking fcuntains in the main thoroughfares of the town are gradually and surely disappearing from our midst, and to the fact that the town does net possess a single drinking trough for horses, summer weather has suddenly burst upon us as if to empha-
A DRINK THAT COULD NOT BE GOT AT WARRINGTON,

div.head: VALUE OF WATER.
div.p: THE VALUE OF WATER.
T WINWICK.

Some may be inclined to under- rate the value of drinking foun- tains along our main roads, but there can be no doubt that they are of vital importance to the man on the road whose needs are great and whose resources are small. Water will cover all needs in the drinking line and cover them quite efficiently, as the testimony of soldiers in the most arduous cam- paigns completely proves.

Thus in 1896 General Sir Francis Grenfell stated : "The campaign in Egypt was a teetotal campaign. We drank the Nile and nothing added. I took over the rear guard on the occasion of the finish of the campaign and in no other part of the world have I seen a force of men so fit and so well as that force which was employed upon the Nile."

div.head: SNAKE FOUND AT BRIDGE FOOT.
div.p: SNAKE FOUND AT BRIDGE FOOT.
MYSTERIOUS APPEARANCE OF A NOVEL KIND OF VISITOR WHICH STARTLED CORPORATION WORKMEN.

div.head: Photograph by Burre'l. THE SNAKE IMPRISONED FOR PHOTOGRAPHIC PURPOSES.
div.p: Photograph by Burre'l. THE SNAKE IMPRISONED FOR PHOTOGRAPHIC PURPOSES.

Workmen employed by the Corporation in the demolition of property at Bridge Foot recently made an unusual find. A quantity of bricks and other material had been deposited on the site of the old bedstead works off Knutsford-road, and the workmen were in the act of placing the heap on a cart for removal when they were somewhat startled by the appearance among the debris of a snake. However, the novel visitant

proved perfectly harmless, as it was merely a fine specimen of an English grass snake. The curious point is as to how it got in such uncongenial surroundings as Bridge Foot, for snakes are generally found on marshy or moist land where there is a plentiful supply of such delicacies as frogs. The snake,which is about thirty inches in length, was taken to the Beamont School where a home has been found for it in the nature study room.

There was a great chat of it in this country, and it was a condition of things that was rapidly growing. Mr. Hamilton, the newly-elected Conservative mem- ber for Al trincham, has received the following message from Lord Roberts :
