The minutes of the Gas Committee which were oon- firmed showed that the net profits for the year ending March 31st were 4:14,448 16s. 53., which Aide rtnan JOHN EVANS said was remarkable. TRAMWAY MEN AND SUNDAY LABOUR.

The Electricity and Tramways Committee considered the request from the tramway employes for time and a half for Sunday labour, and, after consideration and a report on the conditions of service from other towns, it was decided that no advance be made on the time and a quarter now paid for Sunday labour. Considerable discussion took place on the above minute.

Councillor BROADHURST said his conscience would not allow him to let that minute be passed without raising his voice in protest. In moving that the minute be referred back he said that that application from the men was only what was made in every first-class works. There was not a single trade unionist but who believed that the tramway employes were entitled to time and a half for Sunday work. The Manchester Corporation had granted to all the tramway employe 3 2s. per week more than the standard rate of wages for the district. As a trade unionist for 22 years he considered that the Eiectricity Department was not doing its duty until it paid time and a half for Sunday work for those who were compelled to sacrifice the Sabbath. Alderman Smethurst had told them that there had been a record sear in the working of the tramways and the men were entitled to some consideration. Whenever a well- salaried official applied for an increase the application had never been rejected, and why, then, refuse the men who had made the undertaking one of the greatest successes in the country to-day. The Warrington drivers and conductors were second to none in Great Britain. Why should the committee be ruled and guided by what obtained in other towns in such a matter ? They ought to have the courage of their con- victions and be able to see whether the men were entitled to a decent rate of pay for Sunday work. He hopad the committee would reconsider the resolution and give to these men that to which they were entitled. (Hear, hear.) Councillor WILSON seconded the amendment to refer the minute back. He considered that the tramway employes, who performed their duties exceedingly well, were fully entitled to the payment asked for in respect of Sunday labour.

--Councillor CH FUMES supported the amendment. He stated that Corporation employes in other departments received time and a half for Sunday labour and often worked side by side with the tramways employes. Any man doing wore on Sunday was doing work that could not Le done in the weektime and ought to be recompensed for it. CJuncillor PEMBERTON spoke in favour of the amend- ment. Ile remarked that the men worked constantly on Sundeye. They had heard of the magnificent profits earned by the undertaking, and the payment ot time and a half would make very little difference to the profits. The fact that employes in other departments received time and a half was calculated to create grave disostisfect ion. Councillor DICRENSOII also supported the amendment. He thought it was only fair and just, after what they bad heard from Alderman Smethurst of the wonderful profits made by theldepartment, that the minute should be re-considered. The tramwaymen had got to rub shouldere with men who got time and a half, and it was not is fair state of things. Ile supported the amendment on principle. Councillor Gouon said that the Corporation were ideal employers where highly-paid officials were con- cerned, but why they should stumble ashen the workmen asked tor what was just, and when they asked for equal treatment in the various departments, he did not know. The MAYOR believed that only two Lancashire towns paid time and a quarter for Sunday labour and that all the others paid single time. Councillor HAWTHORN said the committee decided the application on the question of conditions and rates pai,l in other towns. A report was presented showing that only two towns in Lancashire paid time and a quarter and the others paid the single rate for Sunday work. There was not one town in the county where time and a half was paid. They were now ahead of moat Lancashire towns and would be ahead of other of the towns in the county if the request were granted. Councillor LINDLEY supported the minutes. It was understood when drivers and conductors applied for jobs that they would be called upon to do Sunday work. Some of the men had only just received an increase in the rate of pay. He thought the men were fairly well dealt with, for they understood that there was Sunday work when they took on the jobs. Alderman SMETHURST said it was only three months since the Sunday pay was raised to time and a quarter, and now another application had been sent in simply because the men had heard one or two councillors talk- ing. The report submitted to the committee was to the effect that of 21 Lancashire towns with tramways only two outside Warrington paid anything extra for Sunday labour. Warrington, Wigan and Birkenhead were the only towns in this part of the country paying time and a quarter for Sunday labour. Councillor BROADHURST.—WeII done, South Lanca- shire.

...... Alderman SMITHURST said the "committee arrived at their deoimion on that report, but he did not care if the Counoil did send the minute hack. The amendment was carried by a large majority, only Alderman Smethurst, Alderman Burton, Councillors Lindley, Hawthorn, Birtles and Taylor supporting the minutes.

div.head: ELECTRICITY DEPARTMENT'S PROGRESS.
div.p: ELECTRICITY DEPARTMENT'S PROGRESS.

Alderman SMETHURST said that the balance sheet for the Electricity Department showed there had been a large increase in the consumption of current for power and lighting, despite strikes and advances in coal prices. The financial result was very satisfactory indeed, and showed there was a profit of close upon £3,000. Councillor Goucui, referring to a letter asking on what terms the Corporation would be prepared to supply Winwick Asylum with electricity, asked if it was the Intention of the committee to supply the asylum at the same price as Warrington ratepayers or at a less price. The MAYOR: We have no power to supply.

div.head: BRIDGE.
div.p: THE BRIDGE.

In proposing the confirmation of the minutes of the Bridges Committee, Alderman SMETHURST mid be thought everyone would now see they were making very forward progress with the new bridge. The Me:YoR seconded. Alderman BENNETT said they all agreed that when the bridge was constructed it would be a fine structure, but its dignity would be lessened by the shurteuing of the training walls on the north-west side. The minutes were confirmed. LOVELY-LANE RECREATION GROUND.

A short discussion in regard to a recreation ground for WhitecroEs arose when Councillor HAWTHORN proposed "That the Town Hall, Parks and Baths Com- mittee be requested to lay out at an early date the land in Lovely-lane, purchased in 1911 for a recreation ground, and to make provision in their scheme for the construction of a bowling green." The land was pur- chased for a school site and recreation ground in November, 1911, at a cost of £5,750, and the sanction of the Local Government Board was obtained to the borrowing of the money in 1912. The Board of Educa- tion had since approved of the plans for the proposed school,which would occupy a portion of the site nearest the Cheshire Lines Railway, but no buildings had been erected. He could not say the land had not been used, an football and other athletic clubs had made good use of it in its bare state. The Corporation had already provided means of recreation in other parts of the town, and Whitecross Ward should have some consideration. Alderman BENNETT seconded the motion. Councillor ROBERTS cordially supported the motion. The MAYOR: It is not an organ. If the men who are supporting this bad opposed the organ being provided I should have opposed this resolution. (Laughter.) Councillor GOUGH opposed the motion, not because he was against the provision of a recreation ground,but because he thought it premature. Bewsey wanted a recreation ground. Alderman JAMES EVANS and Councillor PEMBERTON supported the motion, the latter expressing the hope that there would be no delay in beginning the work. The MAYOR: How many bowling greens equal one organ? Councillor PEMBERTON : Fifty, sir! Councillor DICKENSON thought it was an insult to the

Town Hall, Parks and Baths Committee that the matter should be brought forward in the Council before being laid before the committee. (Criea of "Oh, no.") It wad an insult.
..... Councillor HAWTHORN 'aid no insult was meant. It was just a little driving power. The MAYOR said he was only sorry that the same

interest was not taken in catering for the music lovers. Ile thought they could get bowling greens two at a time every fortnight, but they could not get one poor little organ without every pretext and plan being taken to oppose it. He quite agreed to the bowlers being looked after, but thought the attitude upon the organ war, dovrn-ight mean and unjust. The motion was carried. LATCHFORD WITHOUT AND THE FIRE BRIGADE. PROPOSED AGREEMENT.

At a meeting of th 3 Fire Engine Committee it was resolved that the Committee would be prepared to give the services of the Warrington Fire Brigade and appliances for coping with outbreaks of fire in the parish of Latchford Without on the following conditions An annual payment of £23 to be made by the Parish of Latchford Without to the Corporation. This sum to include out-of-pocket expenses, and the Parish Council to recoup themselves by charging insurance corn.mnies and othars for fire expenses in their district. The Parish Council to provide and maintain any fire alarm which they coasider necessary. The motor fire engine, when delivered, in addition to the steam engines and appliances, t, be available for extinguishing fires in the Parish of Latchford Without. At least one practice per annum to be held in the parish. The rule as to attendance of men at country fires in so far as attendance in Latchford Witnout is con- cerned not to apply. The Parish Council to be liable for any claim which may arise in respect of the abstraction by the Fire Brigade of any water from any pool, canal or stream, in or adjoining the parish. The Corporation to have first call on the services of the Fire Brigade, fire engine and appliances, for use in the Borough. The above terms to be subject to revision every three years. Alderman BURTON, in moving the confirmation of the minutes, said the Borough Treasurer had gone to a con- siderable amount of trouble in comparing the rateable value of Latchford Without with that of other localities, and it was found that a fair sum for the parish to pay would be £2B per annum. In a few months they would have a new motor fire engine and they would have sufficient equipment to deal efficiently with all conflagrations in the borough aud in Latchford Without. Councillor CUNNINGTON seconded.

Councillor GOUGH took exception to Latchford Without being granted such a concession. They ought not to be on the same terms as the borough. If they allowed that, they would not want to come into the borough. They found that the outside districts had to pay more for gas and he thought that was only right. Latchford Without would make a profit on the people who wanted the services of the brigade. They would have the first call of any outside district for the £2B. The bi igade cost the borough a penny in the £ and be thought that Latchford Without ought to pay £35. He moved that that minute be sent back for further consideration so that ratepayers of Warrington would not suffer, as be believed they would, if the con- cession were granted. What, he asked, about electricity? The MAYOR : We don't supply the outside districts yet. UOUnCillOr GOUGII : It would not be easy to supply the outside districts at as cheap a rate as the ratepayers of the borough. this minute has been thrust upon us. Councillor CUNNINGTON : It has not been thrust upon us at all. Alderman BENNETT seconded the amendment proposed by Councillor (lough. When such important questions as amalgamation were looming ahead it did seem a little bit unwise to make such an agreement. It was as well to have some power of arguing with the people who were asking tor the Caine privileges on the'same terms as the people in the borough. Councillor WILSON supported the minutes. If the privilege had been granted they would, during the last ten years, have made a prok of at least 200. He thought that in any as eat tuey were covered by the stipulation that the terms were subject tu revision after three years. Councillor DrcicEN'soN : This thing has been thrust upon us. Ido not know whether it is altogether wise for the matter to be discussed. _ _

Councillor BROADHURST strongly objected to the members of the Council coming forward and posing aq defenders of the ratepayers and I practically making it appear that the other members of the committee were wasting money. tie wished Councillor Dickenson had geue more fully into the matter. They had to consider that those rates we re based on the laws of average and what the costs were to the fire brigade who attended fires outside the district. They had had every detail brought before them. He did not think Councillor Cough was such a big rate- payer.' property owners were not the biggest ratepayers. They had to remember that there had not been a fire in the district in question for the last 30 years. They stood to gain £8 for the ratepayers of the town, and yet Councillor Cough said that they were giving something to the ratepayers of Latchford Without which they were not going to give to the ratepayers of Warrington (" Shame.") ‘Varrington people would certainly have the first call on the brigade, and it would not be as Councillor Cough asserted, that Latchford Without would have the first call. They could alter the arrange- ment after three years if they found it, unsatisfactory. He was there to look after the interests of the rate-

_ payers as well as Councillor Gough. Councillor PEMBLItTON : We know Councillor Broadhurst always looks rater the interests of the rate- payers according to himself. 'act:MA:Yon : Don't be personal. Councillor PEMI3ERTON : He has made a personal attack on Councillor Gough. Councillor Gough and Councillor Broadhurst, he continued, had a right to their own opinions, but he thought it was unfortunate that the matter had been discussed publicly. It would be much better if the agreements were first brought before the General Purposes Committee. Some of the councillors did not know what was to the general good of the whole Corporation. He proposed that the matter be referred back and thrashed out, at a General Purposes Committee meeting. Councillor WILKINSON intimated that he would vote against the resolution being sent back. He thought the proposed charge would work out at a good average. Before Lritchford could say she could make a profit there would have to be a fire in the parish. Consider-

ing that there had not been a fire for such a long time the Council had taken up the right position in placing the services of the brigade at the disposal of the parish. The MAYOR: It has not been submitted to them. We don't know whether they agree with it or not. Councillor WILKINSON : We know this is a good sitting committee. They would sit an hour over ts ss. job. (Laughter.) The 111 Avon said he quite agreed that people outside the borough should not have toe same advantages from the Corporation as those who lived in Warrington. On the other hand he understood that the Fire Engine Committee had made exhaustive inquiries and con- sidered the matter very carefully, it was practically a vote of "no confidence" in the committee if the amendment were passed. On that ground he would support the minutes. Alderman BURTON said he did not quite understand Councillor Pemberton. He seemed to be a man with many sides. One time he came and accused the members of doing things in the General Purposes Committee and he criticised them that night because they had not brought the matter before that committee. The Fire Engine Committee had considered the matter fully at a special meeting, and how anyone could say the matter was being rushed he could not say. It seemed now, seeing that there had not been a fire for so many years, very questionable whether Latchford Without would accept their terms. On a vote being taken, the minutes were confirmed.

div.p: AFTER TWO YEARS OF SUNDAY TRADING PROSECUTIONS.
RUNCORN MAGISTRATES AND INEFFECTIVE
PENALTIES.

The Sunday-trading proseottions which have been going on fox the last two and a half years at Runcorn continue to be the subject of much controversy. On Monday, Dr. McDougall, chairman of the Bench, addressing the eight defendants, said that the adminis- tration of the law was becoming a farce and a mockery. The defendants turned up every Monday ith their money, ready to pay, and opGned their shops again the following Sunday. He thought the time had arrived either for the infliction of costs as well as a fine, or the dropping of the prosecutions altogther. A meeting of magistrates would be held to consider the matter. Superintendent Bunion mentioned that there was a tendency for the number of shopkeepers who opened on Sundays to increase.

div.head: ST. HELENS HORSE PARADE.
div.p: ST. HELENS HORSE PARADE.

The twelfth May horse show and parade was held at St. Helens on Saturday, when upwards of £lOO in prizes and trophies was offered for competition. The show ir well patronised each year, Mr. Arthur Robinson being president. The horses and the turn- outs assembled at the Town Hall for judging, and afterwards paraded the town, headed by the Ravenbead Prize Band. Mr. J. Willis was ch,sirman of the com- mittee, and Mr. John Cotbam secretary. The winners of special prizes were : Greensll, Whitley Cup.—Messrs. Pilkington Broa. (J. Mower and W. Pennington). SUGGESTED TESTIMONIAL TO MR. BURNS. A letter was read from the editor of "The Poor Law Officers' Journal" suggesting that the work of Mr. John Burns at the Local Government Board was worthy of suitable recognition by Poor Law Unions. The Board would, he felt sure, desire to join in the move- ment, the object of which was so thoroughly laudable and which was obviously likely to;be widespread among Poor Law representatives.

The Rev. A. M. MITCHELL: Is it because of Mr. John Burns's poet,ry that this is being done? (Laughter.) I don't think we ought to waste time- over it, as £5,000 a year is a very comfortable amount. The letter was ordered to lie on the table.

div.head: WARRINGTON BOARD OF GUARDIANS.
div.p: WARRINGTON BOARD OF GUARDIANS.
Relieving Officer Appointed.

The Warrington Board of Guardians held its fort- nightly meeting at the Workhouse on Wednesday. Mr. E. L. Bent presided, and there were also present : Mrs. Collingwood, Mrs. Simnson, Mrs. Hall, Revs. T. R. Matthews and A. M. Mitchell. Messrs. A. J. Jolley (vice-chairman), J. Billinge, W. C. Brooks, W. Furness, R. Lee, Philip C. Garnett, J. A. Hughes, P. Longton, T. Robinson, W. Flanagan, W. Seton, T. Dale, A. Bottomley (clerk), R. T. Partridge (assistant clerk) and W. J. Brown (master). REGISTRATION AT HAYDOCK.

The Finance Committee considered the application of the Haydock Urban District Council for an extension of the hours for the registration of births and deaths at Haydock. The Clerk having given information as to the number of cases registered at Haydock, with the time of attendance by the registrar,it was recommended that the Clerk be instructed to arrange for a weekly evening attendance of the registrar at Haydock, such attendance to be in lieu of one of the three evening attendances now given at Newton. It was recommended that it be an instruction to the relieving officers to pay all relief weekly, without regard to the districts in wnich the recipients may reside. APPOINMENT OF RELIEVING OFFICERS. The committee considered the question relegated to them by the Board, of the advisability or otherwise of appointing a relieving officer for the No. 1 district and generally as to the allocation of work of the relieving officers. After careful consideration, the committee came to the conclusion that it would be unwise at the present juncture to recommend the Board to make any alteration in the number or districts of the relieving officers. The Clerk presented 109 applications for the position of relieving officer of the No. 1 relief district. It was recommended unanimously that Mr. J. H. Constable, workhouse porter and assistant relieving officer for vagrants, be sppointed -relieving officer for the No 10 district at a salary after the rate of £lOO per annum, rising by annual increments of £lO to a maximum of £l3O per annum, subject to the provisions

div.head: DEATH OF MR. W. FORD.
div.p: DEATH OF MR. W. FORD.
A Former Co-Operative Official.

One who was for many years officially identified with the Co-operative movement in Warrington passed away on Tuesday, in the person of Mr. William Ford, 37, Froghall-lane. A native of Warring- ton, Mr. Ford was educated at People's College and afterwards at the Manchester Technical School. At the age of nineteen, he entered the service of the Pearson and Knowles Coal and Iron Co., Ltd., as a clerk in the Dallam offices. He remained there for

twenty-five years, and on resigning to take TIIE LATE Ma. , up the duties of cashier to the Warrington Co-operative Society he was presented with a handsome marble clock as a token of the respect in which he was held. Mr. Ford was a most efficient and conscientious servant of the society and on retiring about three years ago he was granted a pension. One of his chief interests in life was music and he was for many years a member of the Musical Society, as well as being one of the original members of the late Mr. Parkinson's orchestra, which met in Golborne-street. He was a Congregationalist and for many years had been a regular worshipper at Wycliffe Church. In politics be was an ardent Radical. He leaves a widow and four children, two sons and two daughters

div.head: FUNERAL.
div.p: THE FUNERAL.

div.head: Passing Week.
div.p: The Passing Week.
THE ROYAL VISIT.

The Mayor's request to the manufacturers and tradespeople of Warrington to observe July 7th, the date of the visit of their Majesties the King and Queen, has, we hear, met with almost unanimous approval. The reception Committee have decided upon one very appropriate permanent form of com- memorating the event and impressing it upon the memories of the school children. They propose to present three shields—to be known as the George V. Shields—for competition in swimming and athletics among the scholars at the local elementary schools. The trophies will be held for twelve months by the successful school. We are informed that, as on the occasion of the visit of the late King Edward VII., stands will be erected in front 0.4. the Town Hall for the accommoda- tion of councillors, magistrates and their families.
MR. ARTHUR CROSFIELD.

Mr. Arthur Crosfield addressed two highly successful meetings during the week, one at Orford and the other at Bridge Foot. He gave one of his masterly reviews of the political situation and clearly showed that he was ready to take his place in the thick of the fight that is to result in the Liberal party rounding off, in fitting manner, one of the most progressive periods in social and political pro- gress that the present generation has seen. An extension of the care of the legis- lature for the unorganised and therefore badly paid worker, the land, and education are items that lie immediately ahead for treatment of the Liberal party—portions of a constructive policy, for which Conserva- tives are sighing and seem destined to sigh in vain. Mr. Crosfield's welcome at Orford was of the heartiest description, and there was a large and intelligently interested audience at Bridge Foot.

div.head: ALEXANDRA DAY.
div.p: ALEXANDRA DAY.

A very large number of ladies have volunteered to sell roses on Alexandra Day, Saturday, June 28th, and the work of organ- isation is going merrily on, giving every promise of the most successful results. Patrons of the fair saleswomen may purchase flowers of any value, but it is unnecessary to say that, although the lowest charge will be one penny, there will be no limit in the other direction, and any sum tendered will be accepted as a gift to the Infirmary. Owners of motor cars and carriages, it is hoped, will enter into the spirit of the carnival by decor- ating their conveyances with flowers, which can be obtained on reasonable terms before- hand, on application to Mrs. Henry Greenall, the hon. secretary. Stockton Heath, Dares- bury, and other outlying places are joining in the festival.

TRAMWAY MEN AND SUNDAY DUTIES. Alderman Smethurst was able to tell the Council a month ago that the tramways had had a record last year, and that the profits had been no less than £2,981, out of which £1,500 would go to relieve the pressure of the rates. Up to date the trams have assisted the rates to the extent of £6,000, be- sides which the department has a reserve fund of £lO,OOO, and a balance in hand of £1,820. Councillor Broadhurst, good smith that he is, struck while the iron was hot. He noticed, he said, that the Tramways Com - mitte were considering an application from the tramways employes that they should be paid time and a half for Sunday labour and he hinted that the time when record profits were in the air was a favourable one for the I making of such a concession. However, the committee, having make investigations,found that Warrington and Wigan were the only places in Lancashire where extra was paid for ' Sunday labour to tram employes and as it was only three months since the Warring- ton men had their application for time and a quarter granted, they now decided to make no further advance. This brought Councillor Broadhurst to the fore again and on Tuesday- night he carried an amendment that the re- commendation of the committee be struck out of the minutes. Only ten voted with him but in a small Council it was sufficient and the matter will be reconsidered by the corn- mittee.

How EXTRA INCOME MIGHT BE EARNED. So far as the writer is concerned he sees no objection to the tram men receiving pay and a half for Sunday labour especially if, as was stated, other workmen in the Corporation employ have that consideration shown them. What he and many of those who use the cars with him do not like is the bad habit ' some of the conductors have of making the customers sprint after the cars from the starting point. When a car sets out there are invariably a few customers within sight but often the conductor is admiring the features of those inside instead of noting the gesticulations of those who wish they were inside. They might earn their extra Sunday money by taking in all the people who wish to ride.
PICTURE PALACES AND THE PUBLIC HEALTH.

The rise of the picture palace has been one of the most widely discussed topics of recent years. Its influence and potentialities have been brought before us in a variety of aspects such as perhaps no other form of entertain- ment has suggested. This week the health side of the living picture boom receives notice from Dr. J. Coote Hibbert, medical officer of health, in his annual report. He states : The preset-day popularity ot such places of amusement as picturedromes, which offrr a form of entertainment spcially attractive to children and within the reach of their slenderest resources,

must tend to the spread of infectious disease unless close attention is paid to the ventilation of these buildings and more care is taken by parents to keep away children who are either themselves in an infectious condition or have come from infected homes. It is by no means uncommon to find that a child who has been excluded from school on account of there being non-notifiable infectious disease, such as measles and whooping-cough, at home is allowed to visit a picturedrome where he is a possible source of danger to other children who may be present. _

We have no doubt that the proprietors of our local picture houses are fully alive to the requirements on which the medical officer lays stress, with regard to the proper ventilation of their buildings. Parental apathy or carelessness is, however, difficult to overcome. The secret of this apparent indifference is, we believe, to be found in the fact that the seriousness of such diseases as ' measles and whooping cough is not fully appreciated by the majority of the people and their ignorance constitutes a menace to the community. As Dr. Hibbert suggests, compulsory notification would no doubt do a great deal to disturb unwarrantable com- placency and to impress the public with some sense of their responsibilities with regard to the spread of infection.

div.head: SILENCE.
div.p: SILENCE.

In the " Examiner "of April 19, we drew attention to the fact that at the annual meet- ing of the Warrington Women's Unionist and Tariff Reform League there was a marked dearth of reference to the great object that originally and mainly bound together that greatest organisation of its kind in the kingdom. We suggested that that annual meeting was held by ladies oblivious of the fact that their leader, Mr. BONAR LAW, had killed Tariff Reform and buried it 'in the Colonies; but, if his Warrington adherents had not heard of his latest doings, Mr. BONAR LAW hqs evidently heard of them, for last week he imitated their method of procedure. He was the chief speaker at the annual meeting of the Women's Amalga- mated Unionist and Tariff Reform Associa- tion held in London. One would have thought that in this Upper House of Women Tariff " Reformers " Tariff "Reform," the chief plank—if a plank that has been whittled down to a lath may still retain its name— would have received some attention. The leader's subject was "The Party's Progress," and there was not a word about Tariff Reform in the speech ! There's progress for you ! After ten years of progressing backwards the question has backed itself out of sight and out of speech, even of Mr. BONAR LAW when addressing Women Tariff "Reformers." It is a silence that must be oppressive in some quarters.
AMERICAN AND BRITISH EXPORTS.

The Tariff Reformers are delighted because in 1912 the total exports of the United States exceeded those of this country by £5,000,000, the relative figures being £492,000,000 and £487,000,000 respectively. "The United States," writes Mr. GRAHAM ANDERSON, of the Tariff Reform League," has won from us our historic position as the leading exporting power." But it happens that in 1901 the U.S.A. exports were £304,000,000 and the British £280,000,000; so that our exports have advanced faster than theirs since that date. The United States, though suffering under a tariff which Mr. CHAMBERLAIN has called "an abomination," has a population more than twice as great as ours, an area more than twenty times as great, enormous natural resources, and climatic variations which enable them to produce practically every- thing. It would be a curious thing if, with such advantages, their exports should not increase, especially as their indebtedness to foreign countries increases every year, and their credit has to be maintained abroad by means of exports. Moreover, it must be noted that £25 7,000,000 of the exports of the United States last year consisted of surplus food and raw materials, including £33,000,000 worth of bread stuffs and £130,000,000 worth of raw cotton. There was also £21,000,000 worth of mineral oil exported, and £10,000,000 worth of raw tobacco. It is in items like these, which we do not produce, that the United States have been enabled to increase their exports so immensely. Their exports of manu- factures were some £150,000,000 smaller than OUTS.

It is amusing to find the export test once more trotted out by Tariff Reformers like Mr. GRAHAM ANDERSON, after being shut up in the stable so long. Last year, it may be remembered, the "fatuous jumble" test was the favourite. Next year it will probably be something else. The fact that many of our great industries are now being compelled to refuse orders, that there is a shortage of labour in several of them, that wages are rising all over the country, and that our unemployment rate is now considerably lower even than what the "Daily Mail" called the "bedrock minimum," weigh for nothing with the "Reformers," whose busi- ness it is to show that everything is still going wrong, and who have perforce to keep on trotting out self-stultifying " tests " to prove it."

div.head: " TARIFF REFORMERS."
div.p: " TARIFF REFORMERS."
An 111-fated Movement that was routed by National Prosperity.
HON. GEORGE PEEL'S WITHERING SUMMARY OF THE SITUATION.
[By C. E. Parker.]

The Hon. George Peel, who bears an honoured Free Trade name, has written a racy little book on the history of Tariff Reform. The Hon. George is of the same faith as his grandfather—Sir Robert Peel— the statesman who abolished the corn taxes, and wrote in 1850 :—" If others entertain doubts as to the wisdom of the commercial policy adopted from 1841 to 1847 I entertain none, and shall do everything in my power to prevent the reversal of the policy or the restoration of protection in any shape on any pretence whatever."

A Troubled Life. Mr. Peel gives a graphic and accurate description of the troubled life of the Tariff Reform movement from the date, now ten years ago, when Mr. Chamberlain launched his ill-fated project. According to Mr. Chamberlain, unless we adopted his scheme the Empire would tumble about our ears. " Agriculture has been practically destroyed. Sugar has gone. Iron is threatened. Wool is threatened. Cotton will go." "Our workingmen are like sheep in a field being led to the slaughter," and so on. We have recorded the details of the holding back, the clever wriggling of Mr. Balfour, who saw that public opinion was not ripe for such an arrangement, and was clearly doubtful if it ever would ripen, who had no settled convic- tions .on the subject, who hedged so ingeniously that no one knows to this day if at heart he is a Tariff Reformer or Free Trader. He let Mr. Chamberlain go into the wilderness on an irresponsible crusade, he himself kept in cover as long as he dare, for years mystifying his own party, until they could stand it no longer, and 8.M.G., "Balfour must go," became the watchword. Then we have the placing in power of the bold Bonar Law, the "strong man" on Tariff Reform, the man who would keep the flag proudly at the peak, the man who was to lead and need no pushing, the man who said, "We cannot have Preferential trade without a tax on food.' Mr. Law, naturally a mild and reasonable man, felt bound to play up to the part assigned to him by his supporters. He tried to make up for the poverty of his arguments by the violence of his words and actions. He set up his own standard, an ignoble one. His own .words were "The standard of success which I set up is the amount of irritation which my speech has caused to my opponents., He was expected to lead the charge, to take the Free Trade fortress with a rush and plant the Tariff Reform flag upon its highest battlement. But, alas ! for the fortunes of this imperial leader, scarce had begot into the saddle, waved the flag and sounded the charge all along the line, when he was obliged to sound the recall. What had happened? While Birmingham was mounted and eager for the fray, Lancashire and Yorkshire held back. Birmingham and a section of Warrington cried " Forward," the North cried " Wait," and the bold leader, incapable of leading, chafed in his saddle, and waited for orders from his valiant followers. The reason for this indecision was, as Mr. Peel points out, partly economic and partly political. The silent, stern facts of the general prosperity of the country, as evidenced by trade and employment returns, were proving too much for the main arguments on which the Tariff Reform case rested and neutralis- ing their influence. Again, food taxes were thoroughly disliked in the north, and no amount of money poured into Tariff Reform coffers to equip lecturers to prove that food could be made cheaper by taxing it had any lasting effect. There had been a limited adhesion—to part of the programme as far as it affected manufacturers in manufactur- ing districts. The idea of making the foreigner pay our taxes had caught on with the ignorant class. Perhaps the thought of the Tariff Reformers in the north was best evidenced by a speech of Lord Newton in which he said :

"Much as Lord Newton personally admired Mr. Chamberlain, firmly as he believed in his policy, it had always seemed to him that Mr. Chamberlain, in advocating his policy in the way he did at that parti- cular moment, committed a serious tactical error. His error was that he tried to persuade the country to adopt two courses at the same time. He preached Tariff Reform and Colonial Preference simul- taneously. Lord Newton had no doubt that every man almost in the country, and almost every woman, was at heart a Protectionist to a certain degree, and he honestly believed that there was nothing that appealed to the English workingman more than the prospect of making the foreigner pay." Here we have the secret of any strength the Tariff Reform movement has in the manufacturing north. It is thoroughly Pro- tectionist, but, of course, only Protectionist in what they themselves make. The idea of Colonial Preference involving food taxes never caught on, just as Protection to manufac- tures without Protection for farm products will not be supported in agricultural districts. Army of Arguments in Flight. We all remember how the bold leader somewhat sulkily obeyed the orders of Lord Newton and his fellow Protectionists, lowered and defaced the flag hoisted and unfurled by Mr. Chamberlain ten years before. But what of Birming- ham—the Tuileries of Tariff Reform?

There was no strong revolt. "There was an electric thunderstorm silence, as when cloudland is too big with storm." Both Birmingham and Warrington, after a feeble protest, accepted the change of front, obeyed the new command, and took their place in the new party formation. Meanwhile, Tariff Reform was put into cold storage for a time, and its advocates ordered to talk against the Insurance Act. As the "Morning Post" put it at an election:—"At the Unionist lurry the orators had 'instructions to say nothing about Tariff Reform,' and that 'the whole thing savours of madness.' " Mr. Peel puts it thus :—" Some in touch with the stable thought they had a better horse than Tariff Reform entered for the Grand National, and that they stood to win on a chaser which originally had been voted an outsider by the ring." The point was all along how they could win ; the cost in consistency- mattered nothing.
Mr. Peel graphically describes the set back of Tariff Reform as follows :

"Then suddenly, at the close of December, was witnessed a singular spectacle—a whole army of arguments in flight. There was no attack from without, for the Free Traders, entrenched in the facts of the situation and commanded by the best of generals, looked on with amused surprise at the amazing move-

Bicycle Thieves. An expert gang of liicycle thieves is believed to be at work in South Lancashire. Several machines have disappeared from Warrington during the past week and have not been recovered. Cyclists are therefore cautioned against the practice of leaving their machines standing near the doors of houses or places of boBite3s.

div.head: Sunday Trading.
div.p: Sunday Trading.

With a view to checking Sunday Trading in Warrington, the Chief Constable has warned the shop- keepers concerned that they are alleged to be break- ing the law by opening their premises for business on Sunday. This action is the outcome of the petition recently presented to the Watch Committee by a deputation of clergy and ministets. On that occasion it was stated that a census had revealed the fact that GOO shops were regularly open on Sunday. Whether, in the event of a continuance of the trading, Police Court proceedings are contemplated has not yet trai,spired.

The 'Rector and Secondary School Religion. The current issue of the " Warrington Parish Church Magazine" contains an expression of the Rector's satis- faction at a letter published recently from a parent pro- testing against the methods adopted by the Education Committee for imparting religious knowledge to the scholars in the Secondary School. The Chairman and other members of the Committee (says the writer of the magazine article) have stated that the parents, so far as they know, are quite satisfied with the action of the Committee. The Rector hopes that this letter will open their eyes and show them that they are mis- taken, and he earnestly trusts that it will be followed by others from parents who know from their children's own lips the solemn farce which is now being enacted in this important day school.

div.head: National Association of Head Teachers. _ __ .. _
div.p: National Association of Head Teachers. _ __ .. _

The Council of the National Association of Head Teachers has decided to hold combined meetings in various centres by linking up certain associations. For this purpose the following associations are acting in concert : Manchester, Oldham, Rochdale, Salford and Warrington. Oldham is holding the second of this series of annual meetings On Saturday, June 14th, in the Music Room, Werneth Park, Oldham. The subjects to be discussed include: "Some thoughts on Educational RefJrm," to be introduced by Prof. H. Bompass Smith, M.A., Manchester University, and Some kinds of work devolving upon education authorities," to be introduced by Mr. J. (Rennie, Secretary of Education, Oldham. The Late Rev. H. R. Wild.

The one incident that has engrossed the thoughts of all the parishioners during the last ten days or so (says holy Trinity Parish Magazine), has been the unexpected death of the Rev. H. R. Wild, on Tuesday, the 20th tilt., at his brother's house at Diming, near Glossop. There was a remarkable expression of feel- ing at the funeral from Mr. Wild's old friends and associates at St. Luke's; and beautiful wreaths were sent from the members of the congregation, the following gentlemen, along with the Vicar, attending on their behalf —the churchwardens (Mr. Oldfield and Mr. Taylor), Mr. Sutcliffe, Mr. Armstrong and Mr. Warburton, jun. The white presentation stole given some time ago to Mr. Wild by the members of the congrtgation was sent by them that it might be worn by and buried with him. Sweated Workers. The Rev. Thomas Jackson, president of the Primitive Methodist Connexion, held a large congregation spell- bound at the Legh-street Church on Thursday evening while lie unfolded to them the story of " East-end sweating and rescue work in Whitechapel." It was a narrative in which the grave and the gay were blended. There was righteous indignation in the president's voice as he held up to scorn the vile system of the sweater, but he allowed a pretty wit full play when dealing with the brighter side of rescue work. The President is intensely practical. Be had brought with him a collection of articles produced by sweated labour, and he invited members of the congregation to appraise their value. We had" The Song of the Shirt" in real life, for Mr. Jackson showed us a shirt which a widow —providing her own thread and hiring a machine—had made for the sum of one penny. Mrs. Henry Speed, of Rock Ferry, presided at the lecture. The choir creditably sang the anthem "By Babylon's wave." Children's Athletic Festival.

The fifth festival promoted by the Warrington and District Teachers' Association is to be held on Monday evening at 5.30 p.m. A record entry of over 1,500 has been received and the teachers appeal to the parents and everyone interested in sports to give them a record gate. The programme consists of 17 events for boys and 16 events for girls. A championship competition between the various schools,which is teeing held for the first time, has created a healthy rivalry and a keen contest is promised. Two trophies have been given—one for boys, the other for girls. To give every school, as far as is possible, an equal chance of gaining the trophy, all competitors must be under 13 to score points for their respective schools, and only certain events count for the championship. A first prize winner in championship events gains a prize and 8 points for his or her school, a second gains 6 points, and so on. The school gaining the most points holds the trophy for 12 months. Cham- pionship shields have been given by the King's visit reception committee and will be presented on the day of the King's visit.

Striking Empire Day Celebration. The boys of Heathside school have kept Empire Day this year on more ambitious lines than previously. In the afternoon the whole school assembled upstairs to see "The Crusaders "—a romantic play in five acts, The room was tastefully decorated and hung with streamers, a platform had been erected, special scenery procured, and everything done that could be done to make the afternoon enjoyable and instructive. The actors were all in correct costumes. Kings, dukes, knights, abbots, soldiers—all of the twelfth century— lived once more, and walked about to the evident amazement of the smaller boys. The first scene showed most of the characters (including King Richard I. of England, the Duke of Burgundy, and the Duke of Austria) on the Walls of Acre in July, 1191. From there, through the eight scenes, the boys followed with the keenest interest the changing fortunes of the king for whom they have such admiration—the lion- hearted Richard. The acting was splendid and deserved the hearty applaus3 which it called forth. Special mention must be made of J. Blotneley, P. Bradburn and F. Davies (principals), J. Deakin (Blondel), S. Makin (the Merchant), and E. J. Newall (Hadmar von Kuenring). Mr. T. Edden and Mr. F. J. Emson trained the boys. Cancer and its Causes.

During a recent discussion on " Vivisection" at a meeting of the Warrington Field Club the Mayor (Councillor Dr. Joseph) explained the fact that cancer was very rarely found in animals by expressing the view that the disease was, to some extent, due to worry. A similar view- is stated by Dr. Greenhalgh the medical officer of health for Accrington, who, in his annual report just issued, says :—" In studying the antecedent circumstances of large numbers of persons affected with cancer, great worry, of one form or another, seems to be a more common factor than any other condition. Peace of mind in carrying the troubles from which no-cne escapes would seem to be a valuable preventive means in avoiding the invasion of this terrible disease." A circular on the prevention of cancer containing information extracted from most of the medical journals says that chronic irritation and injury are the chief pre-dis- posing causes of the disease. The following rules are laid down :—Remove warts, moles and other skin growths exposed to irritation ; workers in tar or paraffin should be treated for hard growths, sweeps should have daily baths, and workers with x-rays should be protected; avoid smoking to excess which pre-disposes to cancer of the lips, tongue and cheeks; avoid irritation of the tongue and cheek by jagged teeth and lips by inferior clay pipes ; avoid excessively hot food and drink which induce cancer of the throat; avoid iced drinks and ices as digestion ceases when the temperature of the stomach is reduced below the normal ; imperfectly chewed food causes chronic internal irritation which sets up cancer in various organs; money spent on the teeth bring a greater return than any other investment; avoid constipation; avoid alcoholic drinks as they are a pre-disposing cause of cancer and diminish the average prospects of survival by 30 per cent.

div.head: Examiner, Saturday, June 7, 1913. DEATH OF MR. A. H. CLIVE. THE ROYAL VISIT. End of an Active and Promising Career. EMPLOYERS ASKED- TO DECLARE A GENERAL HOLIDAY.
div.p: The Examiner, Saturday, June 7, 1913. DEATH OF MR. A. H. CLIVE. THE ROYAL VISIT. End of an Active and Promising Career. EMPLOYERS ASKED- TO DECLARE A GENERAL HOLIDAY.

A promising career has been cut short by the death of Mr. Alfred Henry Clive. auctioneer and estate agent, who passed away at his residence, Nordene, Grappen- hall-road, Stockton Heath, at 2.45 on Saturday after- noon. Mr. Clive, who was only forty years of age, was seized with serious illness on Christmas Day. For several weeks his life was despaired of, but he partially recovered, though not sufficienty to return to business. A fortnight ago he had a relapse and succumbed to liceornorrhage on Saturday. The circum- stances of his death are more deeply saddening by the fact that his youngest child, aged sixteen months, died so recently as Tuesday of last week, the funeral ' taking place on Friday. Widespread and sincere is I the sympathy extended to the widow and three children in their hereavement. .Aithough only a comparatively young man, Mr. Clive had already established himself in the business life of the town by consistent and painstAking effcrt. A son of Mr and Mrs.

Edmund Clive, of Pcwell - street, Air. Clive received his *4l. early education at People's College, and afterwards sbrwcarcoisiA . nel,a proceededs to the B.)teler articled to the late Alderman Thoma,4 Suttou,auctioneer and with lvhom he irictome-tascollector v re- mained for 14 years.

TE Mn. A. H. CLIVE. In 1903 he was ap- pointed to the sec- retaryship of the Warrrington Permanent Benefit Buil,!ing Society and entered into business on his own account., Subsequently, he took up the profession of an auctioneer and estate agent, and his sound training, aptitude and conscientiousness gained for him general confidence and an ever-increas- ing circle of clients. He conductei some of the most important property sales in the district and theie appeared to be no doubt that he was marked out for a very successful career. Mr. Clive took a great interest in the Warrington Horse Parade and for a number of years had rendered the committee invaluable service in the position of hon. secretary. He dis- charged the dulies with that thoroughness which characterised all his work and it was in no small degree due to his skilful direction that the parade so completely fulfilled its purpose. Mr. Clive was also secretary to the Private Estates (Warrington), Ltd., and Atkinson's Cafes, Ltd. He was a well- known Freemason, being a member of the Friendship Lodge. He was also identified with the Warrington Cricket and Bowling Club and devoted his interest particularly to the bowling section. Mr. Clive was of a frank, genial disposition, courteous and hard- working, and his charm of personality made him a great favourite with the many friends ‘vho deplore his untimely end.

THE FUNERAL. Impressive testimony to the respect in which Mr Clive was held was to be found in the large and repre- sentative attend:lnce at the funeral which took place at St. Thomas' Church, Stockton Heath, on Tuesday afternoon. The service, which was characterised by great simplicity, was conducted by the Revs. James Collins (vicar), and E. W. Clarke. Mr. Arthur Down was at the organ and played appropriate music, incluling "0 Rest in the Lord" and the Dead March from "Saul." The body was borne to its last resting place by six old school friends of Mr. Clive—Councillor °abort(' and Messrs. Sam Bertles, S. Wallhead, 11. Milling, W. H. Payton, and T. Chirilaw. The principal mourners were Mr. E. Clive (father), Mr. Ted Clive, jun. (nephew), Mr. J. Gerrard and Mr. R. Roberts (brothers-in-law), Mr. G. Smith (cousin). Mr. A. J. Willett, Mr. J. Atkinson, Mr. N. Dowswell, Mr. A. Warburton, Mr. J. Wilkinson (Stockton Heath), Mr. S. W. Cookson, Mr. W. Hollingdrake and Dr. Langdale. The members of Mr. Clive's (ace staff were represented by Messrs. R. Chalmers, A. I'. Huglacs and C. Swinton.

Other representatives in attendance were : Permanent Benefit Building Society : Messrs. W.. 7. Shaw (president), T. Critchley, S. W. Dallow, C. H. Hibbert, T. Ince T. P rtridge, R. Shackleton, F. Timperley, W. H. Woodcock (auditor), and A. Cook (treasurer). Private Estates Limited : Messrs. J. Dolan, IL B. Houghton, H. Hughes and B. Silcock. Atkinson's Cafes, Limited : Councillor Wilkinson (chairman`„ Messrs. Joseph Wilkinson, J. Jackson and J. E. Richardson. People's College : Mr. E. Wallington. Horse Parade Committee: Mr. W. Fletcher and Mr. G. Venn. Freemasons: War. Bro. H. F. Greenough, Bro. J. H. Clarke, P.P.G.5.8., Bro. T. Cooper, Bro. S. Tuustall, Bro. E. J. Sutton, 8r0.2 Illidge, War. Bro. John Cooper, Wor. Bro. John Saillcock, Wor. Bro. W. It Woodcock. Bro. J. TeAre, Bro. A. Bottomley and Bro. F. A. Jenkins. Among others present were Messrs. J. Lyon Whittle, A. T. Hallaway, T. H. Spinks, J. Gray, A. S. Wright, J. Mainwarine, F. Hickman, R. Lowe, J. H. Gittens, T. A. Sutton, H. Cooke, E. Cowdell, D. E. Watson, F. Barber, T. D. Ames, T. Cooper,T. Welsby, W. Mclntyre, E. Bradshaw, W. Roberts, H. Rogers, S. P. Silcock, E. England, F. A. Morris, A. Taylor, H. Johnson, G. C. Howard, E. Morris, C. H. Hoult, W. Chalmers, H. Parkimon, W. Parkinson, 3. Smith, J. Welsby, J. Cooper, J. Turner Cooper, J. Jackson, Li. Cookson and many others. In addition to the many beautiful wreiths sent by relatives and friends, florar tributes were received from "The office staff." members of Lodge of Friendship, 2,963, directors of Permanent Benefit Building Society, members of the Warrington Cycling Club, directors of Atkinson's Cafe, Ltd., directors of Private Estates, Ltd.," The old tenants at Widnes." The funeral arrangements were carried out by Mr. H. F. Greenough, Heathside, Warrington.

div.head: MENACE OF "THE TRADE." -- Citizens' Temperance League's Campaign.
div.p: MENACE OF "THE TRADE." -- Citizens' Temperance League's Campaign.

The work of the Warringten Citizens Temperance League is so well-known that we feel confident that the summer open-air campaign which was commenced with a meeting at Longtord-street, Orford-lane, ou Wednes- day evening will be as successful as ever. Mr. J. Griffiths presided and the principal speaker was Mr. P. Taylor, of the Manchester and Salford Union of Temperance. At tee outset the CHAIRMAN said that they were plPased to find that in the aggregate tl.e evil of drink- ing was a diminishing one. It was, however, of such a formidable character that it was found necessary to educate all in tbe temperance movement. To do that they could not find a better medium than opm-air meetings. (Hear, bear.) Mr. TAYLOR said they had a recipe which would cure a preat number of ills from which the community bad suffered a good deal. He was never so silly as to say that the whole of the poverty came from drink but he would say that a good deal of it was due to excessive drinking. If drink was not the cause of poverty, it aggravated the poverty which did exist. (Hear,hear.) Illustrating what the drink evil did in the way of poverty he referred to tnree districts in Liverpool. In district "A " there was one public-house for 250 people, and there was one pauper out of every 28 of the population. District "B " had only one public- house to 450, and the proportion of paupers was one in SO. In district "C " they had no public-houses. The population was 50 000 and there was only one pauper out of every 1,000. But they might say that Liverpool, with such a largo foreign element could not be classed with a town like Warrington. He would take Burnley, where in one district which had 696 people to 15 public-houses and two off licences, there were 338 in receipt of relief and in one 3ear people went into the Workhouse. That represented 476 pauoers our, of 696 people and the cause la; in the 15 public houses and off-licenses. Drink was a great menace to every community. Another reason why they should oppose and crush the drink traili:3 was because there was no trade in any country which sweated its workers like the drink business. The " trade " worked its employes longer hours and paid less wages in pro- portion to its capital than any other industry known. Strong drink blighted the character and shortened life.

div.head: COLBORNE-STREET BAPTIST CHURCH. Sale of Work for Building Fund.
div.p: COLBORNE-STREET BAPTIST CHURCH. Sale of Work for Building Fund.

The handsome new school premises attalhed to Golborne-street Baptist Church were the scene on hursday afternoon of a very successful sale of work. The arrangements had been in the hands of a very enthusiastic band of workers, with Mr. H. Buckley as stcretary. The sale was opened by Mr. William Roberts. under the presidency of Mr. Norman Balmford. The PASTOR (Rev. H. Ogden) explained that the con- gregation had to raise £5O a year as interest on the loan obiliined for the erection of the new school, and the wile was being held with that object in view, and also to further the work of the church.

Mr. Balmford referred to his early associations with Golhorne-street school, and expressed his indebtedness to his old teacher, Mr. E. James Hall. The most hope- ful part of the work of the Christian churches was that which conc.rned the training of the young. Mr. W. Roberts said the record of that church was an honourable one in the history of Warrington. It had never been blessed with rich men, the congregation always having been composed of the working class; but they had been a united and hard-working people, cheer- ful in the face of difficulties. Mr. Roberts went on to emphasise the fact that a minister could not do his duty without visiting the homes of the people, and said he believed they had in Mr. Ogden a pastor who would do his utmost to make that church the success which it deserved to be. He (the speaker) congratulated all the Baptist churches in Warrington and district on their ministers, and said he did not believe that at any time during the past forty years had they been better served in that respect than at present. (Applause.) A vote of thanks was passed to Mr. Roberts, on the proposition of Mr. B. FEW, seconded by Mr. E. WYNNE JONES.

div.head: FREE CHURCH BOYS' BRIGADE.
div.p: FREE CHURCH BOYS' BRIGADE.
AN ORGANISATION THAT IS CALCULATED TO DEVELOP REAL PATRIOTISM,
Photograph by Burrell.
THN.: BAND AND OFFICERS.

div.head: To the Rear : Quartermsster Lieut. 11. Appleton, Rev. J. S. Chedbnrn, Captain Fernley, Lieut. Borney, Lieut. Wilkir.son, Captain A. Appleton, Lieut. Banks and Colonel Grounds.
div.p: To the Rear : Quartermsster Lieut. 11. Appleton, Rev. J. S. Chedbnrn, Captain Fernley, Lieut. Borney, Lieut. Wilkir.son, Captain A. Appleton, Lieut. Banks and Colonel Grounds.

An effort to give the Boys' Brigade movement a prominent place in Free Church life has taken practical shape at the Baptist Church, Latchford, where a flourishing corps now exists, and on Thursday evening there was e, large gathering to witness the presentation of instruments to the bugle band. The ceremony, which took place at a special service, was performed by Mrs. James Dodds, of Penketh. The Rev. J. S. Chedburn presided and was supported by Col. A. Grounds and Quarter-master Appleton. Lieut. Homey was at the organ. The Rev. J. S. Cbedburn pointed out that the principle underlyirg military organisation and discip- line were rapidly coming to be recognised as possessing a moral end educational value ent;,rely apart from their general warlike application. Boys' Brigades had, in spite of much adverse criticicism and many acknow- ledged weaknesses, proved in the main to be a most powerful influence in developing a robust and practical type of Christiaa .character. It would generally be found, moreover, as the result of careful and unpreju- diced investigation, that there was no purpose so far from the minds of those responsible for such institutions as the development of Jingo militarism, or that spurious patriotism which signified not love for one's own country but hatred and jealousy towards other countries. The object was to present Christianity to the lads in the aspect best calculaeed to appeal to their natural instincts : that of a mighty army waging incessant warefare against every form of sin and

wrong; and inoidentally to train them, by the means which a military form of organization afforded better than anything else, in habits of obedience, discipline, reverence and self-respect. He earnestly hoped thin the time was not far distant when the movement would be more generally embraced by the other Free Churches in the neighbourhood to their own lasting and permanent good. (Applause.) Mrs. Dodds then presented the bugles, which were of regulation pattern and very handsome in appearance, to the lad 4. The instruments were supplied by Mr. G. Shakeshaft, Mersey-street, and each bore an en- graved inscription with the name of its respPctive donor. The donors were: Mrs. James Dodds, of Penketh, Quartermaster Lieut. Herbert Appleton, Mr. James A. Banks, Mrs. W. S. Chedhurn, Rev. J. S Chedburn, Captain N. Fernley, Mr. Thomas Ford, Mr. Alfred Ground-: Colonel), Mr. Frederick Pendlebury, Mrs. E. A. Russell, CAptain James Smart, R.A.M.C. (T.F.) of Aberdeen, Officers of the Staff.

Mrs. Dodds delivered an address warmly eulogising the work of the brigade, as it helped the boys to cultivate both character and physique. She urged the members to form high ideals and live up to them, and hoped they would continue to serve in the corps even when they had pacsed the years of boyhood.
A
STANDARD BEARER FOR LOCAL
LIBERALISM.
Mr. ARTHUR CROSFIELD AT ORFORD
AND BRIDGE FOOT.
MINIMUM WAGE FOR THE WEAK AND UNORGANISED.
Progressives Ready for Another Move Forward:
Land and Education.

Mr. A. H. Crosfield addressed two open-air meetings in Warrington and Orford in the earlier part of the week. He had splendid receptions from large and enthusiastic crowds and his speeches on the foreign and domestic policy of the Government were followed with great interest and approval. As Mr. C. E. Parker put it, in proposing a vote of thanks, Mr. Crosfield's speeches are characterised by breadth of outlook, and, it might be added, be always lifts political controversy to a high level.

extremity of folly to intensify mankind's suffer- ings by the butchery and bloodshed of war. (Hear, hear.) ADVANCING SANITY OF CIVILISED RACES. There had been encouraging evidence of the advancing sanity of the civilised races and of their determination to settle their differences without resort- ing to the stupid, futile and barbarous system of war. (Applause.) In many a critical and difficult issue we had, thank heaven, seen the triumph of commonsense and of wise diplomacy. Let us hope and believe that the smaller Powers, seeing what the, larger Powers had done, would rise to the occasion and ensure that the splendid victory they had won, by heroic courage, b aindless self-sacrifice and real patriotic devotion, should not be besmirched by any dreadful internecine struggle. (Applause.) The spontaneous tributes of praise which they heard coming from the different nations of Europe to the sagacity and statesmanship of Sir Edward Grey— (applause)—was surely a matter of deep satisfaction to all Englishmen, and he would like to express one's sense of appreciation of the patriotic manner in which the Opposition, quite as much as the Progressive side, had supported Sir Edward Grey in foreign policy in these critical times. (Applause.) Without wishing to make it a party matter, he thought they as Liberals were entitled to feel a special degree of pride in the fact that so great a diplomatic triumph had been achieved by a Liberal Foreign Secretary —(applause). —and by one for whose line and unselfish character, lofty patriotism, ability, distinction' and devotion to national and international affairs, they felt the deepest respect and admiration. (Applause.) Sir Edward Grey's real disinterestedness had been recognised by all who had bt en concerned in the recent difficult and delicate negotiations and had proved of priceless service to them. His patience, tact, courtesy, and winning personal charm on the one hand, the :courage and decision with which he acted in the case of Scutari, and again the decisive advice and warning which he gave to the allies the previous Tuesday, had won the day. (Loud applause.) THE INSURANCE ACT. Turning to home affairs, Mr. Crosfield said be did not think there would be any difference of opinion between that meeting and himself as to which had been the most outstanding achievement of the past twelve months. Unquestionably it was the event which they celebrated on January 13th—the inauguration of the most stupendous work in the direction of social reform ever undertaken in this or in any other country. Those who attended the Labour League's meetings were no doubt familiar with the main figures that were in themselves so eloquent. For instance, before this year we had only 5,000,000 of our industrial popula- tion secured against the day of adversity; now we had over 14,000,000. (Applause.) As a matter of fact the difference was even more marked, because many of those 5,000,000 were putting their savings into concerns that were more than a little shaky, whereas under the Insurance Act the money which every person set apart for that purpose was as safe as a church. Thus we had established among the mass of the people a security far beyond anything which they enjoyed before. There were, of course, other splendid reforms included in that great and far-reaching Act, but a single figure like that he had quoted was more eloquent to the man who thought what it meant to the country than any verbal description of tbe benefits. (Applause.) If they added to the benefits of the Insurance Act the great advantages which accrued from the Workmen's Compensation Act and the Old Age Pensions Act, and also tried to estimate what" the defence of Free Trade meant to the men and women of the country, they had blessings for the industrial classes of Britain that were to be reckoned annually in tens of millions. (Applause.) He challenged any Tory in Warrington to deny that, and he asked every thoughtful citizen in our town to ponder that simple fact and to ask himself whether that was a situation that the men and women of England could afford to trifle with. (Applause.) ON THE EVE OF FURTHER WORK. It was a position which they as Liberals and Pro- gressives had to defend, but they had also to advance still further because they were on the eve of additional work of the same good kind. (Applause.) It would not be long before they were fighting the great battle of education --(hear, hear) and dealing with the land question—(applause)—and the enormous question of a minimum wage for the unskilled or less skilled labourer. There were four industries in the country to which the great experiment of the Trades Boards Act was being applied—an experi- ment which he knew, from personal inter- course with people on the Continent, was being watched with great interest throughout Etrope. (Applause.) That was only a beginning, but five more trades were to be brought within the scope of the Act, and in that way we had established in England the principle of the minimum wage for those workers who were unable to organise and defend themselves. He had never advocated interference in industries where trade unions could do their own collective bargaining—in fact such interference would be little short of impertinence—but where people were too weak to protect their own interests the State should step in. (Applause.) He was one of those who, verbally and by letter, had been pressing Mr. Buxton to extend the operations of the Act in directions where it was badly needed. (Applause.) AT GRIPS WITH THE POVERTY PROBLEM'. Mr. Crosfield went on to submit that the work of the present Government constituted a direct and practical attempt to deal with the problem of extreme poverty. When they got the old folk looked after by the Old Age Pensions Act, the sick and the unemployed defended by the Insurance Act, and sweating attacked by the Trades Boards Act, he maintained that they were already at close quarters with the whole question of pcv.rty and had taken a long stride in the direction of Poor Law reform. (Applause.) After a period of unexsmplsd activity, there had been a little breathing space and for a few weeks they were on the defensive. That was never a good time for Progressives at by-elections; they wanted to be on the attack. (Applause.) Their hard-working party chiefs had now an interval in which to study and prepare in detail the measures that lay immediately ahead of them, but the party would very soon be in the thick of the fight again, and he said, with absolute confidence, that when they had completed their work of social reform there would ba a record to the credit of this Government for which they might search the pages of English history in vain fora parallel. (Laud applause.)

THE SPREAD OF POLITICAL JUSTICE. Many of their friends who were keen on that social reform, for which every man who looked around hini saw the urgent need, were inclined to say : Why don't you go straight on with that and put all political reform aside? That would not do. He thought one of the most striking successes of the Government was to be found in the fact that they held the scales so wisely, and maintained the progress alike of social and political reform. (Hear, hear.) Thus they had such tine measures as Home Rule, Welsh Disestab- lishment, the Parliament Act, the Plural Voting Bill, and the Payment of Members. They could not describe either the Home Rule or Welsh Disestablishment Bills as coming within the category of bread and butter politics. They constituted sheer, disinterested work for the spread of political justice. (Applause.) The Progressives of the present day had to remember that they were trustees, carrying out the great political reforms which had come down to them as a heritage, and it was well to remember that, but for the way in which their political fathers fought for an approxima- tion to political fair *play and justice, they would not have found in these days the same desire for social reform or the capacity to carry it into effect. He did not think the people of this country had yet grasped the import and the enormous significance to the democracy of Britain of the success- ful carrying of the Parliament Act by the Prime Minister. (Applause.) In whatever
(Continued on Page S.)

div.head: MEETING AT BRIDGE FOOT.
div.p: MEETING AT BRIDGE FOOT.
MR. CROSFIELD AND THE MINIMUM
WAGE QUESTION.

On Monday evening Mr. Crostield snoke at a meeting held near the Old Mill at Bridge Foot, under the auspices of the Progressive Labour League. Mr. E. Wynne Jones (president of the League) presided, and was supported on the platform by Mr. C. E. Parker (president of the Liberal Association), Mr. A. R. Mason (Free Trade Union) and Mr. E. W. James. LIBERALS NOT DOWNHEARTED. THE TORY PARTY AS TIPSTERS.

The CHAIRMAN said Liberals had no need to be downhearted. Liberalism was not going to be over- come by a temporary set-back like the Newmarket or Altrincham by-election. No matter what the Tory party said, the great programme of the Government was going to be carried into operation. He noticed that the local Tory party had turned " bookies " and tipsters. (Laughter.) A placard, announcing the Altrincbam re3ult, declared : " Lay any odds the Radicals like against Home Rule." (Laughter.) He had never made a bet in his life, but he told them frankly that, even to a steady-going Radical, such an invitation was a great temptation. (Laughter.) He would like to ask Mr. Harold Smith what odds he was prepared to lay against Home Rule being carried, in spite of the House of Lords, and becoming ths law of the land. (Applause.) He did not think Mr. Smith would be prepared to risk any odds in that way. (Hear, hear.) The Tories were, however, going in for a great campaign against Home Rule. The Ulster members were not only arranging great demonstrations, but had invited a large number of journalists to go over to Ireland and had promised them plenty of hospitality between the speeches. (Laughter.) Not withstanding all these efforts,nothing they said or did would prevent the passing of Home Rule. He believed that, with the aid of self-govern- ment, Ireland was destined to become one of the most prosperous parts of the British Empire. (Applause.)
TARIFF REFORMERS WHO ATTACKED INSURANCE.

Alluding to the Altrinchara election, the Chairman mentioned the fact that, in his expression of thanks, the Tory member included the Thrift Reform League. That organi=ation, however, did not preach Tariff Reform, but its speakers were engaged in denouncing the great insurance Act of the Liberal party. He predicted that Mr. Hamilton and the whole of the Tory party would come to regret their attitude towards that fine measure of social reform. They professed to be against compulsion, as far as insurance was concerned, but the very same people were advocating compulsory military service. The Insurance Act was going to save life, but these people were prepared to adopt compulsion to train people to kill and not to save.

div.head: DAY OF RECKONING.
div.p: THE DAY OF RECKONING.

A day of reckoning was in store for the Tory party, and he was certain that the time would come when we would wonder how we ever got on without an insur- ance scheme. The opponents of the Act had not a single suggestion to offer as to how it could be amended. The people best qualified to amend the measure were those who introduced it and carried it through the House of Commons. (Applause.) They had the promise of Mr. Anquith that an amending Bill should be introduced, and that whatever hardships were experienced would be rectified —not by the Tory party who would like to see the scheme banished entirely, but by the Liberals who desired it to be made as useful and efficient as possible. Applause.) As far as they in Warrington were con- cerned the first step towards carrying the full Liberal programme into effect was to change the representation of the borough. They intended to leave no stone unturned, so that after the next election Mr. Harold Smith would have plenty of time in which to carry on his business apart from Parliamentary duties—unless the Tory party found him a seat elsewhere. (Laughter.) (A Voice: "Close the public-houses on election day and it will be all right.") He (Mr. Jones) bad been seriously taken to task for suggesting that the Tory party benefited by the public-houses being kept open. Whether they benefited or not, he was certain that if the public-houses were closed the Liberal party would stand a better chance than they did at the present time. (Applause.)

div.head: MR. CROSFIELD'S SPEECH.
div.p: MR. CROSFIELD'S SPEECH.
The Struggle in. the Balkans.

Mr. A. H. CnosFinn,who was received with cheers, surveyed some of the momentous events which had happened since he last had the honour of addresiing an open-air meeting under the League's auspices. First in importance he placed the struggle in the Balkans, whic`a had resulted in the overthrow of Turkish power among the Christian populations of that part cf Europe. Thus a striking chapter in the history of humanity had been written. It was not the end of the story, but the curtain fell last week on a great act in a great and tragic drama. It had been bad enough in years gone by to read of the barbarity and the calculated agony which had been suffered by civilised white nations under a rule which a man in a very high position in the East had told him was, with two or three exceptions, five or six centuries behind the times. (Hear, hear.) But if they had heard, as he had, from men who had been able to study the inner working of things on the spot, if they had had from eye-witnesses accounts of the diabolical cruelty perpetrated in that part of the world they would feel more deeply thankful that, in the Balkans at any rate, humanity stood to suffer less. (Applause.) A VICTORY FOR THE CHRISTIAN POPULATIONS.

The Christian populations had achieved a victory that would have rejoiced the hearts of Bright and Gladstone if they had lived to see this day. (Applause.) He (Mr. Crosfield) did not wish to depreciate the Turk, who, as an individual, was grave, courteous and dignified. The responsibility lay with the system. with the mass of officials taking the hint from headquarters, and with the fury which unfortunately swept large sections of the Turkish nation when race hatred was excited and they were attacking the Giaour. In view of what had been accomplisbed vve ought not to be too ready to jihe at the smaller nationalities because of the differences which had divided them during the last few weeks. We had all seen the tension and the delicate situations that had arisen for years past between the larger Powers of Europe and it was a matter for thankfulness that, while men were fighting so strenuously against the more pitiless part of natural law in the world, they were recognising that it was the
