div.p: A t ,
STANDARD BEARER FOR LOCAL LIBERALISM.

sphere or capacity the Progressives of to-day played their part, they might be proud to follow that gifted band of leaders in the House of Commons, and they had every right, as politicians, to hold their heads high. (Loud applause.) They were working for as fine political causes as ever animated Englishmen at any stage of our history. A defection here or there was nothing, but the democracy of this country, if they were true to themselves, would steadily support the men who were fighting their battle. He would say to all who were banded together in that glorious com- mon cause that they might live prouder and, when the time came, die happier for their association with it. (Loud applause.) TORIES WHO WANTED A CONSTRUCTIVE POLICY.

The CHAIRMAN said be noticed that at a Tory Confer- ence at Widnes on Saturday, Alderman Bennett succeeded in carrying a resolution to ask the party leaders to adopt a constructive pAicy. Some of the delegates did not want to go quite so quickly as the alderman desired. (Laughter.) Liberals had no need for resolutions of that kind, for they had got a real constructive policy and the members of the Progressive Labour League were prepared to support the candida- ture of Mr. Crosfield because they believed he sub- scribed to every measure which found a place in their programme. (Applause.) WARRINGTON'S TEMPORARY LAPSE.

Mr. MASON, in the course of a homely and forceful addri se, said be could not help wondering whet on earth possessed the electors of Warrington to return Mr. Heroin Smith es their member in place of Mr. Crosfield. He (the speaker) never had the pleasure of meeting Mr. Crosfield before that night, but after bear- ing his fine speech, his wonderment was all the greater that Warrington should have elected Mr. Smith instead of such a sturdy supporter of progressive causes as Mr. Crosfield had proved himself to be. (Applause). He ventured to prophesy that, notwithstanding the boasts of their friend the easily, the verdict which Warrington gave at the last election would be reversed at the first opportunity and the town s‘ould again be honoured in laving Mr. Crosfleld as its representative. (Applause.)
(Continued from Page 7.)

div.head: WHY ALTRINCHASI WENT WRONG.
div.p: WHY ALTRINCHASI WENT WRONG.

Having expresseid amusement at the sporting proclivities of the local Tories' as evidenced by the placards in which they rejoiced at recent by-election results, Mr. Mason said he took part in the Altrincham contest and the reason why Mr. Hamilton was returned was because the Insurance Act was so grossly and scandalously misreprclented by the speakers who supported his candidature. (Hear, hear.) They succeeded in deceiving the electors for the time being, hut he believed they would give a very different decision at the next election. The Tories claimed that Home Rule was an Imperial question. He would therefore ask any opponent of that measure if he would be willing to submit it to the Empire as a whole for decision. If so, the overwhelming verdict of the Empire would be in favour of granting that measure of justice to Ireland. (Applause.) Everyone of our colonies had already stated, in emphatic language, that it considered it was the duty of the home government to grant a large measure of Home Rule to Ireland and thus bring about that good feeling between the sister isle and our own country which every sensible man desired. THE POST OFFICE DEPOSITORS.

The Insurance Act was the mcst beneficent piece of legislation ever placed cn the btatute Book. He felt confident that the men who were now misrepresenting the measure and doing all they could to defeat its successful administration would in the near future come to be heartily ashamed of their present action and speeches. The Insurance Act was not to blame for Vie Post Office depositors; it did not make them. Unfor- tunately, their physical condition or character was such that no approved sc 3iety would admit them to membership. Apart from that class, many of the present-day Post Otlic,3 deposit r 8 were wilful obstructors of the Act. They had become Post Office depositors because they were opposci to the measure and had taken the cue given to them by the leaders of the Opposition. Having shown that the Post Office depositor was in a better position now than before the passing of the Act, Mr. Mason said no one would argue that the Act wes absolutely perfect, but the parLy that placed it upon the Statute Book was the. party best qualified to am. I it as experience dictated (Applause.) It was necessary that the Act should be compulsory, for if a man had not sufficient foresight, when in work, to make provision for the time of sick- ness, it was due to the thrifty portion of the com- munity that he should be compelled to do so. (Applause.)

div.head: OUR FOREIGN TRADE.
div.p: OUR FOREIGN TRADE.

During the Altrincham contest the Tories made frantic efforts to place:Tariff Reform in the bsokground yet, strange to say, Mr. Hamilton claimed the result as is triumph for Tariff Reform. Comparing our trade with that of Germany, the speaker pointed out that from 1902 to 1910 Germany, with her population of 65,000,000, increased her over-sea trade of manufactured goods by £82,000,000. He rejoicel in that evidence of the increasing prosperity of Germany, for it would inevitably be refiEcted in greater trade with this country. However, in the same period England, with her population of 45,000,060, had increased her over- sea trade of manufactured goods by £108,000,000. (Loud applause). The Tariff Reformers were quit 3 wrong in claiming that they were on the flood tide of victory. A -set-back here and there would not mean the rout of the Progressive forces. As Sir John Simon put it, the loss of an outpost, the repelling of an attack, must be met by a general call to arms and an attack of the enemy's forces all along the line. (Applaint..) It was for the working-classes to strengthen the hands of those who were fighting their battle, and enable them to bring it ,to a glorious conclusion. (Loud applause.)

div.head: IRELAND'S GRIEVANCE.
div.p: IRELAND'S GRIEVANCE.

Mr. C. E. PARKER, in proposing a vote of thanks to the speakers, recalled tne fact that his grandfather stood by Peet when he was fighting for the abolition of the Corn Laws, and his father stood by Gladstone in his great work of sweeping away almost all the taxes. He (the speaker) was therefore glad to be able to take a small part in supporting those who had teen entrusted with the defence of Free Trade during the last ten years. (Applause.) Mr. Parker then referred to points in favour of Home Rule, which had k' impressed upon hin• during a recent visit to Ireland, end pointed out that the Irish people took little or no interest in projects which ought to concern them—Mr. Parker instanced the construction of a pier—simply because they recognL-d that the money came largely from sources over which they had no control. They were, therefore, inclined to treat jocularly free and easy methods of doing work which we in Engle nd,if we experienced their, would regard -1 a serious light. The whole (potion of local government was closely affected by that attitude. Unless they could interest the people in the money that was spent on the government of their country—whether on piers, railways, schools, or housing—there must necessarily be a waste of funds. The 1 )1145S erected in Ireland under recent slhemes were much needed ,and had proved of great value to the people, but many had been scampsd in their construction. the .consequence being that in some instances the plaster had fallen off the walls. That was an illustration of the need for giving the Irish people that c3ntrol of their own affairs which would assuredly mean a crest accession of interest. Referring to Mr. Crosffeld's speech, Mr. Parker said one characteristic of Mr. Crosfield which he always admired was that he took politics seriously and viewed the affairs of the country in a wide and comprehensive manner. He was also sympathetic and loyal to all the .aspirations of the democracy. (Applause.) The vote was passed with enthusiasm.

div.head: TEA DRINKING AND STOMACH TROUBLE.
div.p: TEA DRINKING AND STOMACH TROUBLE.

"Tea drinking tans the mucous lining of tl- etomach, making it thick and tough like leather," says an eminent authority, apd he is doubtless right. Hot water extracts from tea leaves a powerful astringent known as tannic acid. This tannic acid acts upon the stomach lining just as it acts upon 1eat1.../r, only in a lesser degree, but in the long run the result is the same—the stomach lining becomes thick, bard and loses its power to secrete the gastric juice on which digestion primarily depends. "Tannic acid, however," says this same authority, "may be neutral ised and robbed of all its harmful properties by taking half a teaspoonful of bisurated magnesia in a little hot or cold water after eating. Tea drinkers' indiges- tion and heartburn are 'due to the tannic acid in the

tea, and I personally recommend bisurated magnesia because it not only neutralises the acid immediately and stops all food fermentations, but it also possesses a quality rarely found in neutralising agents in that it cannot possibly upset the most delicate and sensitive stomach. In fact, bisurated magnesia—be sure to ask your chemist for the bisurated, as other kinds are lacking in these particular qualities—promotes healthy and normal digestion in a most astonishing manner by neutralising all acid in the stomach. Its regular use after meals as well as after drinking tea is a fine habit.
SIR STUART SAMUEL. ANOTHER ACTION DISMISSED.,

A second action brought by a common informer to recover the heavy penalties which Sir Stuart Samuel was said to have incurred by sitting and voting in the House of Commons after he had become disqualified came before Mr. Justice Scrutton in London on Wednesday. His Lordship held that in this case, as in the first, the action bad been brought under the wrong statute, and he gave judgment for the defendant, with costs.

div.head: MEETING AT ORFORD.
div.p: MEETING AT ORFORD.
MR. CROSFIELD ON CONSCRIPTION AND UNIONIST DISLOYALTY.

That Liberalism is making good headway in the Orford district was evident from the large attendance at the open. air meeting which was held on Orford Green, under the auspices of the Liberal Association, on Tuesday evening. Mr. A. H. Crosfield was again the principal speaker and had a very gratifying reception. Mr. P. H. Brown presided, and among others on the platform were: Councillor J. Kendall (Manchester), Councillor Peter Peacock (chairman of the Liberal Executive), and Mr. E. Wynne Jones (president of the Progressive Labour League).

div.head: LIBERALISM'S FORWARD POLICY.
div.p: LIBERALISM'S FORWARD POLICY.

The Chairman said Liberals had every reason to be proud of their policy. No Government of modern times had done more to appeal to the democracy than the present Administration, and their record of legislation showed their genuine concern for the masses of the people. Some of the inhabitants of Orford seemed to look upon Liberals as interlopers and to be quite willing to go on as they had done in the past. That, howpver, was a bad policy, as there should be no such thing as stagnation in politics. Liberalism stood for advancement, and he claimed that if the Govern- ment had done nothing but pass the Insurance Act they would have justified their return to power. (Applause.) Another great step in the interests of the democracy was the passing of the Parliament Act, which curbed the power of the House of Lords. In his opinion, that measure did not go far enough, but they had to be content with half a loaf. He hoped that when the Government came to deal with the House of Lords again, they would make it possible for contentious Liberal Bills to be passed in one session, just as Tory measures were. He was pleased to read that Mr. Crosfield had referred to a prospective extension of the Trades DOards Act to other industries, and he fully agreed that those workers who were weak and unorganised should have a minimum wage secured to them by Parliament. He hoped that at the next election Mr. Crostield would once more be the standard- ' bearer for Liberalism in Warrington, and that he would lead them to a great victory. (Applause.)

div.head: MR. CROSFIELD'S SPEECH.
div.p: MR. CROSFIELD'S SPEECH.
His Devotion to the Progressive Cause.

Mr. A. H. CROSFIELD, who was greeted with enthusiasm, said it Wcttl a pleasure to know that, in spite of the adverse political influence that was brought to bear from a neighbouring factory by an old friend of his, Orford had been waking up and Liberalism was making progress in that part of the constituency. (Hear, hear.) Referring to the hint of the Chairman, Mr. Crosfield continued: I have fought Warrington twice successfully and twice unsuccess- fully. Ido not know what the future has in store for us and it would be presumptuous on my Dart if,acting on the kindly remark your Chairman has just made, I was to make any assumption as to who will be chosen to be the standard-bearer next time. But I promise you this: That whether that honour falls to me or to somebody else, as long as I am able to take an active part iu politics, and as long as I see such splendid work for our beloved country as is being done at the present time, I am going to have a hand in the progressive fighting in Warring- ton. (Loud applause.) For political, patriotic and —may T add for family reasons?—(hear, hear)—l should aht ays consider it a privilege to take an active and, as far as health and strength allow, an effective part in Warrington progressive politics. (Applause.)

div.head: MONUMENTAL WORK
div.p: A MONUMENTAL WORK

Continuing, Mr. Crosfield said that the Chairman— one of the shrewdest brains in the Liberal party in Warrington—had pointed out bow the legislation of the present Government affected the lives and homes of the whole of the people ; and every good patriot might well value and feel proud ot the work which this wonderful Ministry had been privileged to carry out. (Applause.) Whether they lived in a centre of red-hot Radicalism or under the as2is of some Tory influences which they told him still existed in that pax t of Warrington, he sincerely believed that all progressive citizens should be thankful to have some share in accomplish- ing work which, in his opinion, was far greater iu its effect than the success of Dick, Tom or Harry in A, Bor C constituency. He felt, with the strongest conviction in his nature, that they were participating in movements which were writing one of the greatest chapters in the history of human evolution. Some of them who were getting on in years were fond of talking of the old times and recailing, from what they experienced in boyhood or from what their fathers hau told them, the events of those great and spacious political days of Bright, Cobden and Gladstone. (Loud applause.) Absorbed as they were in their great schemes of social reform in these days, it was well for them to remember what they owed to those fine and stalwart workers of the old days, who cleared the ground, laid the foundations and paved the way that modern Progressives were treading. (Applause.) Just as those great reformers of the past could not foresee the kind of constructive reform on which their successors of to-day would be engaged, so it was impossible for the present workers in the Liberal cause to foretell the limits of future developments. One thing, how- ever, was certain—that when the work of the last seven years and of the next half,i dozen years —(applatise)—in English history was viewed in its completeness, it would present such a record of social reform that their successors for many generations to come would point to it as a monumental achievement in the great structure of permanent, constructive statesmanship. (Loud applause.)
THE INSURANCE ACT AND ITS BENEFITS.

Touching upon some of the outstanding effects of the Insurance Act, Mr. Crosfield said that since it came into operation four months ago, 5:2,000,000 had been distributed in sick benefits, at the rate of 5:100,000 a week. (Applause.) It did not require a very vivid imagination to realise what that meant to the masses of the people. (Applause.) In addition, ,-2,500,000 had been distributed in maternity benefits - a fact which he would commend to the consideration of the women of Orford. Seven thousand victims of consumption had been taken by the hand, placed in sanatoria, and treated with the best scientific skill, the consequence being that many homes would be saved from the despair and heart-breaking sorrow which the white scourge too frequently left behind it. A reserve of z€:15,500,000, which the Government would increase to Y-20,000,000, had been built up in order to guarantee the continuity and perfect security of the benefits under the Act. (Applause.)

div.head: GRATITUDE TO MR. LLOYD GEORGE.
div.p: GRATITUDE TO MR. LLOYD GEORGE.

A striking and touching incident occurred when Mr. Crosfield was alluding to the comfort which the Old Age Pensions Act—that immortal triumph of Mr. Lloyd _leorge—had brought to 900,000 of our old folk. An old gentleman in the audience fervently exclaimed " God bless Lloyd George! " Mr. Crosfield said he had the plivilege of knowing the Chancellor personally, so be would perhaps take the opportunity of telling him that that was not the first remark of that kind which he had heard in Warrington. (Applause.) It must be an encoutagement to a man who was fight- ing so courageously and with such tireless industry to know that his work was appreciated by the rank and file of democracy. Mr. Lloyd George was one of the most wonderful statesmen we had ever had—a man of high aim, great vision and splendid courage, who was out for nothing less than the regr Jeratic i of the democracy. (Applause.) Of cc 1138, a sta'esman who laid himself out to fight such be tle 3as Mr. Lloyd Gorge had been fighting in the Efouso of Commons waq bound to excite a great deal of resiitment amongst privileged —and sometimes very selfish—classes, and therefore no-one valued more than he every indicAtion that the people did appreciate the great life work he was doing for them. (Applause.)
AN APPEAL TO THE MANHOOD OF WARRINGTON.

Having touched upon the benefits conferred upon the workers by the extension of the Workmen's Com- pensation Act, Mr. Crosfield appealed to the manhood of Warrington as to whether it was quite creditable to our old Roman town, with Its splendid record in industry and in other departments of life, that such historic, magnificent political work should be going on without Warrington playing its part in support of the men who were carrying it through? As to the reforms

gap.desc: skipped/gap: fewer than 20 non-control characters after cleanup

div.head: Examiner, Saturday, June 7, 1913.
div.p: The Examiner, Saturday, June 7, 1913.

of the future, they would soon be in the thick of a great Education measure—the lines of which had been broadly indicated by the Lord Chancellor—and they also knew pretty well the lines upon which land reform was going to be taken in hand. (Applause.) Then there was the projected further extension of the operations of the Trades Boards Act in the interests of those who were too weak and lacking in organisa- tion to do their own collective bargaining, and in this connection he would emphasise the fact that a decent minimum wage must be a condition of satisfactory housing reform. (Applause.) Another matter, which was not really a party question, was the international movement that was gaining ground in favour of the introduction in all continuous industries of the eight hours' shift, in place of the twelve hours' shift. -He was thankful to say that that movement was receiving support not only from Progressives—Liberals Labour men and Socialists—but from enlightened donserva- tives who realised the value of a reform which would help to civilise the conditions of industry. They did not want men to be unfairly treated by excessive and impossible speeding up, any more than they wanted the other extreme of a useless ca' canny " slacking" of work. Whpt they were aiming at was fair, brisk, alert work wi.thin reasonable hours, so that a man could take a pleasure and a pride in his job and finish up fresh and ready to avail himself of the oppottunities which modern civilisation offered of leading a rational .and civilised life. (Applause.) PROTEST AGAINST EXTREME MILITARISM. Mr. Crosfield went on to empha.ise the inter- national, as distinct from the purely industrial aspect of the movement, pointing out that Le had seen Frenchmen, German and representatives of many nationalities sitting side by side and co-operating in the work. Did they not think, he continued, that international co-operation on those lines, promoting international concord, was better than any efforts that might be made abroad— and he was sorry to say they had seen some of them in Warrington—to promote international animosity or to stir up the fires of extreme militarism ? (Applause.) In contrast to the magnificent record of Liberal wc7k to which he had alluded, it was interesting to consider what the Opposition had to offer. (Laughter.)

, remember the McCann and Castledawson affairs. We don't want him in our loyal city. We chased Churchill, the rat, like a Redshank, and we will chase him, too. Let him stay away. We want neither him nor King George to visit our city. We can do without them both. As for the gutter Radical Press of Great Britain, we despise them. The coming 12th will tell the tale, so beware.— Yours &c., LOYALIST (100-1914). P.S —As you will see, I have placed the King's head downwards. It will convey to your mind an imperfect idea of what we really think of him. L. Mr. Harold Smith is going to Belfast. Are we to understand he is going to support " Loyalist " ? That letter is the consequence of the example and the evil instigation of responsible leaders of the party who call themselves ultra-Loyalists. I have given you a sample of the performances of the Opposition ; and I have tried to give you some picture of the work to which, in these strenuous days, Liberals and Pro- gressives, of all ranks in the great army, are devoting themselves. I leave it with confidence to the judgment of my fellow-townsmen to choose between them. (Loud applause.)

div.head: TARIFF REFORM AND TOMMY ROT,
div.p: TARIFF REFORM AND TOMMY ROT,

Of course, there was their 'old friend Tariff Reform. (Laughter.) He would remind the audience that T R. stood not only for Tariff Reform, but for "tornmy rot "—(laughter)—and he thought anyone would be hard put to it to find, in the whole course of English political history, any such example of " tommy rot " as they had had in the last ten years, since Mr. Chamberlain began by driving out the best men of his party from the Cabinet. It was said of the French Revolution th At it ate its own children. Well, he thought they might certainly say that Tariff Reform had shown an extreme faculty for polishing off its own leaders. (Laughter and applause.) The first batch that went included Mr. Ritchie, Lord George Hamilton, Mr. Goschen and Lord Balfour of Burleigh—some very influential names in the Tory party. (Hear, hear.) But the next man to leave the Cabinet held a name even more weighty and, if possible, incl.° respected by all Englishmen, without respect of party,-he referred to the old Duke of Devonshire. (Applause.) Then he did not know whether he could say that Mr. Balfour was polished off, but at any rate he gave up the leadership of the party and they then thought they had at last got a man who would give them the pure milk of the word. (Laughter.) However, Mr. Bonar Law had not been at the head of affairs very long before he turned his back upon himself—(laughter)— and stuffed the food taxes up his sleeve—(laughter)— where they were trying to keep them at present. Thus had the Tory party rung the changes in this amazing political farce. The great high priest of Protection, Mr. Joseph Chamberlain, had told his party—and he (Mr. Crosfield) heard him say it in the House of Commons—that if they wanted Imperial Preference they must put a tax on food. The Tories still claimed that Imperial Preference was the first constructive plank in their platform, bat they were going to have it without food taxes—although not only Mr. Chamberlain but Colonial statesmen and the Colonial Press had tald them that they could not.

Really (added Mr. Crosfield), when you lcolt into the stuff they talk and the rottenness of their ratiocination, all I can say is : Goto " Alice in Wonderland "for a parallel. It is the only place where you will find it. (Laughter.) When I think of their gyrations and contortion., their twistings and turnings, I VII reminded of some sinuous half-back who comes to Warrington and tries to work his tvay through our good forwards. You know he won't get very far—and that in the end they will pretty wll.l smother him. (Laughter.) At three successive elections the Tories have had a very unpleasant dose of it, fighting for their Protection which they will never get. (Applause.) Lancashire may trifle at a by-election here or there, but when it comes to the main issue we will be there when the bell rings and we intend to see to it that Protection never gas a footing in this country. (Applause.)

div.head: TRIFLING WITH CONSCRIPTION.
div.p: TRIFLING WITH CONSCRIPTION.

Having had such a bad time with Protection, one would have thought that the Tories would have learnt a little caution, but, on the contrary, they are now trifling with conscription. Between now and the end of this year we shall have the whole case against conscription thrashed out on our plat- forins. We are having none of it—(applause)----and I was truly glad, knowing as I do that such proposals will not hold water from any point of view, that the Chief Whip came down to Manchester the other ddy and said that the whole massed forces of the Liberal party—yes, and we have got the massed forces of the Labour party with us on that question, too—would offer an unflinching opposition to that short-sighted dangerous and unnecessary policy fJr old England (Applause.) PREACHING SEDITION AND DISLOY

The last psrformance of the Opposition to which I would draw your attention is the way in which ,these people who once called themselves the party of law and order have actually—some of them deliberately— incited those extreme fanatical Orangemen that you have to deal with in a small section of 'lreland, till you get them indulging in ruffianly hooliganism, in. the barbarous ill-treatment of their brother workingmen, and in talk which is nothing less than open unblushing sedition. The party which used to lay such stress on its loyalty ha e gone the length of uttering the most scandalously disloyal sentiments that we have ever read in our time. Only this morning there appeared in the " Manchester Guardian " a letter from one of these misguided fanatics. I don't blame him half* as much as I blame the ~•apable men who have misued their talents in order to lead these men on to their sedition and dis- graceful behaviour. You hear the present leader of the Opposition daring to tell these fanatics in the North-East corner of Ireland that there is hardly any- thing they could do that he would not support. ("Shame.") Imagine that from the man who hopes sume day to lead the country in the House of Commons! Is it any wonder that you hear many of the more reputable section of the Tory party declaring nowadays that they are getting sick of politics, or that you see men like Mr. Balfour and Mr. Austen Chamber- lain severely holding aloof from work of that kind? Still the leader of the Opposition, Sir Edward Carson—and I presume Mr. Elarold Smith—are indulg- ing in this incendiary talk, and now we see whatt;it leads to. Here is a letter addressed to the "Manchester Guardian " by a man who styles himself" Loyalist."

div.head: COMING OF ABERDEEN.
div.p: THE COMING OF ABERDEEN.

Sir,—As you axe doubtless aware, a lot of time- serving traitors in the Belfast Corporation have had the boundless audacity to actually invite Lord Aberdeen to our loyal and Protestant city to open the new abattoir. Now, sir,this is a thing we will not stand, and if we are compelled to it we will let tile world see that the opposition of Ulster is not a sham but a dread reality. The sword of Damocles hangs over the heads of this wretched Government, and unless they change their tactics it will soon fall on their accursed heads. As for the present Royal Family, to tell the truth, we loyalists of Ulster have very little respect for them. And we have no right. The mother of our present Sovereign, Alexandra, was a supporter of the vile separatist policy of the late Mr. Gladstone. And lam afraid we must place King George and his wife in the same category. Let me tell his Majesty here plainly that we are fully determined to fight for our blood-purchased rights. We will not have Home Rule. If we are driven to it we will let his Majesty see what we will do. If he signs his name to this accursed Bill it. will be fatal for him and his family. Our sainted forefathers had to call in a William, 6efore to def end their- rights. We, their sons, may have to call in another William to defend us from a faithless King and venal, time-serving, opera- bouffe Parliament. As for Aberdeen, we will blow the abattoir up some night rather than let him desecrate it by his presence. We have no confidence in him. We should we? We

div.head: MENTAL DEFICIENCY BILL.
div.p: THE MENTAL DEFICIENCY BILL.

Councillor J. KENDALL delivered a telling address He pointed out that the verdict of Altrincham was that the Liberal Government was worth 250 more votes to- day than it was two and a half years ago. Referring to the attitude of the Tory Party with regard to the Insurance Act, be characterised it as one of the most bhameful pieces of political chicanery tbe world had ever seen. The policy of regard for humani life and health ran though the whole gamut of Liberal legislation and in this connection the speaker dwelt upon the Old Age Pensions Act, the Children's Act, and the Insurance Act. A question had been handed up, asking how the Slental Deficiency Bill—which the Tories had promised should not be a contested measure—would affect the attendants employed at the Winwick Asylum. Councillor Kendall replied that it would not affect them at all adversely. The only effect of the Bill was that if a man served his time as an attendant, the institutions of that kind would be multiplied as a result of the Bill, and his chances of earning a livelihood would be much more certain in the future than they had been in the past. In conclusion, Councillor Kendall said that any workingman who was true to himself and his family would cast in his lot with the progressive forces which were ever seeking to improve the conditions of the workers.

div.head: "UNMITIGATED BLUFF."
div.p: "UNMITIGATED BLUFF."

Mr. E. WYN'NE JONES said the threatened trouble in Ulster was nothing but unmitigated bluff. If there was any fighting to 134 done, they could take it for granted that the Harold Smiths, the F. E. Smiths, and the "King " Carsons would be very far from the fighting line. (Liugbter.) They would rather march to the law courts, with brief bags in their hands, than march to Cork or anywhere else. (Laughter.) A vote of thanks to the speakers concluded a success- ful meeting.

div.head: CROSFIELD FAMILY'S GIFT.
div.p: CROSFIELD FAMILY'S GIFT.
Bust of the Late Mr. John Crosfield for the Town Hall.

div.head: MR. CROSFIELD AND THE COUNCIL.
div.p: MR. CROSFIELD AND THE COUNCIL.
Before beginning the usual business at the meeting of the Warrington Town Council on Tuesday evening, the Mayor read the following letter from Mr. A. H. Crosfield
39, Hyde Park Gate, S.W., May 28th, 1913.

Dear Dr. Joseph,— I have just heard from Alderman Tinnion that you stconthd a resolution which he brought forward at the meeting of the General Purposes Committee of the Town Council on the 20th in regard to the placing of a bust of my late father in the Town Hall, and which was carried unanimously. Mrs. Crosfield, senior, is at present on the Continent, and we do not expect her back in England for some little time, but as soon as I can get in touch with her I know she will appreci- ate as deeply as I appreciate myself your courtesy and kindness in supporting the proposition, and seconding it at the meeting, and may I beg of you to kindly convey to the members of the Council, on behalf of both Mrs. Crosfield and myself, our sincere appreciation of the way in which they have so kindly, and without dis- tinction of party, signified t.teem for the memory of my dear father? He was, of course, a keen party man in his day, but he loved the dear old town, and loved it well, and I know you will agree with me that he sought to serve it in many ways wholly without regard to any party distinctions. It is just for that very reason that we respect and deeply appreciate the unanimity of this kindly and valued tribute to his memory. I daresay you know that in the first instance all Mrs. Crosfield thought of was a bust for the Memorial Hall. It was only then that some of our friends in Warrington remonstrated and said that if a posthumous bust was to be prepared there ought to be one in the Town Hall. Again thanking your Worship and the members of the Council very warmly, believe me, dear Dr. Joseph, Very sincerely yours, A. H. CROSFIELD.

div.head: ROUND THE WORLD IN TWO HOURS.
div.p: ROUND THE WORLD IN TWO HOURS.
Celebrated Film that comes to Warrington Next Week.

A picture which is believed to have reached the acme of perfection as an auxiliary educational force will begin a seven days' run at the Picturedrome on Monday evening. It bears the ambitious title "Round the world in two hours," and the fact that the Liverpool and Southport educational authorities gave facilities for their children to witness the show and that they were highly gratißed with the results spaks
MR. RICHARD SAKEII, who will describe the scenes and events.

for the manner in which i the picture substantiates itH claims. The journey, in imagination, aided by the picture and the expert services of Mr. Richard Saker as lecturer, begins and ends at the Picturedome dc 3r, proceeding by way of Sankey-street, the Central Station, going round the globe and home again by Bank Quay Station. The intervening stages include Queenstown, New York, and the sights of America and the Atlantic, Panama, the Pacific, New Zealand and the East (Asia and Europe). Africa, London and Crewe Special arrangements are being made in respect of the schools.
TERRA NOVA'S HOME-COMING.
The Lord Mayor of Cardiff on 1 hursday received a telegraph from Commander Evans announcing that the Terra Nova,the ship of the Scott South Pole expedition was due to reach Cardiff on June 13th.

LYMM Boys' SCHOOL.—The vacancy of ssistan master at the Lymm C.E. Boys' School, created by Mr. Pate's severing his connection with that institution,has been filled this week by Mr. Frederick Arthur Mayor, late master of Much Woolton C.E. Boys' School, Liverpool. Mr. Mayor should be a decidediacquisition to the local school, tle is an exceptionally clever draughts- man, having won the South Kensington bronze medal for design, besides gaining several book prizes and certificates. GRAMMAR SCHOOL SCHOLARSHIPS.—The result .of the recent competitive examinations for scholarships tenable at the Lymm Grammar School for four years has been announced as follows :—From Oughtriogton C.E. School, Grace Timperley ; from Lymm C.E. Schools, Rupert Allan Oddie. Miss Timperley is the daughter of Mr. W. Timperley, stationmaster at Heatley ; whilst Master Oddie, ii the younger son of Mr. R. Oddie, the popular headmaster of the Lymm Boys' School. We congratulate both scholars on their success. BROOM EDGE PRIMITIVE MFTIIODISTS.—The birth- day celebrations of the Broom Edge Primitive Methodist Sunday School were observed on Sunday. Owing to the unfortunate indisposition of the appointed preacher, Mr. G. L. Welford,the services were conducted by Mr. Schofield, of Manchester, who d slivered stirring sermons at both the morning and evening services. At the former service he impressed his hearers with the importance of attending to the smaller things of life, afternoon while at night he spoke about Antipas, the martyr. In the afternoon a children's service was held, at which Mr. J. D. B. Smith gave a most suitable address. Mrs. J. H. H. Warham contributed a solo, and recitations were supplied by Mrs. Lawson and Messrs. A. Appleton and J. Perrin. WILLIAM HILL.—The funeral of the late Mr. William Hill, whose sudden death came as a painful surprise to the local inhabitants, took place at the Lymm Parish Church on Tuesday afternoon. As the cortege left the deceased gentleman's house on Lymm Bridge one noted that most of the tradesmen in, the village had drawn their blinds as a last token of respect for one who was looked upon as a most just and upright man. The Rev. G. B. Thurston was the officiating clergyman. The chief mourners were the Widow, Mr. Frederick Hill (brother) and his wife, Mr. William Whitelegg (brother-in-law), and the Misses Sarah and Tilley Whitelegg (nieces). Other friends who attended to show their sympathy were Messrs. Alfred Guest. T. Knowles, James Weeks,and Councillor Lockyer. The Tradesmen's Association was represented by Mr. W. E. Hillier (presi- dent). Councillor Gotobed, and Messrs. J. Beswick. H. S. Brown, S. Hinde, H. Kemp, C. Richards, A. B. Richardson, F, Warburton and F. Wilson. Floral tributes were sent by the following The Widow, Mr. and Mrs. F. Hill, Mr. and sirs. W. Whitelegg, Mr. and Mrs. Weeks, Mrs. Hammond (Fara- worth), Councillor Lockyer, Mr. and Mrs. R. Kemp, Lymm Tradesmen's Association, Mr. ann Mrs. Fred A. Morris, Master Joe Morris, Mr. and Mrs. Neese and Mr. George Clark. WEDDING AT OUGHTRINGTON.—St. Peter's Church, Oughtrineton, was the scene of a very pretty wedding on Tuesday morning, the bridal pair being Mr. Horace Finninglev Oxley and Miss Olive Smith, daughter of Mr. and "Mrs. 0. G. Smith, of "Fox How," Lymm. Owing to the recent death of the bridegroom's mother it had been decided that the wedding should be of a quiet nature, but the popularity of the happy couple caused a large number of friends to assemble at the eacred edifice. The bride, who was charmingly attired in an ivory satin dress, with wreath of orange blossom and veil,was given away by her father. The bridesmaid was Miss Oxley, whilst the bridegroom's brother per- formed the duties of best man. The Rev. J. Edwards- Evans, M.A.. of Ring way, late headmaster of the Lymm Grammar School, was the officiating clergyman. A special feature of the service, which was fully choral, was the singing of a hymn written for the occasion by Mrs. I'. J. Itidgway,with a musical setting composed by the bride's father. Mr. Jack Smith presided at the organ. A small party were entertained to breakfast at "Fox How," after which Mr. and Mrs. Horace F. Oxley left for Scotland, where the honeymoon is to be spent. On their return they will reside at Higher-lane, Lymm. Needless to say, the newly-married couple were the recipients of both a numerous and choice selection of presents. WESLEYAN ANNIVERSARY.—On Sunday the Lymm Wesleyan Sunday school successfully commemorated its 108th anniversary,the attendar se being satisfactory, whilst the collections exceeded last year's total. The special preacher was the Rev. Thomas Gladding, of Macclesfield(formerly of the Warrington Circuit),whose discourses at the morning and evening services were greatly appreciated ; his subject at the latter service being " Conversion " (Acts 111., 19). In the after- noon Mr. Gladding presided over a young people's service, at which he gave an interesting address on" How children should be like arrows," i.e., well balanced, sharpened, and directed. At this service recitations 'were given by Gladys Leigh, " The finger family" ; Florence Gitsham, "The Healer" ; and Leslie Brown," Suppose." Solos were contributed by Edna Jones, "I love to hear my Saviour's voice; and Bertha Leigh, "Jesus wants me for a sunbeam," the latter item appropriately followinglithe primary song "Merry Sunbeams." The effective arrangement of the programme was further shown by the combination of the primary song "Ring bells, ring," and the scholars' hymn "Joy bells." Throughout the day the primary department, under the care of Miss Rogerson, took a prominent part in the services. Other soloists during the day were Cissie Wright, " Saviour, teach me day by day " ; May Winstanley, "If I had lived when Jesus did" ; and Esther Soanes, "Rock of Ages." Mr. H. S. Brown played the organ with his usual efficiency. YOUNG MEN'S CLUB.—With the purpose of augment- ing the funds of the recently formed Lymm Sunday School Young Men's Club a concert was given in the Primitive Methodist Schoolroom on Wednesday night. There was a very fair attendance to enjoy the mis- cellaneous programme provided. Miss Florence Gavins was a pleasing soprano, her enunciation of the follow- ing songs beiug excellent, "It I built a world for you," " The Rosary," "0 Flower of all the world," "Nobody else," and "The Carnival." Other vocalists were Mr. John Moss, solo "The Sailor's Grave; Mr. J. Ellis, solo" On the Banks of Allan Water " ; Messrs. J. H. Brazendale and E. Waterwortb, duet " Watch- man, what of the night ?" ; Messrs. Brazendale, Champ, Moss, and Waterworth, quartette" Two Roses 's and the Lymm Male Voice Glee Society, "Com- rade's Song of Hope," "My love is like the red, red, rose," and "Farewell." Miss Armstrong proved to be a popular elocutionist with her pieces "Miss Edith helps things along," and "The high tide," her dramatic deseription of the latter being very good, Miss Hinde contributed some clever whistling solos and Messrs Andrews and Champ a violin and 'cello duet. The most striking feature of the programme was the masterly violin playing of Mr. Andrews, whose delight- ful performance of "II Trovatore " was vociferously applauded, his encores and selection from "Poet and Peasant" being further musical treats. The duties of accompanists were skilfully discharged by Mrs. Walker and Mr. F. Champ.

WESLEY Glmn.—The monthly devotional meeting was held in the schoolroom on Welnesday evening when there was a good attendance. The address was given by Mr. F. Wright, of Padgate, the subject being " The nature songs of the Psalmist." Mr. Wright dealt very ably and helpfully with the wonderfully way in which God is depicted in Nature and so admirably expressed in the language of the Psalmist. In the absence of Mr. Lawton, the meeting was presided over by Mr. Warburton.

div.head: "I REMEMBER-
div.p: "I REMEMBER-
REMINISCENCES AND STORIES OF OLD WARRINGTON.
GLEANED FROM MANY QUARTERS. Thought It Was Something Worse.

I remember a good story—and a true one too—which was told about the Lion Hotel. The child of one of the proprietors made a pet of a little pig which used to follow him into the kitchen and run about the premises after the fashion of a dog. This was quite amusing whilst the creature was small, but as it grew and fattened its presence on the hearth sometimes gave a shock to strangers. It is told that a commercial traveller who was staying at the hotel, and who had been indulging over-much the night before, came down rather unsteadily to order a glass, which was to serve as a pick-me-up. He entered the guests' parlour and settled down to await the coming of the liquor. It happened that the pig had settled down in the parlour before him, and, as the waiter arrived, it jumped up with a snort. The apparition was too much for the traveller, who bolted excitedly through the doors and into Bridge-street. He thought it was an attack of the delirium trem ens.

Knutsford Road Sixty Years Ago. I was brought to Warrington as a child in 1851, and as some of my early,7years were spent in Latchford I will attempt a descrip- tion of Knutsford-road as I first remember it.

The first large building on the left hand was Waterloo factory, which stood on the river bank and was entered at a point now marked by Water-street. This has quite disappeared. Next was a timber yard under the shadow of the factory and two houses. The old large building which still stands in partial ruin was known as Latchford Cotton Mill. It had a date stone A.D. 1805. Then came the site of St. James' Church. The building had been demolished, though the new one on the Causeway was not yet begun. A high wall hid the graveyard from the road, but there was a centre doorway over which was placed a granite tablet inscribed with gilt letters to the effect that "Here the gospel was preached by a succes- sion of faithful men."

I cannot recollect the exact wording, but as it remained there until about 25 years ago many of your readers will recall it. There was also inscribed the text "Except a grain of wheat fall into the ground and die, it abideth alone; but if it die, it bringeth forth much fruit," probably a reference to the bodies which were buried there. Immediately on the other side of the grave- yard was another mill known as Latchford Old Cotton Mill. This has disappeared. I have heard it said that this was the first mill to be driven by a steam engine. Another timber yard and then the Golden Lion Inn. Yet another timber yard, and next the Pin factory. At that time not only pins but tools and files were made there. There was a long open space which extended to Preston Place. This last-named consisted of six or eight houses. Then came another long open space, and beyond it two small houses, known as Lime Kiln Houses, stood nearly opposite to the Vicarage. These with their pink-washed fronts can still be seen. There was nothing else on the left-hand

side. Coming back to the Bridge and travelling along the right side the buildings extended to a point about opposite the Golden Lion. As they mostly remain I need not describe them. The first street on the right was School-street, taking its name, I suppose, from St. James' Infant School, which had been built at the corner. _ _

Next was Sparling-street, and the next Prince's-street. Off Prince's-street was a small street of about eight or ten houses,called Green Doors and at the end was a public pump. It is now Fountain-street, but then it was a quiet and rather nice little pocket street. lam supposing that the place took its name from the houses having been decorated in green, but this is only a guess. There was no building until Mersey House was reached. This was a square house which stood back from the road and had a large garden. Adjoining it was Wellington Place, where a dozen houses had been built. After two open fie:ds was the Vicarage, or, as it was then called, the Parsonage. The building still stands quite smothered amid modern buildings and hidden by the Co-operative Stores. Then it had a fine garden and grounds and had a leisurely and dignified look. Of course, it had not then been blackened in soot. Mersey View, which adjoins it, had just been built. There were perhaps twenty-fly e houses, and they were regarded as quite in the country. A number of working folk who went to live in them were regarded as rather adventurous people to live so far" out," and so remote from the comforts of civilisation. Thereiwas not anything else, I think,except the Smithy and Black Bear Inn, but these remain with us yet and need not be described.
GROUP NEAR THE STOCK

Members of the Sunday School Union visited Grappenball last Siturday afternoon, and enjoyed a survey of the church and village, under the leadership of Mr. A. Mounfield. His lecture on the village and its antiquities will have wide itAcrest, and we Lerewith present verbatim.

- Tea was served in the Independent Methodist Chapel, and at 6 30 Rev. J. S. Chedburn presided over a public meeting. In an opening address, Mr. Chedburn took oppor- tunity to desci ibe his experience of Boys' Brigades and Girls' Guilds as a branch of Church activity. Such organisations, he said, provided interests suited to the needs of young people at a certain stage of life. Their boys and girls were not held by Bible classes; some- thing more was needed, and it must be their study to discover something. There was no greater peril in the life of the young than that they should have nothing to do. His own experience had been that the Church had come to have a larger p7ace in the affections of the youths and maidens where Eomething had been designed to provide an outlet for their energies. He stated that three companies of Boys'
SUNDAY SCHOOL UNION SUMMER MEETING.
Photograph by Burrell. :S, GRAPPENHALL CHURCH.

Bligades had been formed in the neighbourhood. Miss Crosbie (of Liverpool) gave an address on "My Ideal Sunday School Teacher," which was full of good points. She asserted that the teacher was, after all, the chief factor in Sunday school life ; that whatever the building or equipment, the thing that mattered most was the teacher. The ideal teacher would be a present teacher a punctual teacher, a prepared teacher. Under these heads Miss Crcsbie put in a plea for diligence in attendance, for scruputius punctuality and for careful preparation. The second part of the address was devoted to the activities of a teacher between Sundays. The work done upon week-daya was declared to be of more importance than the teaching given on Sundays. Emphasis was laid upon visiting as the best means of gaining contact and influence, and of securing the full interest of the scholars. The address closed with an eloquent statement of the claims of Sunday school work.
A conversatiln followed, and Miss Crosbie was heartily thanked for her address.

div.head: AGAINST CONSCRIPTION.
div.p: AGAINST CONSCRIPTION.

ASSOCIATION FOR VOLUNTARY SERVICE. An influential committee of a non-party character has been formed to defend the principle of voluntary military service. Colonel Brcmley Davenport, vrho was Financial Secretary to the War Office in Mr. Balfour's administration, is general chairman, and the objects of the organisation are to preserve the privilege of undertaking military service voluntarily, to promote voluntary training in preparation for national defence, and the moral and physical training of the boys and girls of the kingdom, and to spread information E howl ng the vital importance of our naval supremacy and the moral superiority of voluntary service.

substance of it :—For some time an important issue had been discussed, and the terms of agreement were practically settled, when an inexperienced labour representative, a man of wild, unbalanced zeal, lost restraint of himself and poured out a long vituperative harangue of the kind with which we are all familiar, growing more and more violent as he worked himself up to his climax. Then, at a well- selected moment, the chairman of the employers quietly held out his hand, and asked for one moment's interval. The speaker stopped, and turning to the other chairman the first said, "It has just this moment occurred to me that in the terms of settlement we have made we forgot to mention so and so." The subject was perfectly trivial, but the men's chairman,with tact bred also of much experi- ence, took it up and turned it this way and that, and so for five minutes a small thing, absolutely of no importance, was debated with calmness and solemnity. Then the chairman turned again to the speaker, apologised for having found himself obliged to interrupt, and requested him to continue. But the fire had gone out, the excitement had subsided, and the fire-eater, after a lame attempt to mend the broken string of eloquence, subsided into silence.
The Examiner, Saturday, June 7, 1913.

div.head: GRAPPENHALL AND ITS CHURCH.
div.p: GRAPPENHALL AND ITS CHURCH.
A Picture of Latchford aftcr the Conquest.
"TWO FREEMEN, TWO SE RFS, ONE VILLEIN AND THREE BORDARS. "

div.head: Lecture at Grappenhall to the Sunday School Union.
div.p: Lecture at Grappenhall to the Sunday School Union.
BY MR ARTH

The first mention of Grappenhall (or Gropenhale, to use the ancient name) is in the famous Domesday Book. By the order of William the Conqueror, after the conquest, the country was placed under survey, and his commissioners were to put on record the names of those who held the land in the days of Ed ward the Confessor, the extent and nature of the areas, how many mills and fishponds, how much the land was worth in Edward's time, and how much after the upheaval of the Conquest. This is bow Grappenhall is reported upon : Osborn (Fitz Tezzon) holds Gropenhale and Edward of him, He and Dot, both freemen, held it as two manors. There ;s one hide and half a virgat of land ratable to the gelt. The land is two carucateS, one and a half of which are demesne; and there are two serfs and one villein and three borders. There is a wood one league long and forty perches broad. There are two hays. Its value in King Edward's time was five shillings (a year) it is now worth six shillings. When it came to the Earl of Chester it was waste.
The information is slight, but it is interest- ing. The areas we call Latchford, Latchford Without and Grappenhall are held in Saxon

div.head: R MOUNFIELD.
div.p: R MOUNFIELD.

Hugh de Boydell is given the right to levy a toll upon those using the fords of the river. The date of this falls in the early part of the reign of Richard I. possibly about A.D. 1190. So long has Latchford had its name. In 1250, as an act of homage to the Church William le Boydell. by a charter gives " acquittance " to the Abbot and Monks. He confirms to God and the Blessed Mary that "the said Abbot and Monks for ever shall pass through my vill of Latchford with all things belonging to them without any- thing being required for the said passage. And for this grant and quit-claim neither I nor my heirs shall ask anything except their prayers and supplications." In a later charter dated 1308 Sir John Boydell gives to the hermit friars of War- rington, the members of the religious house at Bridge Foot, "a free pasgage through the vill of Latchford' for their wain, by ',ghat namo soever they may be called, so that every priest brother of the colvent celebrate mass on the dty of my
anniyer.ary." This he does " for the health of my

days by two men named Edward and Dot. The sword and fire of the Conquest devastate Cheshire, and Hugh Lupus as Earl of Chester divides the county among his followers. "It was waste," says the record;and under that pitiful word lie materials for the most tragic volume that could be written, a story of brave and simple men de6troyed, their houses and crops burned and plundered. England changed hands amid pillage and blood and the smoke of ruin filled the land- scape.
WHEN LATCHFORD AND GRAPPEN- HALL HAD FIFTY INHABITANTS.

The change that took place at Grappenhall was typical. Edward and Dot the two Saxons are put in charge under the new owner. To cultivate the 2,400 acres they have two serfs, one villein, and three bordars Allowing that all may have had families, the population of Latchford and Grappenhall will scarcely reach fifty. In the wood three miles long they may hunt the deer, the free- men taking the venison, the serfs and bordars eating the umbles or remnants in the form of "urnble pie." Beyond a guess that they lived the simple life, and a confident statement that Latchford Without was not famous for villa architecture we cannot say much about the home life of Edward and Dot. Did time drag heavily we wonder when there were no drainage schemes to discuss,no Local Government Board inquiries to keep the rustic mind from stagnation, and not even the excitement of reading placards about foot and mouth disease?

Possibly we can picture Grappenhall with the pigs that feed upon the acorns in its forest and the serfs and villein who tend them. But of Edward and Dot we hear no more. They come and go in that one sentence in the Domesday Book. THE NEW OWNER.

But we must take notice of the new owner to whom the Conqueror gave the land, because he was the ancestor of the Boydells and the Middlehursts, and his children's names fill many a musty charter. Osbern Fitz Tezzon, the Norman, was a man of some note. Possibly he saw little of Grappenhall and Latchford, for he held also Lymm, Warburton, Appleton, Hanley, Gresford and some other places. What is more important, he held, under Hugh Lupus, the Castle of Dodleston, a very exacting post on the Welsh border. _ _ _

Osbern left Grappenhall to his son Hugh Fitz Osbern, who in turn had a son named Osbern Fitz Hugh. This Osbern the third had a son named Helto, who called himself Helto de Boydell. Thus came in the name of Boydell, which was destined to be associated with the village for centuries. THE FIRST MENTION OF LATCHFORD. Helto's son was named Hugh de Boydell, and I propose to drag him into my lecture because it is in one of his documents that the name Latchford first appears. Here it is : "Randle, Earl of Chester, sendeth greeting, &c. Be it known to you that I have granted to Hugh de Boyden, the way in Latchford, with the passage of the water of Mersey, between Runcorn and Thelwall, and that no wain of two horses shall pass the said way and passage except by the allowance of the said Hugh and his heirs." Which probably means in plain terms
body and the safety of my soul."
GRAPPENHALL AS A FEUDAL PRESERVE.

These charters give us the only glimpses we have of Grappenhall when it was a pre- serve of its feudal lord. The exchanging of privileges for prayers and masses by written 6 greement was quite characteristic of the period. Sir John will allow the monks to pass along his roads and through his "viii of Latchford "without paying the toll which is exacted from everybody else; but they must covenant in solemn charter to celebrate an annual mass for him on his anniversary day. The feudal lords held the land, but the Church was careful to get what hold it could upon the lords. Other writings of the ancient Boydells have come down to us, and they contain many things that arrest and half-amuse the modern reader. There are for instance grave charters written in Latin which allow the landholders' pigs, for a consideration, to eat the acorns which falls from my lord's oaks. Such a document, dated 1270, is in the name of William Boydell, whose effigy reposes in the Church, and this William, it may be noted, advanced the fortunes of his house by marrying Alice, a daughter of Hugh de Dutton.

The visitor may see the spot where the Boydells lived. On the high ground at Reddish Hall they were "monarchs of all they surveyed." The old house has gone, but the moat which surrounded it remains. THE CHURCH.

Now a few words about the church. We do not know by whose fostering a church first arose at Grappenhall. It is hardly likely that there was a place of prayer here at the time of the conquest. The Domesday Book with its mention of a church at Lymm suggests that Lymm would be the religious centre of the Osbern territory. . _ _
But there is little doubt tliat a church was built at the beginning of the 12th century, and of this structure one interesting portion remains.

The foundations which were uncovered forty years ago show it to have been a small building. It would have round-headed Norman windows and possibly a porch. Happily for our interest a scrap of the old building is left. When rebuilding took place in the 16th century, instead of demolishing the south wall, as they did the north, it was pierced and arches placed within it. The upper portion was therefore left and with it the corbel table and gurgoyles of the Norman Church. These quaint faces carved by the early builders have looked down on the worshipper for about eight centuries. Formerly upon the outer wall of the church, they are now sheltered by the roof of the south aisle and are seen from within. THE ANCIENT FONT.

Another relic of the first church is the ' Norman font. This was rescued from oblivion forty years ago. Rejected in favour of a new one in the 16th century it was found buried beneath the church floor. Many fine old fonts came to grief at the hands of restorers during sleepy periods of our history
(Continued in next column.)

div.head: LITERARY GLEANINGS
div.p: LITERARY GLEANINGS
A MIRACLE IN THE EAST.

"If anything could be more startling," says Mr. H. N. Brailsford in the "Contemporary Review," "than the rapidity with which the Balkan League destroyed the Turkish Empire in Europe, it would be the ease with which the Western peoples have adjusted them- selves to the miracle. There has been no larger territorial 3hange, no bigger historical event in Europe since the resurrection of Italy, and even that change was in some respects less momentous. "But the really significant transformation is that the whole population of this broad region has acquired between last autumn and this spring a new mind and a new morality. For the first time in six centuries the forbidden chimes will ring in the belfries of the church. For the first time since the Ottoman conquest, a man will reckon quite certainly on reaping what he sows. The wayfaring peasant will question no longer whether the man who approaches down the highway carries a rovolver and a knife. Christian women will walk unescorted in the border towns, and peasants dare to build their cottages on the hillside and out on the plain, far beyond the crowded safety of the huddled village."

div.head: ONE DAY IN SEVEN.
div.p: ONE DAY IN SEVEN.

" A striking revelation of the seriousness with which the workers of the country regard the weekly rest-day was provided at the annual meeting of the Imperial Sunday Alliance," says the "Christian World." " The speeches of the representatives of the workers were intensely interesting. An electrical worker said he had worked seven days a week for sixteen years. A sewage worker had had twelve Sundays off in twelve years. We don't want to become machines,' he said, pathetically. ' Some of us are only young men.' A Jewish tailor supported the Alliance in what he said was really a fight for the Jewish Sabbath as well as for the Christian Sunday. "But perhaps the meeting was most touched by Mr. Charles Coborn, the famous old music-hall singer, who finished a breezy little speech by saying, Because we sing frivolous things you must not think we don't think seriously. We would not like to lose our Sunday, a day to rest and to thank God for the bread and butter we have had during the week.'" MR. DOOLEY WANTS TO KNOW WHERE MAN IS GOING 'lO.
What ar-re ye readin '? ' asked Mr. Hennessy," according to the "London Budget."

"'A comical little piece in th' Sunday pa-aper on th' Descent iv Man,' said Mr. Dooley. 'Ye get a good dale iv knowledge out iv th' pa-apers whin ye're not lookin' f'r it, an' a fellow that's paid a penny to find out where Christahel Pankhurst spint her vaca- tion, if he doesn't stop there but goes on r-readin,' is li'ble to end up as an idjacated man.

" Maybe ye'd like me to read somethin' out iv this here fable in slang. Well, thin, listen to th' profissor : " Such habits not o'ny tended to develop the motor cortex itsilf," he says, " but thrained th' tactile an' th' kin—th' kin—l'll spell it f'r ye—k-i-n- -a-e-s-t-h-e-t-i-c—pronounce anny way ye plaze—senses an' linked up their cortical areas in bonds iv more intimate assocyations with th' visyool cortex— ' " " What kind iv a language is that?' Mr. Hennessy interrupted.

"'lt's scientific language,' said Mr. Dooley. I've been thryin' to wurruk it out mesilf with th' aid iv a ditchnry, but I cudden't put it together till Dock O'Leary, who's great at these puzzle pitchers, come in. Fr'm what he said I guess that th' pro-fissor that wrote it meant to say that th' raison man is betther thin th' other animals is because iv what's in his head. I suspicted as much befure an' have often said so.

" ' Mind ye, I don't blame this doe. fr thryin' to make us all—th' Dooleys, an' th' Honezollerns,an' th' Vere de Veres—mimbers iv th' same fam'ly. His name is Smith. But if he'd frgit about th' origin iv th' race an tell us not where man conies fr'm but where he's going to I'd take an intherpter aroun' an' listen to him.'"

and they are constantly being rescued from base uses. Many of them have served as pig troughs. It is a gratifying thing that in the Tudor period there were throughout England minds sufficiently astute to perceive that a good large font would make an admir- able feeding trough. I say it is a gratifying thing because events have proved that the fonts were safer with the pigs than with the humans.

Many fine Saxon and Norman fonts have been restored to their original use after being for centuries in the safe custody of the pigs; this one after serving as font for four and a half centuries was buried under ground as being ugly and out of date. Placed upon its new pedestal it is now one of the treasures of the Church.

Before leaving it let me describe it. In measurement it is two feet seven inches long, two feet wide, and one and a half feet deep. It is of local red stone and decorated with Norman arches of rather rude workmanship. There are one or two traces of history upon it which are too interesting to miss. In 1236, the Archbishop of Canterbury required that all fonts should be covered and locked. At a later time, possibly at the Reformation, the cover has been removed. The marks of the staples and the injury done in wrenching it away can be seen in the stone, though the broken portions have been restored.

div.head: PARISH CHEST.
div.p: THE PARISH CHEST.

Another relic of the Norman Church rests in the Warrington Museum. This is the Parish Chest and is about as crude as a chest can well he. It consists of a portion of the trunk of a tree about seven feet long, a slab forming the lid. A cavity cut in the tree about two feet long would, hold, perhaps, the altar vessels, but little more. It is a hollow log,chopped smooth by an axe, and,as a piece of church furniture is almost unique. (To be continued.)

div.head: JUNE BIRTHDAYS.
div.p: JUNE BIRTHDAYS.

With the King's Birthday on the 3rd of June and the Prince of Wales's on the 23rd, nobody need be ashamed of the month as a birthday month, I think. The King is now 48, and the Prince of Wales will be nineteen when his natal day arrives. I will mention three oTher famous men who were born in June, a great preacher, a great engineer, and a beloved writer.

The preacher, who was born in June, was a little boy who appeared at Epworth Rectory in Lincolnshire on June 17th, 1703. His name was John Wesley. Ten years ago Methodists from every quarter assembled at Epworth to celebrate the 200th anniversary of the day that gave John Wesley to the world. And well they might, for his influence quite changed the current of English life and history. Another man who was born in June changed the land in quite another way, and indeed has changed every civilised land. lam referring to George Stephenson, the maker of the locomotive and pioneer of railways. George was born in 1781 on the 9th of June. He was a poor man's son and went to work when quite a lad. He worked as an engine man in the village of Killing- worth near Newcastle, and I daresay you have read of how he used to spend his Satur- day afternoons in taking the engines to pieces and putting them together again. He had a real love for machinery and lived to make the first railway engine and construct the first railway.

If you ever travel through Darlington don't forget to look at his first engine. It is placed on a pedestal inside the railway station. It looks very crude alongside the fine engines that pull us to-day, but this awkward- looking piece of machinery is one of the most important relics in the world, and its inventor is one of the most important of our national heroes.

The writer I propose to mention is Charles Kingsley, who was born at Holme Vicarage, Dartmoor, June 12th, 1819. I shall not need to say much about Kingsley. Every boy- feels that the man who could write " West- ward Ho" must have been a dear fellow. So he was. He was much beloved by all who knew him and will not soon be forgotten.

div.head: ROMAN FORTS FOR GERMAN
div.p: ROMAN FORTS FOR GERMAN
SCHOOLBOYS.

The Berlin correspondent of the "Times" reports something interesting from Mainz. The Emperor William has arranged for the erection of two Roman fortresses in order thac schoolboys may have brought before them in the most real way the operations and methods of the Romans. It is said that the Emperor is himself giving supervision to the work, and to make it as real as possible the work is being done by Roman tools. This is what the writer says : "The work is done with tools, made at the Emperor's order, after the Roman pattern,' a two-edged kind of hoe, or military spade, held together with rivets instead of nails, axes, pickaxes, and billhooks. One ' fort ' is already finished. The other is to be about 50 metres on each of its four sides, and will be surrounded with a ditch and with a wall which is made of earth and staves driven in upright into the ground by a wooden hammer of the ancient pattern, and bound together with wattle."
What a happy and easy way of learning about the Romans! And how nice to see those forts after they are finished.

div.head: NAMES OF THE MONTHS.
div.p: THE NAMES OF THE MONTHS.

"I know just why the months were natned," Said little Johnny Sea. He stood straight up with folded arms, And rapidly spoke he: " The first of all from Janus comes, Because this Roman god Ruled over all beginnings With his head-shake and his nod, "And Febus, Roman festival, Our February bore, And March, of wind ar.d windy ways, From Mars, the god of war. "Sweet, dripping month of April, With its bursting leaf and bud, From the Latin word to open— Open flower and bud. "A certain fair divinity, Called Maia, don't you know, Was worshipped on our May day By the Romans long ago. "And June, with blushing roses, And its tender glowing skies, From June, Queen of Heaven, Her of the smiling eyes. " July from Julius, becaut e Of Cmsar's natal day, And August from Augustus For the luck it brought his way. " September and October In the Roman Calendar Were the seventh month and the eighth month, Septem and Octo, hear. "And November and December," Said little Johnny Sea, "Were the ninth month and the tenth month— And that is all." gasped ha. —Louise I?. Baker.

div.head: WEEKLY SMILE.
div.p: THE WEEKLY SMILE.

Mr. Roosevelt likes a good story, and he can tell an amusing one. He recently told a story of a man who was always very careful of his things. One day he exhibited a hand- some umbrella. "Its wonderful how I make things last," he exclaimed. "Look at this umbrella now. I bought it eleven years ago. Since then I have had it re-covered twice. I had new ribs put in it last year, and last month I exchanged it for a new one in a restaurant, and here it is after eleven years as good as new."
