div.head: COMPLETE ' EXAMINER ' STORY.
div.p: COMPLETE ' EXAMINER ' STORY.
(ALL RIGHTS RESERVED.)
RAMERTON'S CHOICE.
BY OSWALD WILDRIDGE
author of "Margery Manestv," "Paul Mus- grave," "A Disappointing 'Relation," "The Outcast," &c.

Again and again, as the train from Over- :he-Sands makes its zigzag round of the Bay, Mr. Harold Hamerton, barrister-at-law, ex- tracts a letter from his wallet, and reads :herein the message which the hand of Mary Bradley has sent him. "It is all mystery and darkness "—this is what she had written—" but I'm full of con- idence ; you will see that all will turn out right in the end. I never knew dad act so iueerly before; but, then, he has no one else nut me, and he doesn't know you, and I'm :yertain that as soon as he sees you every atom of his doubt will vanish. I suppose it is no use you writing to him again, and so you must slip away to the dale as soon as those horrid law-courts will spare you; once lad learns what manner of man you are he'll give you all the trust you can desire." Hamerton shakes his head gloomily as he re- stores the letter to his pocket. "I'd like to be- lieve my task was going to be as easy as that, he thinks, as he again mentally reviews the situation; "but fathers can be very stubborn when they set themselves, and I fancy that this is going to be a case of very special pleading. It is rank mystery from beginning to end. Her father and I have never met; probably until a month ago he had never even heard my name. My position in the world, so far as I can see, is more than equal to his own; no man can level a finger at me, and yet—when I ask him for his daughter he makes a flat refusal, won't even discuss the matter with me. nut dismisses it as an absolute impossibility." And, after this, he recalls Richard Brad- ley's further refusal of an interview, and the singular condition with which his surrender on this point has been accompanied—that Mary shall not be informed of her lover's visit to her home; and, finally' he turns his thoughts to the girl herself and the pleasant surprise he is hoping to spring upon her, and he is still engaged in this fashion when the train deposits him at the station marked upon the map as Dalefoot. Here, this side of the Lake Country being an unknown land to him, he makes certain inquiries, and then crosses the sidings to the tiny terminus dignified as the headquarters of the Dales express, and in one of the toy carriages of the toy train is by-and-bye trundled away through the gorge which forms the gateway to the mountain lands. And, away in his home of solitude, Richard Brad- ley awaits his coming with terror and wrath seething madly in his heart. Though livinc, the life of the dale, breath- ing its atmosphere, Bradley was not a dales- man; nor in the real activities of the fellside had he any part or lot. Indeed, in the inter- vals of the daily round that were not devoted to sheep and cattle, the people of the hamlets would occasionally discuss the man and his manners, and invariably they summed him up as "a gey queerish mak"—a man whose peculiarities might not be fathomed nor weighed. Two years ago he had slipped quietly into the dale from the outer world of busy men in busy towns, and had settled with his daugh- ter in the solitary house which stands between the Black Tarn and the Green. To the girl the dalesfolk had at once opened their doors and their hearts, for she was a winsome lassie, unspoilt by any make-believe airs and affectations, natural, responsive; and when she tripped lightly down the winding path- ways to the plains the people who dwelt therein realised that, somehow, a glint of sunshine had come to them from the dun heights of the brooding fells. Richard Bradley, however, rarely came among them. All his rambling was done in the lonely haunts of the mountain sheep, and when the shepherds met him he had rarely a word for them in response to their greeting, but only a nod of his grey head—and some- times not even that. "An ill-favoured carl," the shepherds were wont to pronounce him, and were glad when they spied him in the distance and were able to avoid a meeting. And yet not one of them could lay a single flagrant offence to his charge. He was not a religious man, but no one had ever found him guilty of open impiety; his past was without a flaw, for anything they knew to the contrary; his aloofness was his outstanding characteristic; *above and beyond everything else, he was a man who desired to be alone. From the ban pronounced against his fellow-mortals he made one exception. In all these other people of the hills and plains he manifested no interest ; but hie daughter seemed to fill and make complete the round of his life. He made few demands 91 com- fort or of luxury for himself; but where she was concerned, his desires were beyond satisfying. For her he had turned that old house on the fells into a dwelling fit for a • queen, and in its furnishing he had shew n himself a man of artistic taste and judgment ; pictures and books had all been selected for he-: joy, dresses the daintiest that London could supply, and when her schoolgirl friends came from the far-away towns of the south to spend their holidays on the fellside they declared her to be the luckiest girl in the land. On this matter of visiting, Richard Bradley • had attempted, when lie settled in the dale, to establish a rule that was decidedly one- sided; while Mary might receive her friends in her own home, she was not to be permitted to visit them in theirs. It was a foolish ex- pectation on which his rule was based, one that took no account of those other fathers and mothers, nor of the force of English cus- tom, and it broke down in its second year, when he found that Mary was threatened with a measure of isolation almost as com- plete as that which he himself was content to court.

And now he was to pay for his surrender. This was one of his burdens of reflection while he gazed over his garden-hedge at the far-away train as it wriggled along the twist- ing, snakelike track, bearing Hamerton into the kingdom. of the dales. Mary's last round of visits had proved a journey of romance; she had met Harold Hamerton and given him her heart; and now he, Richard Brad- ley, was doomed to pay. It was hard enough that he should have his treasure wrested from his keeping, but, now that the mills had begun their grinding, the penalty of discovery must be added to the burden of loss, and, to the uttermest farthing and the last drop of blood, the debt must be paid. And the price must be his own soul-agony and his daughter's broken heart.

While the train was yet in the jaws of the dale, Richard Bradley went round to the stables with an order for the governess-car, When it stopped at the bandbox station at the Green, he helped his daughter into the car and despatched her upon an unimportant errand to Dalehead. As he turned to go back into the house Mary was moved to pity by the greyness which had overspread his gaunt face so very often in these later days, by the droop of his shoulders., and the weary shuffle of his gait. Ever since he returned from his travels and took her from the school he had been an old man; 'but now a load of years seemed to have been suddenly thrust upon him. Surprise would have been added to pity if she had seen how, when he entered his room, he drew the curtain slightly so as to dim the already sombre light, and how he took his seat as far back among the shadows as possible, and remained there with craven heart and trembling limbs, listening for the click of the gate and the tread of feet upon the gravel path. He offered no word of greeting when Hamerton was admitted to his presence, but curtly bade him be seated, and then suggested a speedy ending to the interview. "I have already given you my answer to your pro- posal, Mr. Hamerton," he added; "your visit can serve no purpose. and the sooner it

Is ended the pleasanter for both of us." "You have given me your answer, it is true," Hamerton replied, "but you have shewn me no reason for it. I claim to be an honourable man. my career is full of hone: even now 1 can oner your aauguter ali that you yourself are giving her; my character"— the man in the shadows winced, but the movement passed witnout, notice—" my char. seer will stand any test you care to apply to it, and I claim that for your refusal of my suit I am entitled to some account." "You will receive no account. I never explain." "Not even when your daughter's happiness is at stake "

"Man "—here Richard Bradley breaks into passionate protest—" who are you to come here with your law-court manners, hec- toring and lecturing? My daughter's happi- ness is the only aim that I have had since she was born. It filled my thoughts and made my dreams for years and years before she ever heard the whisper of your name. And I'll never explain. If I did, my words wouldn't mr.he your way easier, they wouldn't make my girl your wife; they would part you—ay, part you tar more completely than my own rejection of your demand. Go back to your life in the city and the courts, make your name and your fame, but leave Mary Bradley to the simple lic-3 that I have chosen for her here among these hills." "As if that will content her," Han-ierton scornfully replies; and then he begs again for explanation, only to be once more re- pulsed with a blank negative. And after this he ceases to be the lover pleading for his bride, and becomes the man of law, the shrewd, keen-witted counsel, sifting a case of baffling mystery, plying this man, whose face he has but dimly seen, with questions, some of which have lancet - points and double blades, and some have no apparent point at all ; but every one is directed with subtle skill to the exposure of the secret which has been interposed between his sweetheart and himself.

At first Bradley makes some show of fence, but suddenly it dawns upon him that this man, who has come to the dale as a lover, is now giving play to his professional skill, that he himself is being treated merely as a wit- ness under cross-examination, and the dis- covery chills anew with fear and firmly seals his lips, so that he sits there silent as the Sphinx. Still, in spite of all his precaution, he is in the toils of a stronger intellect than his own ; and wrath is feeding upon fear, and at last hatred and anger force him to his feet, and he orders his tormentor from the house.

" I'll not be played with any longer," he cries. "Away with you back to your own life, and be glad that I've refused you. I'm not hard and cruel and senseless. It's a kindness I'm doing; for if you marry Mary Bradley, the day may come when you willl curse the hour of your meeting." " Is love such a very flimsy thine." "Yes—the love such aa you would give her. I've no faith in it. The only love strong enough to stand my test is the love of fatherhood—that is equal to anything, it will dare anything, and bear anything. Your love would run if it heard a whisper of the truth." "Try me." "How?"

" By telling me the truth." " Gad ! I've a good mind to. I'd get rid of you, then. But "—his voice sinks to a whisper, and he points again to the door— "there's my girl to think of. I'll never tell— and you must go." Here he is smitten by the fear that he may have said too much, and he falls into further confusion. Thanks his visitor for the honour of his proposal, tells him he is glad that Mary Bradley has won the love of a good man, and wishes that lie could listen with favour to his suit. He regrets, however, more than 114 can tell, that there is an insuperable barrier to their marriage—Hamerton would be the first to admit this, if explanation were pos- sible—and, therefore, he must beg of him to end an interview which is painful to both of them, and has already lasted too long. And ever, while the old man is rambling thus, memory is reminding Harold Hamerton of a tale he had almost forgotten,, adding link to link and coil to coil. Suspicion of ghastly form uprears itself, and now he too begins to to with dread and look fear in the face. All the time the other is speaking he is -thinking, thinking, turning over a heap of forgotten facts, eagerly watching this other man's manners and noting his tricks of speech and style, and at last he resolves to put suspicion to the proof, and to this end he cuts into Bradley's protestations with the utterance of a name: "Michael Bradshaw ! "

At this moment Harnerton has almost for- gotten Mary Bradley. For a few dramatic seconds he is the man of law, intent on the prosecution of his case, and when Bradley, with a gasp of dismay, sinks back in his chair and makes no effort at defence, a touch of exultation thrills him, just as though he had passed through the maze of a prolonged cross-examination to the triumphant exposure of convicting proof. "Murder will out, Mr. Richard Bradley— or Mr. Michael Bradshaw—whichever name you prefer," he says at length. "Eight years is a pretty long time to keep one case in mind amongst so many, and I'd almost forgotten yours, but now I think I've got the points pieced together. You were indicted in the name of Michael Bradshaw, weren't you? And your offence was forgery. I had a stiff tussle to secure a conviction, but I managed it in the end, and, unless I'm very much mis- taken, you were sent into penal servitude for seven years. That, I take it, is the period that Mr. Richard Bradley is represented to have spent travelling in foreign lands. Per- haps—"

here the world seems to jerk and then spin round, taking from his presence this broken man with the grey hairs and the tainted past, and bringing within his ken a girl with trust- ing hazel eyes and wavy brown hair; one who holds his own joy in her keeping, and has vowed that she will never give her love to any other than himself . . . and she is a convict's daughter . • , and he has asked her to be his wife.

The world jerks and spins again, and now the old man has returned and is standing before him, pouring out a wild stream of •words, partly confession, and partly a pitiful plea for mercy. "I was mad at the time . . . and I did it for her. . . . I didn't want the money myself, and the other man was rolling in riches, and so I forged his name. . . . I couldn't bear the thought of my Mary ever feeling the sting of poverty, and I did it to make her safe. . . . So far my shame has never touched her—the double name and the shortness of the public memory and the solitude of this dale have been an all-sufficient guard, and now— " She was only a child when it happened. She was told that I'd been called away— abroad—on business—and her aunt sent her to a school until I—was liberated; then I brought her up here—did it with money that my brother had left me while I was prison— brought her here into this land of solitude where the people are few and not much given to talk. And I fancied that I might keep her all to myself, and no man ever learn of the blot that I'd put upon her name. And now— it seems like a tale out of a book—you—the man who did more than any other to fasten my guilt upon me—have fallen in love with my lassie, and now you have her at your mercy. I don't count—it is she who will 'suffer if you speak. What are you going to do?" A silence deep as that which rests upon the hills settles on the room, but Hammerton has not yet made his choice, and Bradley gives to his appeal a new turn. "Your love-story is ended now. The chil- dren must suffer for the sins of the fathers. You can't wed the daughter of a convict—and if ever she learnt the truth Mary would marry neither you nor any other man—it would be a life of horror to you, of degradation, of re- proach, of brutal impossibility. . . . But your love is not dead yet, and in the name of that love I beg you to shield my lassie. Don't let her know that her father bears the brand of the felon, that the name she bears is covered with shame."
Again he returns to his chair and cowers in

div.head: Examiner, Saturday, June 7, 1913.
div.p: The Examiner, Saturday, June 7, 1913.

is depths, veiling nis lace oeninu his halms. Hamerton, however, gives him no attention. It is no concern of his that this man is a con- vict, but it is everything to him that he has given his love to a convict's daughter. Again and again he reviles the scurvy trick that fate has played him; again and again he tries to edge away from the dominating fact in this hideous exposure; tries to argue that black may be white, and dross the purest of gold, but always he is driven back upon this—that ne is naroiu namerton, barrister-at-law, and that Mary Bradley is the daughter of a convict. A strange spectacle they make, these two men. The father, crouching in his chair, the Lover sitting bolt upright and well forward, his hand malting a rest ior hi 3 cheek, his eyes resolutely fixed upon the narrow strip of win- dow-pane. All the lines of his face, though he knows it not, have grown very hard, and moisture is standing in heavy beads upon his brow. From the moment of revelation his heart also has been steadily hardening, for he has allowed self-pity to fill it, and has cast out that compassion and mercy which ought to have ruled. He sees clearly that if he marries Mary Bradley he must share her father's shame, sees that through all his days he may have to bear the stigma of the broad arrow and the stripe. One by. one an ugly array of hateful circumstances parades before him ; he beholds even his mother and his sisters touched with this man's infamy ; looks again and sees the finger of scorn outstretched by people who themselves are steeped in mean- ness, and finally thinks of the d -•,y when he may stand up in his place in the court of assize only to find that men are sneering at him for his own living contact with crime. Indeed, this new thought strikes with deadly power; they are almost bound to sneer him out of his profession [lnd cast him among the flotsam of the human sea.

Thus and thus does he deal with the crisis into which he has been thrust, and all the time the man in the chair watches him with hungry eyes and awaits his verdict. Ever and again love cries to him for mercy, but he stops his ears; love looks him in the face— love is a maid with hazel eyes and wavy brown hair—but he makes himself blind ; he is determined to think of none but self. And all the time his heart grows harder, and when he rises self has conquered. "I'll leave you now," he says, speaking in n harsh, strained voice. • "I'm glad I came. This discovery—afterwards—would have been frightful. . . . I'm sorry for you—your crime has only been half punished yet. Still, you have deserved yours, and I have done nothing to merit mine. . . . Good-bye-----we shall not meet again." "Never again? Thank Heaven for that.. You don't blame me for the course I - have taken?"

"No ; I thank you for it. You have dealt honestly by me. Honesty may be terribly cruel, but its end is often kind." " And you will shield my lassie from shame? " " Your secret is as safe as though you had not spoken. . . . I—l will not see her again if I can—avoid a meeting. . . . Broken heart 3 may be healed, but shame cannot be wiped . . . I will write to her. . . . Good-bye." A clicking of the door declares that Harold Hamerton has left the room. The convict drops upon his knees and wrestles in an agony of prayer that his child may be strengthened against the blow. "Let me bear it all—all," he cries, "for the sin is mine."

Like a man in the toils of a hideous night- mare Hamerton passes through* the garden, beloved by Mary Bradley as one of the fairest spots on earth, and pauses at the gate. Far away beneath him lies the dale outspread from the foot of Great Howe to the dunes on the fringe of the sea • overhead the sun is shining with unspeakable glory, but for him the heavens are black and the world an arid desert. He has made his choice—and love is dead. He opens the gate—there is the grind of wheels and the pad of hoofs on the fellsidc way. He steps out into the road, a light car whips round the bend, and at that moment he is granted a vision of hazel eyes and wavy brown hair, and the honestest face in the whole world—a vision of a maid who believes that his love and his loyalty are not for a day but for all the days and all the years—a maid who calls his name vs-iih tell-tale •joy, and then runs to his side with fear because of his hag- gard face and his sorrow-laden eyes. And then the nightmare ends, he takes her in his arms, and the dale again becomes a place of bewitching beauty, and the sun re- gains its light. " No, dearest, I'm not ill, only tired," he tells her—" very, very tired. . . . I've been engaged on the greatest case of my life lately, and—and I very nearly lost it. But now—l don't mind anything so long as I have you, little girl. . . . I'm willing to face anything so long as I have you—and nu going back to your father to tell him so.
[THE END.]

div.head: HERKOMER AND TENNYSON. ---- A Strange First MeetinT.
div.p: HERKOMER AND TENNYSON. ---- A Strange First MeetinT.

Sir Hubtrt von Horkomer has bean telling some interesting things about his early struggles. He worked at the decorations of the So ith Kensington Museum for ninepence an hour and tags how he got away from a common painter's job by sending a sketch of some gipsies to the "Graphic." He began portrait painting in 1881, and when dis- cussing this branch of his art told bow he sNent to paint Lord Tennyson, from whom he obtained a sitting only after much trouble. " Getting to the station rather late, I left my things at the station, not knowing what sort of reception I might g( t. After I had been teceived by Mr. Hallam Telinys9n, the present Lord Tennyson, old Tennyson came shuffling in—he had a shuffling way of walking becausl he was very near-sighted and shook hands with me. I hate your coming,' he said; 'I cannot abide sitting.' That did not seem very promising. However, after we had conversed for some time he said: Where are your things ? ' I explained, and thereupon he got up, rang the bell, and told a servant to fetch my luggage. You had better put up here,' he said. I felt I was getting on. At eleven o'clock I went to my room, still wondering whether I should succeed in my mission or not. Shortly afterwards there came a rap at the door, and I said: Come in. I turned round, and saw Tennyson standing at the door. He said : I btlieve you tire honest. Good- night,' and thereupon departed. It was his way of making amends for the rather dubious way in which he had first met rue."

div.head: WOMEN'S QUESTIONS.
div.p: WOMEN'S QUESTIONS.
A Triumph of Organisation and Endurance.
THE KING AND THE CORSETS.

Letters to the newspapers air( ady foreshadow the usual yearly discussion as to whether it is best or not for Lusbands and wives to spend their summer holiday separattly. This plan is recommended because it affords (lie wife a welcome rest from hcusehold cares and family worries, and enables husband and wife each to choose the particular kind of holiday they enjoy most Such ideas do not (1 course appeal to people with eld-f ishioned pr-clivities, but a new movement The Week End for Wives Guild has been started in Loudon to pr, mote holday changes fi.,r women. Ile professional or business man often sei ds forward his bag, and g es (if himself for a week-end outing. Why should not the wife do the same? The answer is that there is no particular reason, if means and family circumstances permit. Accordirg to the promoters of this feminine wr ek-end movement., it would arable the husband left at home bet t- r to realise and understand the worries and responsibilities of housekeeping, and :fiord the wife a respite from the monoton, us routine of home-life. One is inclined to tlink that the Guild's sphere of us, fiances has its limitations, but it is certainly the fact that there is a very general impression that women are less entitled to holidays than men, although they have none of the little daily chanEes and cacitiments which fall to the husband in going to and fro to his woik or place of business.

div.head: AN_ AMERIC kN WOMAN EXPLORER.
div.p: AN_ AMERIC kN WOMAN EXPLORER.

M:s.. Fanny Workman, an Anrrican, who was the only woman in the recent exploration of the Rose Glacier in the Himalayas, adv, cates this work as a career for wimen. She, in company with her husband, a glaciological expert, camped for six weeks at an altitude of 17,000 feet ; climbed to a height of 23,000 ler t, and explored an unknown country of 900 miles. She undertakes the financinv, organising and all the details of the expeditions she accompanies. The work is similar to that of Polar exploration, as above 11,000 fer t all earching has to be done on ice and snow. The col I is intense, and the south-west mor soon may be compared to an Antarctic blizzard. The difficulty of breathing is great in these high altitudes, yet Mrs. Workman persevered in her determination to reach the top of the Nun Kun Teak, and in addition to her other occupations took her time in the geographical work of mapping the hitherto unknown d:strict. The work of organisa ion alone was a triumph fora woman, and the results of the expedition are a testimony of Mrs. Workman's skill and ccurage. THE WORK OF THE BLIND.

Basket work to-day offers possibilities never dreamt of years ago. Any sisitor to the old-establ:shed depot f the Blind Association in Tottenham Court-road, London, will be abtonished at the number, not only of btrong and servicealde articles displa3ed, but at the ingenuity and skill that have devised such a quantity of pi etty and really artistic objects in almost every colour. The quaintest of tea cosiea,with pixels of a check like pattern, and folding sereers that would seem impossible iti straw are quite desirable possession. The latter have the most whimsical frames, set off with tufts of gay colours most cunningly woven. Mats of every description made chicfly tf half-irctl ribbon straw, in two contrasting colours, such as yellow and green or red and blue, interlaced to form a zig-zag pattern, still sell well at bazaars and sea-side resorts, although they hare been made up for many years. Rough bass in conjunction with skilled embroideries, in silk, chenille and beads, form the most charming Watteau baskets, and are filled with roses formed of silk, cotton or glittering tinsel. Baskets suitable for the river and ccuntry, as well as the pretty trifles for toil( t and other uses, are endless in novelty and useful as they are beautiful, THE LINGERIE BLOUSE.

The quite plain lingerie blbuse is one of the favourite styles of the hour, and nothing could be more suitable for wearing during a spll of hot weather with tailored skirts. Only the firmest and finest lawn is used for the better makes of this blouse, so fine , indeed, that it is almost tear sparent. The cut, too, is irreproachable, and the trimming some light lace, pre- fer bly Valenciennes. The buttons give a touch of individuality. One model has barrel shaped buttons, which instead of being fastened to the Meuse, were suspended on a thick thread about an itch below the hole. There is usually a yoke at the back, and a little fulness below in front which is slightly pouched over the belt. For the oi en blouse, which many people like to fill in, and yet not be obliged to wear an inset of a special make, the new camisole of embroidery and net is an idea that should be welcomed. The net forms the upper part, and may be decorated with soft ribbons arranged as frills, or with lace and tucks. The emlTeidery Irma the lower part of this useful little parole Lt. TUNICS AND SASIIES.

Tunics are deservedly as popular as ever. In cliiftor a plain and p.inted, and in lace, of which the variety is infinite, they are indispensable in the reno- vation of last year's frocks, whether attached to the gown or separated from it. In shape they are equally varied, and whilst some are simply straight all round, others are short in front and fall nearly to the hew behind. The sash or girdle is at the moment an important item of the toilette. The former usually swathes the waist, disappearing eomewhere in that region under draperies, and then emerging on the left side is seen falling to within ten or twelve inches to the hem of the skirt, where it is finished with a hand- acme fringe. THE CORSET OF TO-DAY.

Styles change with ti e passing hour and the dray ries if this season demand a difference in the line of the corset. Years ago one shape remained in fashion for years, but nowadays every few months a modification of style becomes necessary. Often the difference is so slight it is not noticeable to the uninitiated eye, but it is there all the same. It is said that after George T. had danced at his first Court Ball in Loud na he e nnmented on the hard bones of the feminine portion of Lis new subjects. It was explained to him that English women wore heavily-boned vice-like corsets bud that these accounted for his quite natural conclusion. But all that is changed now. The high model with its " hard bones" has disappeared with the wasp-waist and the far more hygienic, natural, and comf rtable shape, hard'y two inches above the waist litre, has taken its place leaving the upper part of the body quite free. Some of the new shapes; slip over the head, and are then drawn in to the figure. All have very few bones and have their length below the waist. The materials used are very supple and elastic, an open mesh being favoured, as is also webbing.

div.head: Well Dear, what News?
div.p: Well Dear, what News?

'Nothing very particular Mother; Baby's got a tooth, and Marjorie has bought a new hat—and, oh she sends the recipe you asked for." "Oh yes dear, I quite forgot to tell you of the lovely Chocolate Cream and Trifle which Marjorie made when I was there last week." Shall I read the recipe Mother? It seems awfully good, and so easy."

Marjorie's recipe to maize Chocolate Cream: Take Milk, 11 pints, Sugar, 15 lumps, and 1 packet (from a 4,1 or ”d. box) of Chocolate Flavour 1311Z1Y5 13LANC-MANGE POWDER, With 3 table-spoonfuls of milk well mix the powder in a basin into a thin smooth paste. Boil the rest of the milk with 250z5.. or 15 lumps of sugar. and whilst still thoroughly boiling pour all at once into the basin. stirring well. When cold serve from a glass dish. For a delicious Chocolate Trifle take 4 sponge cakes, a little milk or sherry, sonic Ratafia biscuits and jam. Split the sponge cakes, spreading with jam, and join again cut in half longways and lay the pieces in a glass dish, soaking with either milk or sherry. Prepare the Chocolate Cream with Bird's Blanc-mange Powder as above, and when half cold pour very gently over the sponge cakes. Garnish the top with some Ratafias or Glace-Cherries, or crystalised fruit. Marjorie says:" The Blanc-Mange MUST BE BIRD'S; there is nothing else so rich and creamy. There are 2 packets in the 4d, box, and 4in the 71d." 13Ntiou

div.head: CRICKET NOTES.
div.p: CRICKET NOTES.

It is surprising—and aggravating to the enthusiastic cricketer—bow the undesirable weather gravitates to the week-end. This was once more the case 011 Saturday wht n, after a spell of delightful conditions; rain came just in time to interfere with cricket Warrington should have met Prescot away, but the ou.t. look was so hopeless that the match was abandoned, The secJnd eleven entertained the Prescot secoea contingent, but rain stopped play when the visitors innings was young. The Warrington me?' however, were favoured in being able to take their full turn at the wicket, and so lustily did they Pile O- the runs that the closure was applied IN hen the score bad reached 181 for nine wickets. J. Thompson digi tinguished himself with a fine display which realiee 48 ; H. Havvtle)rn was also in first-class form for h!ti 31, and W. Howard carried out his bat with 25 to lite credit. The first PrescA pair to bat had kept their wickets intact with a score of 60 when play W. Seplitoa having knocked up 27 and A. Sirumcease 29. d,

-- In the Wariington and D.stiict League tournPY the) Warrington Conservatives ad an easy task in d loos" jug cf Orford. Dismissing the villagers for 36, th.erz responded with 92 for the has of 8 wickets, it Hunter heading the E cores with a splendid 39. and Green shared the bowling honours.

Cairo-street Unitarians made a poor show agal.niBnt Rylands' Recreation, who secured a majority of The visitors could mike no headway against bowling of Waywell and Carter, and not one of the!! players reached double figure. There were £00:10 interesting friendly encounters Whitecross and Latchford Baptists had a keen strugg_,l6d the wire men having to admit defeat by the nu run. The scoring rn both sides was very I°`c:i Egerton captured five wickets for 14 runs, an" Maybury five for 5 runs.

Bold-street Wesleyans met Walton Junior!, t/t5 Walton and gained a creditable victory. The violt°' opened in poor fashion, losing their first three wickets without scoring a run. However, R. Weevre! and W. Stringer put a different complexion on maY.°';'. ihe pair scoring 55 runs in 40 minutes, before Stringe, was caught for a brilliant 21. This was an excellen` stand and quite pleased the Bold-street supportero: The innings closed for 73, R. Weaver contributing.3l)i The Walton batsmen failed to make headway agalt ;he deadly bowling of R. Weaver and Stringer, °Pt? mustering 18 runs, including a brilliant ii by ' • Barlow. The last seven wickets fell for DO run Even " extras " failed to score. R. Weaver Stringer bowled well for the victors, the former ,1" 1.3 overs capturing four wickets for no runs and tile latter four wickets f )r five runs.

Padgate Wesleyans trod conclusions with Fairfiela and won by 10 runs. W. Hodgkinivm clntributed Is c tpital innings of 19 for the losers. There were scl notable I»wling achievements, Mellor taking 81. wickets for 7 runs, Jackson eight wickets for 14 rtiu" and Monks two wickets for 18 runs. Winwick gained a smart victory over Eccleston b 51 runs, the figures being 116 against 65. Winwie owe their success chiefly to Walker, for his fine battiel performance. He went in third wicket dowel cariied his bat out for a wer.pla)ed co. The wicket put on 53 runs, Hilton scoring 25. PelvBfit kn-cked up 16. div.head: NOTES AND COMMENTS.
div.p: NOTES AND COMMENTS.

Keen disappointment was felt in Warrington last 6aturday when it was reported that the only local team to lose in the County Championship was Bull's Head, who were beaten by the Roebuck men at Newton-le-Willows by five points. Both Rylands and Cemetery advanced further in the competition. The Recreation second team won by 64 points over Angel Hotel at the Ship Hotel, Irlam, and the Junior Con- servatives beat Ited Lion, Prestwich, at Chorlton, by 34 points.

The final game in the first round of the "Finlayson" Cup Competition in connection with the Warrington Works Association was played on the Horse and Jockey Green. and the first five matches in the second round were also decided.

One was rather disappointed on looking through the results in the "Peter Peacock" Challenge Cup Competi- tion to notice so many walk-overs. The absence of many of the players was attributed to the fact that owing to the postponement of the games from May 10th a misunderstanding kept some of the players from turning up at the proper time. This also seems to have affected several of the teams.

Play was marred by herq showers at Newton-le- Willows where the Warrington Bull's Head repre- sentatives succumbed to the Roebuck contingent, but they were in no way disgraced, for their defeat was only one of four points.

The Roebuck men showed determination from the first game, when J. McNield lost to A. Regan (Bull' Head) by the odd point in 31 ends. Regan started exceedingly well with the jack, leading 17-7 at the 186 end. At the 24th end he had an adv:Antage of 20-10, but before he could secure the winning point Mcneld had peeled at the 30th end, only to lose on the next length.

F. Casey bowled exceedingly well in his game with A. C. Mace, winning 21-19 in 31 ends. The players kept evenly together up to the 20th end when the game was 13-13. Casey had then a beautiful run of six and led 20-14 at the 27th end. Mace got a single and two doubles, but Casey brought the issue to a conclusion on the next length, winning by a couple.

The last four players for the Bull's Head t earn tried hard to gain sufficient points to win the match, but although they beat their men, the majorities were not large enough to wipe cff the lead of the Roebuck contingent.
We were justified last week in predicting that the match would be keenly fought, and also when we prophesied wins for the other two local teams.

Rylands' Rees had matters practically all their own way at Peel Green, where they defeated C.W.S., Irlam, by 23 points. W. Roughiey, the Recs. captain, beat the opposing skipper, D. Ogden, by 21-S in 23 ends. • --

J. Woods (Rylands) put up a good fight against G. Shaw, and one felt very sorry that he had eventually to knuckle under by three points. At the ninth end Shaw had 11-2, but so well did the wireworker run his woods that at the 29t1i end he was only 18-19 in arrears. This, however, proved to be his final score, and Shaw ran to game with a couple of singles.

11. Langley and A. Sandwith were a well-matched couple, and the xvireworker had all his work cut out t) gain his two point victory. The game was a keen one from the first end, and at the 26th end Sandwith led 19-18. Langley then got the jack and landed a double and a single in capital fashion to win.

There wag a good attendance at the Roebuck, Fliston, on Saturday, when the Cemetery team beat Newton-le-Willows by 35 points. The latter team only won on four individual games, and in the majority of cases the e.3emetery men gained praiseworthy victories.

One would naturally have thought that W. Butter- worth (Cemetery) would have succeeded in his game with A. Harrison, seeing that he led 17-14 at the 26t end, but no such result accrued, the Newton man securing the jack and winning the game with a beauti- ful run of eight.
This was one of the best games in the match, although each of the other contests were of a very interesting nature.

Rylands' Recs. second team were by far tbs better team against Angel Hotel, at Irlatn, and they thoroughly deserved their 64 point, victory. The first six wire- workers to take the green won magnificent victories and the Angel Hotel players had hardly a look-in.
The Works competition is proving decidedly popular, and the games ca Saturday were full of interesting incidents.
Robinson's gained a magnificent victory over Robertson's, winning by 43 points, only three of their men lost individual games.
The County Asylum men are going strong, and if they continue on present form we have every hope of their success. They were up against the Warrington Tanning Company on Saturday and won by 36 points.

The other teams are all playing well and keen interest is being taken in the matches. The games for next week are : Whitecross Wiredrawers v. Richmond's, Academy - street. Locker's v. Crosfleld's No 1. Rylands' No 1 v. Mersey White Lead. St. Heleps Cable No 1 v. Fennel-street Tannery. Castle Rubber v. Crosfield's No 3. Referee, Mr. T. Humphreys.

div.head: CYCLIST'S NOTE BOOK.
div.p: THE CYCLIST'S NOTE BOOK.
Motor Cars Have Brought Improved Roads and Taught Carefulness.
ATTRACTIVE RESTING PLACES.
[BY "SILVER-STREET."

It is often given as a saddening piece of intelligence in the cycling papers that the club life of the earlier days is dead. Various reasons are given to account for this—foremost and always, the motors and the increasing dangers of the open road are held to be the offenders.

But anyone who sees the Wesleyan Cycling Club turn out on a Saturday afternoon from the meeting place at Victoria Square, Stockton Heath, anywhere between 20 and 30 strong will be inclined to think whether there is any need for such decay. On Satur- day last the run to Davenham was just such a success. Through Hatton to Acton Bridge, where the that halt was made for a breath and a smoke, through Weaver- ham village and Hartford was the route, and tea was at once taken at Mrs. Booths', next door to the Church Schools.

Then cycles were resumed and a quick run made down to Hartford Bridge and along the towing path of the Weaver River. (No motors there, anyway). The rain which had threatened so long caused a halt under the viaduct ; only for ten minutes, however. The lock-keeper kindly promised to look after the machines while the party first had photographs taken, and then went through Vale Royal Park for a delightful evening stroll.
The return through Leftwich to Northwich, through Baruton and Little Leigh to Whitley and home was a charming ride, and will long be remembered.
MOTORS AND DUST.

Whatever we cyclits may blame motors for, we ought to drop the word dust." Those of us who remember the solids and the cushion tyres of the eighties know what dust is. The main roads were "a la this way.". Repaired with limestone, ragstone,

sandstone, according to the nearest quarry, they were quickly ground up into a grey powder which always stood a half to three-quarters of an inch deep in summer and mud in winter. (By the way, what has become of those old road scrapers, made in many sections, and dragged backwards by the old roadmen ?) Those were ea', s when the cyclist was a hardy wight. He set out spick and span with mighty coloured tops to his stockings, a wonderful sweater, and a gorgeous tie, and after an afternoon's run came back absolutely unrecognisable for dust. Now-a-days the motor raises a cloud, nine times out of ten it is blown over the fields, and we are in it a half minute ; but there is no dust left for us to raise. You can prove this by trying a run along the Moore-Runcorn road after a spell of dry weather. Few motors bother you, but the dust! Besides, think of what the motors have taught dogs and especially their owners ; to children, and espec- ially their guardians ; to policemen, who used to be our bêtes noires. If we keep off the footpath and keep to lightingeup time the road is our own Fancy the days when an officer used to hide in a convenient spot in the hedge and pounce on a score of cyclists in an afternoon, and on the Monday, the beak, oh! didn't the beak enjoy it? A glorious chance of paying off old scores. for didn't the adjectived cyclist come racing and ringing past his dear little tit, as he and his wife in the trap bowled along behind her over the road that had for a score of years been unsullied by the presence of any user, except the farm slaves? No. the motor has a lot to answer for, but I cannot for a moment admit that cycling has suffered from it. Where middle-aged people have dropped the pastime, and say, " Oh! the motors have destroyed all the pleasure of cycling," I just shut one eye and look for the real cause with the other. It's not very bard to find one somewhere about the dinner-table. CHESHIRE REST HOUSES.

I have been surpised to find how many Warrington cyclists have never seen Arley. In these articlettes to coin a new word suggested by a term pretty well bandied about now-a-days,— I don't propose to des- cribe the route to these places where refreshment may be obtained. If you want to know the way you must ask a policeman, or consult your map. Mrs. Mather lives at a delightful little cottage at the Ashes, Arley. Everything is as clean as a Warrington pin, and for a shilling anything reasonable in the shape of a country tea may be obtained. The cottage is just in the centre of a district beloved of the photographer, and his subjects include Arley Lake, the old mill, the mill house, Arley Green and School, Crowley Lodge, Garland Hall, Stockley Hall Farm, and especially the group of farm cottages called" The Ashes "; and for the curio-bunter there are the rhyming sign-posts which are unique, composed and erected by a former lord of the manor. The hall and grounds are open to the public once a year, and can be inspected and pictured by permission almost at any time. Long live the laird of Arley ! As it is impossible for any individual to know all the rest houses. I should be glad to hear of others from my correspondents. I will add that these notices are and will be entirely disinterested except' for the readers of this journal, as I shall not even inform the subjects of them that such notices have appeared.

div.head: YOUTHFUL MARRIAGES IN GERMANY.
div.p: YOUTHFUL MARRIAGES IN GERMANY.

A recent publication of the Imperial Bureau of Statistics in Germany gives some interesting particu- lars concerning the age oi parties who contracted marriage during the yeek. 1910. The youngest bride- groom was only fifteen years old; but of youths a year older sixteen were married and one was already a widower. Marriages at seventeen years of age were much more numerous; for there were sixty-three youths married at this age, of whom one was a widower. At the ago of eighteen marriage is by no means an excep- tional condition. for 511 young men of eighteen were married, six were widowers, and one was even divorced

div.head: Penketh Right-of-Way Question.
div.p: Penketh Right-of-Way Question.

The monthly meeting of the Warrington Rural:l District Council was held on Wednesday afternoon in Bewsey Chambers. Mr. G. Mather presided, and there were also present : The Rev. A. M. Mitchell, Messrs. W. Furness, J. Backhouse, J. W. Knowles, P. C. Garnett, P. Longton, Robinson, J. C. Sutton (clerk), B. S. Newcombe (surveyor), H. H. Burnage (assistant surveyor), F. Kerfoot (inspector) and Dr. Sepbton (medical officer). PENKETH RIGHT- OF-WAY QUESTION.

The CLERK stated that the sub-committee appointed to consider the closing of the alleged right-of-way at Fiddler's Ferry had met on the.site. The subject involved points of law and utility. Mr. BACKHOUSE said the general opinicn of the sub- committee was that there was an undoubted right. They had an interview with a man 84 years of age who said he could remember the path for 80 years. Unless an Act of Parliament had been passed at some time with reference to it, he did not see that they had a right to cut off the privilege of the public using the footpath. Mr. FURNESS supported Mr. Backhouse, and said he remembered using the road several times 30 years ago. It was decided to write to Mr. Bates, agent to Captain Hughes, telling him that after careful considera- sion the Council were satisfied the road should not be closed.

div.head: SANKEY ROAD IMPROVEMENTS.
div.p: SANKEY ROAD IMPROVEMENTS.

A letter was read from the Clerk to the County Council regretting that he had been so very long in completing all the matters relating to the purchase of land for the improvements. He had not yet completed the agreement with the Railway Company relating to the canal bridge and that had been the cause of the delay. The Railway Company had been insisting on clauses as to penalties in the event of the oanel being interfered with during construction. He thought, however, that he would be able to agree and complete in the course of two or three weeks. Owing to the Ring's visit it had also been found impossible to commence the new canal bridge.
INCREASE OF SALARY. The salary of Mr. H. H. Bnrnage was increased by £2O per annum as from April Ist.

FRIEND OF GLADSTONE,
Death of Lord Rendel, "Member for
Wales."
Lord Rendel died in London, on Wednesday at the age of 79. The barony, which was created in 1894, becomes extinct, there being no heir.

During the 14 years in which he represented Montgomeryshire in the House of Commons, Lord Rendel worked with great zeal on behalf of Liberalism in Wales, and became popularly known as " the Member for \Vales." He was leader of the Welsh Liberal Party and the constant friend and companion of Mr. Gladstone. It was at Lord Rendel's house in Carlton Gardens that a famous meeting was held between Mr. Gladstone and a deputation of Irish members after the Parnell expcsure, and there practically began the split in the Nationalist Party.

div.p: Halton won by 15.
ANGLING NOTES.
Warrington Workingmen's Angling Association (N.A. Centre).

The workingmen anglers of Warrington have had quite enough of close season angling and they are patiently awaiting the 16th. It is a pity that the open- ing day falls on a Monday, as it will delay many taking coarse fish for nearly a week, but no great harm can he done by this. We heard it suggested that societies ought to take the Sunday in this season, as anglers locally have behaved in the best possible way in adhering to the Mundella Aot. But as we are guarded by rules, I see no reason why Warrington should be the first to break them. We know that close season angling does not provide the same sport as we all would like, and we are tired of travelling to the Gowy for a few eels, but taking everything into consideration our sport will be all th 3 better for the long rest.

div.head: GOWY.
div.p: THE GOWY.

The Gowy was visited by a fair number of local rods without anything out of the ordinary being done. A member had four runs out of a good pike before they parted company. There is little doubt that it would have beaten all records, because his tackle was capable of taking one up to 151b5., and it was the hardest of luck that he lost him. One or two trout were taken, but nothing to upset those already weighed in, and the best bag of eels we heard of was 16, the largest being about Soz.

div.head: BAY HORSE.
div.p: THE BAY HORSE.

This society has now got the shield which will offered for competition this season, and by Saturdt next it will be on view at the club-room. It wi, probably be presented to the society on the night the open their new room. A report will shortly be given of the winners of the close season specials.

The Cooper's Arms Club now has a membership of over thirty and some nice specials are to be won for home waters. The novice should stand a capital chance here of securing one or two. HEADQUARTERS.

A general meeting is to be held here on Thursday evening next, at 7.45 p.m. Mr. G. Hamblett has kindly consented to give a lecture on "How to tell different species of fish." As that is the first lecture of the kind held at beadqutirters it should prove very profit- able both to old and new members. The specials for this year have also to be allowed to different waters, and there is other interesting business to be transacted.

WARRINGTJN CO-OPERATIVE SOCIETY. Committee Appointed to Inquire into Conditions of Employment. TRADE UNION MATTERS EXCEPTED The 210th quarterly meeting of the Warrington E. I. Co-operative ociety, Limited, was held in the Co operative Hall, Cairo-street, en Monday evening The l'resident took the chair at 8 o'clock, all the committee excei t Mr. Bibby being present, and also from 300 to 400 members. The rep n-t of the com- mittee showed that the sales for the three months er.ded April 22nd, were £83,107, an increase of £13,161 over the corresronding period, and that the membership stood at 12,848, a net increase of 310 on the quarter; all departments of the society's business having contributed to the increase. The report also included the appreciation of the services rendered by Mr Ha;gh and Mr. England during past years to the com- mittee, these gentlemen having now to retire accord- ing to rule. The report was taken as read and adcpted, including the payment of an interim dividend at the me cf 3e. 2.1. in the £ on all purchases. An application had been received for an increase in the shares held in the North-Western Convalescent Hem( a Association, the holding of the society being at the present time £l7O, and because of the require- ment of new capital for extension the members were asked to sanction a further investment of £ll4 This was sanctioned. —An application had also been received for an ir creased subscription to the iccal branch of the St. John Ambulance Association, and by a large mojority the members decided to increase the subscription from £1 is. to £3 3. A notice of motion had been received frcm Mr. W Lowe to the effect that a tp.3cial committee should be formed from the members who have never served on the general committee to inquire into all the conditions of employment of the society except such as are purely trade union matters, and whatever the findings of this committee that they be reported to the general c-mornittee and afterwards to the quarterly meeting three months hence. The Secretary pointed out that this committee could not be formed under the xisting rules, becaus) the ruler provided that the President and Secretary must form part of any com- mi tee, and thatjurtheramder one of the eociety's rub s it was provided that any complaints or suggestions to be m ,de by the members must come first in writing to the committee and that no com- plaints should be brought More a quarterly meeting except on appeal. As no details of the rumours which were said to be in circulation had reached the com- mittee and therefore they had had no opportur ity of inquiring into or dealing with them, the formation of a special committee to undertake this work was a con- travention of the duties of the committee of manage- ment. In spite of this, however, on being Tut to the vote 142 voted for the resolution and 129 against. On the question being raised as to what the position now wLs, it was pointed out that the only course that could be adopted was an alteration of rules by a two-thirda majority at a special meeting called for that purpose before the committee could go on with the work suggested.—The election for three members of the committee resulted in the return of Mr. Ferguson, and for the two vacant seats Mr. H. Wardman and Mr. J. Upscn, were elected. RUNCORN RURAL DISTRICT COUNCIL. Roadmen and their Wages. The fortnightly meeting of the Runcorn Rural District Council was held at Dutton on Tuesday, Mr. C. E. Linaker presiding. TENDERS FOR MACADAM. A committee consisting of Messrs. Woodward,Pilling, and Wright was appointed to consider the tenders for the supply of macadam for the half year. On the committee's recommendation the following tenders were accepted : Macadam, Ponmeaumawr Welsh Granite Co. and Pwllheli Erama Co. ; lime stone chippings, Representatives of the late Jonathan Horsefi,ld, Runcorn ; curbstones and cube sets, Walton Bros., Rawtenstall. The question of earthenware pipes was left open. ROADMEN'S WAGES. REQUEST FOR INCREASED PAY. The Highway Surveyor reported that he had received a letter from four of the roadmen stating that they respectfully asked for an increase in wages, owing to the high price of goods and the increased cost of living. Mr. Linaker (jun.) moved that the matter b 3 referred to the Highways Executive Committee. The Council would endorse the Committee's resolution in the matter. Mr. Lister-Kaye : What do the men get per week ? The Clerk : They vary from 3s. to 3s. 4d. per day. Mr. Lister-Kaye: They ought to get at least £1 per week. The cost of living has gone up 3s. or 3s. 6d. per week during the last eight years. Mr. Antwis : There is also a difference in the quality of the men to the extent of about reir. per week. The question was referred to the Highways Executive Committee. MEDICAL OFFICER'S REPOR Dr. Adams reported ono case of diptheria from Frodsham ; one case of pulmonary tuberculosis from each of the parishes of Frodsham, Kingsley and Stock- ton Heath. The Church of England schools at Budworth was closed on account of measles. The report was adopted. WONDERS OF INSURANCE. Draft of Charter for National Physical Fitness. It would be beyond the power of any man to evolve a perfect system of national insurance in a twelve- month, nor can a statesman be fairly held responsible for errors or meannesses in administration. Wonders have been done in a short time, and though the Act is marred by undue complication and expense, and by its unequal pressure on the slenderest incomes, it contains the draft of a charts r of physical efficiency for the nation. But it is still a draft; and things have been written into it which must clearly be erased if, as a set-off to the material benefits it confers, the people of this country are not to lose the practice of self-goverment which was the basis of the old system of voluntary insur- ance. This was far from Mr. Lloyd George's original design. It can be no purpose of democratic statesman- ship to strengthen or to affirm the hold which the great industrial societies, with their characteristic of high profits and strict official and centralised management, have already acquired.—" The Nation. " NO SUBSTANTIAL ALTERATIONS. The theory that the Altrincham poll was due to the Insurance Act may possiby be accurate, but there can be no greater mistake than to suppose—as seems to be widely done—that the Act is capable of substantial amendment. The new Bill will regularise the addi- tional plunder claimed by the doctors, but it cannot make the electors polite nor thorough in their duties, nor will it terminate passive resistance among the farmers. Still less will it heal the wounded dignity of clerks. Insurance must be either compulsory or voluntary, and if compulsion is retained, as it will be, the rest is tinkering. It might be a good thing to reunite the four commissions in one, but this would not touch the real problem, which is that the Act, however excellently it may be we-king among the industrial classes in urban areas, is being crabbed by farmers doctors, and snobs.—" Truth."

It was further unanimously recommended that Mr. Constable be appointed Infant Life Protection Officer for the No. 1 Relief District at a salary of £2 10s. per annum. The Clerk was instructed to inform Mr. Constable that the would be required to take up duty in three months. Mr. JOLLEY, in moving the adoption of the minutes, said that with regard to the question of registration, the Finance Committee had the somewhat difficult task of reconciling the conflicting interests of two adjacent parishes, but their recommendation was, he believed, as near as possible an equitable solution. On the question of the appointment or relieving officer, the committee were unanimous, and that, considering the many views represented on such a body, was proof that their sugges- tions were eminently reasonable. The Rev. A. M. MITCHELL asked whether the Finance Committee ought not to give the Board the rcasons which led them to arrive at the conclusion that the appointment of a relieving officer was necessary. Had they gone into the matter minutely and made com- parisons between the amounts of relief given now and a few years ago? it seemed to him that there was no grave necessity for the appointment of such an officer and it might well be held over for three months or a little longer. The amount of work coming before the relief committees was very much less than it used to be and it was still on the decrease. If an appointment was to be made, he was quite agreeable that Mr. Constable should receive it,ana he hoped his wife would speedily be restored to health. (Hear, hear.) Finally, Mr. Mitchell inquired whether the application of the lady who sought the post was considered. The CLERIC: When she applied for a form of applica- tion, I wrote and told her-- Mr. Mrremer, : Then the application did not come forward. We understood at the last meeting of the Board that one lady had made application. The CLERK : You asked me if any applications had been made by ladies and I said Yes." The Rev. A. M. MITCHELL It ought to be made quite clear that ladies are eligible for such appoint- ments. Continuing, he said the Finance Committee seemed to dominate the Board. PUBLIC AMUSEMENTS. ROYAL COURT THEATRE. "A Blind Girl's Love." A more beautiful and effective setting to a melo- drama we could not imagine than the Alps, the land of sunshine, snow and health-giving pine forests. Another pleasing feature about this atractive pro- duction at the Royal Court Theatre this week, is the number of vocal specialities introduced. Miss Cherry Vekeyoe gives a sympathetic portrayal of the blind girl, and wins the favour of the audience by her charming manner. Mr. T. Arthur Ellis acts powerfully as Gerald Carfax, the young doctor. Mr. T. Poison Turner impersonates,Juan Fernandez in an eff- ective manner, making the part as repulsive as poss- ible. He is assisted in his villainies by Cora Clemarte a character in the able hands of Miss Adeline Raby. Mr. Elton Morgan is a popular host Bartelot and Miss Flo Norman is quite at home as his wife who is threatened by the anarchist. Vocal specialities are provided by Mr. Erne Turner and Mr. Artie Francis as Peter and Paul and by Miss Hettie Senior as the vivacious Coquette, the maid at the inn. NEXT WEEK. Next week Mr. Frank Lindo and Miss Marion Wakeford will present the drama" His child Wife." PALACE AND HIPPODROME. Kano productions are invariably capital attractions and this week at the Hippodrome large audiences have laughed right heartily over " The Mumming Birds," one of Fred Karno's best. There is a theatre on the , stage and as the several artistes appear "The saucy boy "and " The drunk" cause roars of laughter by the way in which they show their approval or dis- approval of the fare provided. "Sad Sadie," the saucy soutrette, is popular with both,but "The Bread- way Boys," dancers and " singers," are at once given "the bird." As a finale the audience is con- vulsed by the highly ludicrous wrestling matchc.i between Marconi Ali, the terrible Turk, and the occupants of boxes. We cannot do any more than confirm Karno's own description of the production as a "madly merry burlesque." Edgar , Cooke plays the part of "The drunk "in a highly successful manner, and Jimmy Russell as "The saucy boy " is also a clever comedian who knows just how to tickle the audience. The other members of the company are all successful in keeping up the screams. Tom Gott is a clever Yorkshire dialect mirth merchant, being at his best as " The Dame," who in song and story is very severe on mere man. As an encore ony Monday he gave man's views of women, being equ all vindictive and as piquant in his criticism as in the first number. Gott has a pleasing style, and relates a Dumber of side-splitting gags in an irresistible ma.nner! Albert Le ire recounts his adventures in an aeroplane in a humorous song, and is always full of fun and frolic. His " advertisements" number is one of the cleverest laughter-provoking concoctions we have ever heard. A little eccentric dancing con- chides a very smart turn. Marjory Dawson, the i crinoline girl, scores n rather a novel manner, for she captivates the audience by her rendering of such old songs as" What can the matter be," "Old folks at home," "Little brown jug" and "The Spanish Cavalier." The audience join lustily in the chorus and make the scena go with a swing. Sad( s is a smart novelty juggler, whose diminutive comedian assistant gives a burlesque touch to the "turn." Sados is well received, for he performs his tricks with exceeding smartness and celerity. Little Bella and Jules Terry are a couple of juvenile entertainers who amuse the audi- ence with their " green.apple " number and fascinate with their ragtime ghost song. There is an air of refinement about the turn which appeals to all, the specialities at the piano being exceedingly well given. Al Lawson and Francis Nanaon, comedy cyclists and ball punchers, did not appear on Monday and two singers and dancers deputised. NEXT WEEK'S PROGRAMME. The Lorch Family of acrobats head the bill for next week and are described as the unrivalled Risley acrobats. Other turns will be David Poole, original ventriloquist; Anna Schuberth in "The Deputy " ; Miss Sylvia Cavalho and Co., including Clifford Pem- broke in comedy sketch " The husband of Peggy"; Ted Mercell, skater and dancer; John Child, operatic tenor ; Inez and Pim featuring the finest lady gymnast Extant; the Dainty Danes, simultaneous dancers. There will also be pictures on the bioscope. THEATRE ROYAL. "A Man in a Thousand." The Repertory Company have added to their list of successes this week in presenting so admirably the popular drama "A Man in a Thousand." Each member of the company has acquitted himself or herself in a very creditable manner.—The theatre has undergone complete re-decoration, the work having been carried out on the most artistic lines. NEXT WEEK. The great romantic military drama "Man and Wife " will be presented next week. The play is by that popular author Walter Howard, and it will be given by arrangement with Edward Van Biene. • FRIENDLY SOCIETY NEWS. NATIONAL INDEPENDENT ORDER OF ODDFELLOWS. ..V&rrington District.
